outcomes: You can write, closed-book in under 45 minutes, a 200-line bash CLI with set -Eeuo pipefail, EXIT/ERR/INT/TERM traps, getopts with usage(), leveled logging to stderr and a log file, and it passes `shellcheck -S style -o all` with zero disables.

You can read an unfamiliar script and mark every line where set -e will not fire (conditions, &&/||, non-final pipeline stages, $(...) in assignments, functions called from tests) and rewrite each with an explicit `|| die`.

You can take a script that uses `for f in $(ls)` and unquoted variables and make it pass a fixture directory containing filenames with spaces, newlines, globs and a leading dash, verified by a BATS test.

1.topic: Linux internals: processes, systemd, permissions, filesystems, packaging
outcomes: You can narrate, without notes, the boot-to-traffic chain on your VPS from GRUB through initramfs, systemd targets and unit activation to the socket accept, and back each step with a command that shows it (`/proc/cmdline`, `systemd-analyze critical-chain`, `ss -ltnp`).

You can write a systemd unit for a Python HTTP service that scores under 3.0 on `systemd-analyze security`, runs as a non-root account, binds :443 via AmbientCapabilities, survives SIGTERM with a graceful drain, and restarts on failure without tripping the start-rate limiter.

Given only a PID on a host you have never seen, you can determine within five minutes whether it is CPU-bound, blocked on I/O in D state, waiting on a futex/socket, a zombie, or stopped, using /proc/PID/{status,wchan,stack,fd,task} and strace, and say which of those kill -9 will not fix.

2.topic: Networking: TCP/IP, DNS, TLS, HTTP/2, load balancers, firewalls
outcomes: You can narrate, unprompted and without notes, every step from a URL to the first byte (stub resolver, recursive and authoritative DNS, TCP three-way handshake, TLS 1.3 one-RTT handshake with SNI and ALPN, HTTP/2 stream, load balancer to backend) and name the tool whose output proves each step happened.

You can take a failing HTTPS call and, in under ten minutes, classify it as DNS, TCP connect, TLS, HTTP or application using dig, nc -vz, openssl s_client and curl -v, quoting the specific output line that proves the classification.
You can read ss -ti output for a slow connection and state whether it is limited by loss (retrans), the receiver (rwnd), congestion control (cwnd) or the application (lastsnd high, unacked 0).

3.topic: Performance and troubleshooting on a single box
outcomes: You can run the 60-second checklist (uptime, dmesg -T | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1, top) from memory on a box you have never seen and name the saturated resource in under two minutes.

Given load average 40 on a 4-core box with 5% CPU, you can list the D-state processes with their wchan and say whether the wait is disk, NFS or a lock, and show the /proc/PID/stack line that proves it.

You can read one line of iostat -xz 1 and state whether the device is saturated using await and aqu-sz against a stated baseline, and explain in one sentence why %util alone is not evidence on SSD or RAID.

4.topic: Git at depth: rebase, bisect, reflog, hooks, monorepo hygiene
outcomes: You can recover a branch deleted by `git branch -D` or a commit lost to `git reset --hard` within two minutes using reflog, and within five using `git fsck --lost-found` on a clone with no reflog.
You can take a 4000-commit repo with a known-good tag and a failing test and produce the exact culprit commit via `git bisect run` with a hermetic script, handling untestable commits with exit 125.

You can turn a 15-commit branch with WIP messages into a 4-commit series where every commit builds and passes tests, proven by `rebase -i` with `exec`, and show the reviewer a `range-diff` of what changed since their last review.

5.topic: Docker internals: namespaces, cgroups, layers, networking
outcomes: You can explain to a non-engineer what a container is in under two minutes using only 'a process', 'namespaces', 'cgroups' and 'a tar of files', then prove it by showing the container's process in host ps with a different PID than it sees inside.
You can build a working isolated shell with unshare, pivot_root, a cgroup v2 memory limit and a veth pair to a bridge, with no Docker binary on the machine, in under 15 minutes from memory.

You can draw an image's layer stack from docker history and docker inspect, predict which steps print CACHED before rebuilding, and reorder a Dockerfile so a source-only change rebuilds in under 10 seconds.

6.topic: Production images and supply chain: multi-stage, non-root, SBOM, scanning, signing
outcomes: You can take Dokeo from a naive single-stage `python:3.12` image to a multi-stage image under 200 MB with a dive efficiency score above 0.95, and show the `docker history` line-by-line explanation of where the other 900 MB went.

You can run both Dokeo and DefenderMate under `docker run --read-only --user 10001 --cap-drop ALL --tmpfs /tmp` and under a Kubernetes Pod Security 'restricted' namespace with `runAsNonRoot: true` and `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` without CreateContainerConfigError or a PermissionError at startup.

You can produce a `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1` result of zero findings on both images, with every accepted CVE in `.trivyignore` carrying a written justification and an expiry date, and a CI job that goes red when a new HIGH appears.

7.topic: Kubernetes core: Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, namespaces
outcomes: You can draw from memory, in under five minutes on a whiteboard, the graph Ingress -> Service -> EndpointSlice -> Pod <- ReplicaSet <- Deployment with ConfigMap and Secret edges, and annotate each edge with the component that reads it (ingress controller, EndpointSlice controller, kube-proxy, kubelet, CoreDNS, Deployment controller).

You can take curl -v https://dokeo.example.com returning 404, 502 or 503, name the layer and the three most likely causes within two minutes, then confirm the root cause with kubectl get ingress, get endpointslices and describe pod in under ten.

You can roll out a new digest-pinned image of Dokeo under a continuous curl or hey load with zero failed requests, explain the pod-template-hash of every ReplicaSet in kubectl get rs, state what maxSurge, maxUnavailable, minReadySeconds and the preStop sleep each contributed, then roll back with kubectl rollout undo and prove the old digest is running.

8.topic: Kubernetes production ops: probes, HPA, requests and limits, storage, RBAC, NetworkPolicy, debugging
outcomes: You can take a pod in CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending or CreateContainerConfigError in an unfamiliar namespace and state the root cause with evidence within ten minutes using only get, describe, events, logs --previous and kubectl debug, then apply a one-line fix.

You can read `kubectl describe hpa`, explain each Condition, compute the desired replica count by hand from current utilisation and target, and set stabilizationWindowSeconds and scale policies so a bursty API does not flap.

You can set requests and limits for a Python API and a Postgres StatefulSet with a one-sentence rationale per number, name the resulting QoS class, and prove OOM or CFS throttling from cgroup counters rather than guessing.

You can author, from an empty directory in under 60 minutes, a Helm chart for Dokeo with Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, HPA, ServiceAccount, checksum-triggered restarts, values.schema.json and NOTES.txt, and it passes `helm lint --strict`, kubeconform and helm-unittest with zero warnings.

You can install Argo CD on a kind cluster, register the repo, apply an Application with automated sync, prune and selfHeal, and show a values change pushed to main reaching Healthy in the cluster within three minutes with no kubectl apply.

You can break a deploy (bad image tag or probe path), watch it go Degraded, `git revert` and demonstrate recovery to Healthy, then repeat the recovery with `argocd app rollback` after disabling automated sync, and state exactly what Git and the cluster contain after each path.

10.topic: Kubernetes security: Pod Security, RBAC, secrets, image policy, runtime
outcomes: You can take an arbitrary Deployment manifest and, without a cluster, list every field that violates the `restricted` Pod Security Standard and rewrite it so it admits — including the emptyDir mounts needed to make `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` work.

You can roll Pod Security Admission onto a live namespace using warn/audit first, collect the violations from API server warnings and ReplicaSet events, and cut over to `enforce` with a version-pinned label and a documented exemption list.

You can audit an unfamiliar cluster's RBAC in under 30 minutes and produce a table of every subject with cluster-admin, every wildcard rule, every SA with `get/list secrets` or `create pods` outside its own namespace, and every binding to `system:unauthenticated`, using `kubectl auth can-i --list --as` and kubectl-who-can.

11.topic: Serving models on Kubernetes and GPUs
outcomes: You can take a fresh Ubuntu GPU VM with nothing but the driver installed and, in under 20 minutes, have containerd running GPU containers via nvidia-ctk and a single-node cluster reporting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in Allocatable.

You can write a vLLM Deployment, Service and Ingress from memory with correct GPU limit, memory request, /dev/shm emptyDir, startup/readiness/liveness probes and Recreate strategy, and explain each field to a customer's platform engineer without looking anything up.

You can compute, from a model's config.json and a GPU's memory, the KV cache budget and maximum concurrent 2k-token conversations within 15% of what vLLM prints at startup, and show your working on a whiteboard in under five minutes.

12.topic: Restricted-network delivery: offline install bundle, registry mirroring, private CA trust
outcomes: You can install the full platform on a fresh VM with all egress dropped, from one tarball, and produce packet-capture and nftables counter evidence that zero outbound connections were attempted during the run.
You can relocate every image a chart pulls into an OCI layout and then into a private registry by digest, and prove with skopeo inspect and crane digest that no digest changed in transit.

You can configure containerd certs.d/hosts.toml and k3s registries.yaml for mirroring, path rewriting and a private CA, and demonstrate the kubelet pulling successfully via crictl on a node with no internet.

13.topic: Terraform: state, modules, workspaces, drift, CI
outcomes: You can bootstrap an S3 remote backend with versioning, SSE-KMS and locking (use_lockfile or DynamoDB), migrate an existing local state into it with `init -migrate-state`, and name every IAM permission the CI role needs and why.

You can read any plan and, before approving, list which resources will be replaced and which attribute forces it, then rewrite the change so the plan is non-destructive using moved blocks, state mv, ignore_changes, or create_before_destroy as appropriate.

You can adopt an existing click-ops VPC, its subnets and security groups into a module using import blocks and -generate-config-out, and end with `terraform plan` reporting 'No changes' without -target or hidden ignore_changes.

14.topic: AWS networking and compute: VPC, subnets, SG, NACL, ALB across AZs, EC2, Lambda
outcomes: You can draw a two-AZ VPC (public, private and isolated tiers, per-AZ NAT, IGW, endpoints) from memory and, for every arrow and every SG or NACL rule, state which resource it protects, which direction is stateful, and what breaks if it is removed.

You can stand up an internet-facing ALB in front of an ASG of two EC2 instances in two AZs with Terraform, TLS via ACM, an 80 to 443 redirect and a real readiness health check, and reach a zero-diff `terraform plan` in under an hour from an empty account.

You can take a 'the app is unreachable' report and, within fifteen minutes using only describe-route-tables, describe-security-group-rules, flow logs and Reachability Analyzer, name whether the block is routing, SG, NACL, health check or DNS, with the log line that proves it.

15.topic: AWS data: RDS Postgres, S3, ElastiCache, DynamoDB
outcomes: You can perform a point-in-time restore of a Multi-AZ RDS Postgres instance from the CLI, repoint the application without a config change by renaming instances, and report a measured RTO and RPO with timestamps for a roughly 5 GB database, in under 45 minutes end to end.

You can force a Multi-AZ failover with reboot-db-instance --force-failover while a client loop runs, state to the second how long connections failed, and explain which client-side settings (DNS caching, pool validation, keepalives) would have extended the outage.

You can write a Terraform module for RDS Postgres with encryption, deletion protection, final snapshot, Secrets Manager password, a custom parameter group and log exports, and predict from terraform plan which attribute changes replace the instance, which apply in place, and which wait for the maintenance window.

16.topic: IAM and cloud security: least privilege, roles, IRSA, no long-lived keys
outcomes: You can write, from a blank file and without documentation, a least-privilege identity policy for a queue worker touching SQS, an S3 prefix, one Secrets Manager secret and its KMS key, and it passes `aws accessanalyzer validate-policy` with zero ERROR or SECURITY_WARNING findings on the first run.

You can convert a container that ships an AKIA key in its environment to IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, show `aws sts get-caller-identity` inside the pod returning an assumed-role ARN with a meaningful session name, and decode the projected token to show the exact sub and aud claims the trust policy matches.

You can take an AccessDenied from a customer's Slack message and, using only the error text, CloudTrail and simulate-principal-policy, name the policy type and statement responsible within fifteen minutes, including the disguised KMS and S3 403-for-404 cases.

17.topic: EKS: cluster design, node groups, IRSA, ingress, cert-manager, Route 53
outcomes: You can stand up VPC, EKS control plane, a managed node group, the five core add-ons and the IRSA roles for four controllers from two Terraform root modules with a cold apply under 25 minutes, and terraform plan is clean immediately afterwards.

You can compute the maximum pods for any EC2 instance type from its ENI and IP limits in under a minute, state how many pods a given private subnet can hold, and name the two CNI changes (prefix delegation, custom networking) that fix exhaustion and what each requires.

You can wire IRSA and Pod Identity for a controller with a least-privilege trust policy and prove it from inside a pod with aws sts get-caller-identity, then show the same call denied from an unannotated pod and from a pod trying to reach IMDS with the hop limit at 1.

18.topic: GCP and the multi-cloud Rosetta stone
outcomes: You can take a fresh GCP project with billing linked and, in under 30 minutes and without a service account key, have Dokeo running on Cloud Run behind `--no-allow-unauthenticated` with a dedicated runtime SA, `DATABASE_URL` from Secret Manager, a Cloud SQL connection via the `/cloudsql` socket, and a successful `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)"` against `/health`.

You can produce a one-page service map of the roughly 25 services Dokeo and its pipeline touch across AWS, GCP and Azure, with an analogy-strength column (exact / close / misleading) and a one-line gotcha per row, and defend every 'misleading' entry (global VPC, scale-to-zero, resource groups, deny semantics) to a platform architect.

You can read a Cloud Run revision failure from `gcloud run revisions list` and the revision logs and name the cause within two minutes for each of: `exec format error` (arm64 image), listening on 127.0.0.1 or the wrong port, missing `secretmanager.secretAccessor`, missing `iam.serviceaccounts.actAs`, and `allUsers` blocked by Domain Restricted Sharing.

19.topic: CI/CD and supply chain: build, test, scan, sign, deploy
outcomes: You can, from an empty `.github/workflows` directory, ship a Dokeo pipeline in which pull requests run test, build and scan without pushing, and merges to main run test, build, scan, sign, push to ECR, bump the GitOps repo and wait for Argo CD to report Healthy, with commit-to-healthy lead time under 10 minutes on a warm cache.

You can demonstrate on demand that a failing test and an injected HIGH CVE (an old base image or a pinned vulnerable urllib3) each stop the run at the right job, and that the merge button on the PR is disabled rather than merely red.

You can trace any running pod back to its source: `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}'` to a digest, `cosign verify` to a workflow identity, the OCI revision label to a commit SHA, and the GitOps commit to the run URL, in under five minutes with only CLI tools.

You can produce, from Cost Explorer or a CUR query, a monthly breakdown of the DefenderMate stack by service and by `tenant` tag, and explain every line above 5 percent of the total in one sentence each, including exactly what 'EC2-Other' contains.

You can build a spreadsheet model with a fixed floor, a per-tenant slope and step costs that outputs total cost, cost per tenant and break-even tenant count at 1, 5, 20 and 100 tenants, and it reconciles within 15 percent of a Pricing Calculator estimate and within 10 percent of actuals after one billing month.
You can name three savings levers for the stack with a dollar saving, effort, payback and risk for each, and defend why rightsizing beats a Savings Plan at one client and the reverse at twenty.

21.topic: SRE fundamentals: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, toil, on-call
outcomes: You can write a complete SLO document for DefenderMate with at least four SLIs (API availability, dashboard latency, webhook acceptance, classification freshness), each with a plain-English specification, the exact PromQL implementation and measurement point, a target, a window and a rationale, such that a colleague can reproduce every number in Grafana from the document alone.

You can do the budget arithmetic cold: state the minutes of downtime allowed by 99, 99.5, 99.9 and 99.95 percent over 28 and 30 days, derive the 14.4, 6 and 1 burn rates from the 2%/1 h, 5%/6 h and 10%/3 d budget-consumption targets, and convert them into error-ratio thresholds for any objective.

You can implement multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerts as Prometheus recording and alerting rules, pass `promtool check rules` and a `promtool test rules` suite, and demonstrate live that a 1.5% injected 5xx rate pages within five minutes while 0.05% stays silent and the page clears within minutes of the injection stopping.

22.topic: Observability: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, logs, traces, metrics
outcomes: You can instrument a FastAPI webhook receiver, a queued worker that calls an LLM, and an outbound HubSpot client so that one trace_id links the SERVER span, the CONSUMER span, the classifier INTERNAL span with gen_ai.* attributes and the HTTP CLIENT span, and show the full tree in Grafana Tempo with span durations that reconcile to the provider's reported latency.

You can write an OpenTelemetry Collector config from memory with memory_limiter, k8sattributes or resourcedetection, attributes-based redaction, batch, tail_sampling and OTLP, Prometheus and Loki exporters, pass 'otelcol validate', and prove data flow using only the Collector's receiver and exporter counters on :8888.

You can produce the six PromQL queries of a RED dashboard (rate, error ratio, p50/p95/p99, saturation) for any service given only its metric names, and explain why each rate() window is at least four scrape intervals and why le must survive the aggregation in histogram_quantile.

You can write a k6 script with a ramping-arrival-rate breakpoint scenario, tagged requests, a custom Trend for end-to-end task completion and thresholds derived from the Kaupex SLOs, run it from a separate host, and have results streaming into Prometheus so k6 and application RED metrics share one Grafana time axis.

You can name the first saturated resource in Kaupex under load within 15 minutes using `kubectl top`, `py-spy dump`, `pg_stat_activity` and the k6 timing breakdown, and state whether it is CPU, event-loop blocking, threadpool, connection pool or Postgres, with the evidence line for each.

You can produce a before/after load report in which exactly one variable changed, both configurations were run twice, the environment is recorded down to the image digest, and the p95/p99 improvement at fixed arrival rate exceeds run-to-run variance.

You can take a paging alert on DefenderMate and, within five minutes, have declared a severity, named yourself IC, opened the incident channel with a pinned state summary, and issued one timeboxed mitigation task to a named person, all recorded with UTC timestamps.

You can run a 30-minute Wheel of Misfortune as IC with a friend as game master and be scored by them on the rubric (declaration time, mitigation before diagnosis, update cadence, no unassigned tasks) at or above the threshold you set in the playbook.

You can execute the Kubernetes and Postgres mitigation menu from memory on your k3s cluster: `kubectl rollout undo` to a named revision with ArgoCD self-heal disabled first, HPA minReplicas raised, a blocking Postgres session found via `pg_blocking_pids` and terminated, each with the observed effect written to the timeline.

You can take a customer's architecture diagram and within ten minutes list its failure domains, its hard dependencies with their availability ceilings, and state the highest availability it can honestly promise, with the multiplication shown.

You can perform a point-in-time restore of a self-hosted Postgres from a pgBackRest S3 repository to a named timestamp with --target-action=pause, verify a marker row, promote, and report RTO and RPO with wall-clock timestamps, in under 30 minutes for a roughly 10 GB database.

You can produce a tier table for a workload with objective and measured RTO and RPO for each data store, plus a monthly cost for backup-and-restore, pilot light and warm standby, and defend the recommended tier with the customer's own downtime cost.

26.topic: Supporting a deployment you cannot log into: preflight checks, support bundles, remote diagnosis
outcomes: You can write a Preflight spec for DefenderMate that blocks installation on an undersized node, a missing or wrong StorageClass, an unreachable image registry and an unsupported Kubernetes version, and demonstrate exit code 3 on failure, 4 on warning and 0 on a healthy cluster.
You can ship that preflight as a Helm pre-install/pre-upgrade hook with least-privilege RBAC and prove that a failing check aborts `helm upgrade` rather than leaving a half-applied release.

You can write a SupportBundle spec with collectors, redactors and analyzers, distribute it in-cluster so the customer's command is `kubectl support-bundle --load-cluster-specs`, and produce a bundle from a broken install in under five minutes.

27.topic: Production Python architecture: domain models, repositories, DI, packaging
outcomes: You can draw the four layers of the restructured Kaupex Task Compiler from memory, and `lint-imports` in CI fails the build when you deliberately add `from sqlalchemy import select` to a file under `kaupex/domain/`.

You can run the full service-layer test suite for the Task Compiler in under two seconds with no database and no network, using `FakeTaskRepository`, `FakeUnitOfWork` and a `FakeLLMClient`, and you can show `pytest -m integration` running the same use cases against a real Postgres.

You can swap the LLM adapter (Anthropic direct to LiteLLM or Bedrock) or the persistence adapter (Postgres to SQLite for a demo) with a diff that touches only `bootstrap.py` and one new adapter module, and the unchanged test suite proves the domain and service layers did not move.

28.topic: FastAPI in production: DI, settings, lifespan, background tasks, workers, deployment
outcomes: You can demonstrate, with 10 concurrent curls and a `py-spy dump`, why a blocking call inside an `async def` handler stalls every request in the process, and fix it three ways (async client, `def`, `run_in_executor` with a process pool), choosing correctly between IO-bound and CPU-bound work.

You can start Kaupex with `KAUPEX_DATABASE_URL` unset and have it exit non-zero within one second with a `ValidationError` naming the field, and show that every credential in the settings `repr()` prints as `**********`.

You can write the connection budget for a deployment as (pool_size + max_overflow) x workers x replicas against Postgres `max_connections` and prove it by running the fleet at full pool while reading `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity`.

29.topic: Auth: OAuth2, OIDC, JWT, RBAC, multi-tenant claims
outcomes: You can stand up Keycloak with Docker Compose, create the realm, the confidential BFF client and the audience-restricted API client, export the realm JSON, and have a fresh checkout log in end to end via `--import-realm` in under 15 minutes without opening the admin console.

You can draw the authorization code + PKCE + BFF sequence from memory with every parameter (`response_type`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state`, `nonce`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method`, `code`, `code_verifier`) and, for each, name the attack it defeats in one sentence.

You can write the FastAPI verifier dependency (pinned `RS256`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp` with leeway of at most 30 seconds, required claims, RFC 6750 `WWW-Authenticate` errors) and show a test suite in which `alg=none`, HS256 key confusion, wrong `aud`, wrong `iss`, expired, future `nbf`, tampered payload and an ID token presented as an access token are each rejected with the expected `error` value.

You can take a customer's FastAPI `/openapi.json`, generate `paths` and `components` types with openapi-typescript, and produce an openapi-fetch client where a backend field rename fails `tsc` in CI instead of failing a demo.

You can write a `DefenderMateClient` that connects over stdio or Streamable HTTP, completes the `initialize` handshake, lists tools, calls a tool with Zod-validated arguments and results, and closes cleanly in `finally` without orphaning the child process.

You can diagnose `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`, `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` and `Cannot use import statement outside a module` in under five minutes by reading `package.json` `type` and `exports` and the tsconfig `module` and `moduleResolution` settings.

31.topic: PostgreSQL at depth: planner, indexes, EXPLAIN, locks, transactions, window functions
outcomes: You can take an unfamiliar EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output for a five-table join and, within three minutes and without tooling, point at the node where estimated rows diverges from actual rows by more than 10x, name the cause (stale statistics, correlated columns, function on a column, generic plan, missing extended statistics) and state the change that fixes it.

You can, for WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 on a 10M-row table, write the single index (column order, partial predicate, INCLUDE columns, direction) that yields an Index Scan or Index Only Scan with no Sort node and Heap Fetches: 0, and prove it with the before and after plans.

You can generate 5-10M rows of Zipf-skewed multi-tenant seed data with generate_series, take three real Dokeo queries from seconds to under 5 ms, and explain every line of each before/after plan including Buffers and Sort Method.

32.topic: Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems: RLS, PII, encryption, audit trails
outcomes: You can stand up DefenderMate's schema in a fresh Postgres 16 container and run an RLS test matrix (positive, negative, cross-tenant INSERT and UPDATE, unset tenant, owner-with-FORCE) generated from the catalog across every table in `public`, passing in CI in under 60 seconds; deliberately dropping one policy makes the suite fail naming that table.

You can explain, with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output captured as `app_user`, why a policy written as `(SELECT current_setting(...))` produces an InitPlan and why a non-LEAKPROOF function in the query turned an index scan into a sequential scan, then fix it without weakening the policy.

You can reproduce the PgBouncer transaction-pooling leak (session-level `SET app.tenant_id` visible on the next checkout) in an automated test, and show the `set_config(..., true)` fix turning it green.

33.topic: Redis: caching, rate limiting, idempotency, streams
outcomes: You can implement a token-bucket limiter as a single Lua script (or Redis Function) with per-tenant and per-route dimensions, prove under 20 concurrent workers that admitted requests never exceed capacity plus refill, and return 429 with correct `Retry-After` and RateLimit headers.

You can implement an idempotency layer that claims with `SET NX PX`, fingerprints the request, replays completed responses byte-for-byte, rejects mismatched payloads, and demonstrate by killing the process between claim and completion that the retry recovers and Postgres still holds exactly one row.
You can make a webhook receiver dedup at-least-once deliveries from Stripe or GitHub, ack within one second, and show in a test that replaying the same event id 50 times produces one side effect.

34.topic: Real-time transports: SSE, WebSockets, streaming at scale
outcomes: You can defend the SSE-vs-WebSocket choice for a given customer feature in under two minutes, citing direction, proxy path, auth, and reconnection semantics, and write it as a design-doc paragraph.

You can implement a FastAPI SSE endpoint that relays Claude's stream with matching event names, forwards usage, stops the upstream call within one second of client disconnect, and passes `curl -N` through an Nginx proxy with `proxy_buffering off`.
You can kill the server mid-generation and show the browser reconnecting with `Last-Event-ID`, receiving only the missed deltas from a Redis Stream, with no duplicated or lost text.

You can bring up a three-broker Redpanda cluster from Compose, create a topic with RF=3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`, produce 100k keyed records with `acks=all` and idempotence on, kill one broker mid-run and show zero loss and zero reordering per key; kill a second and show writes fail with `NotEnoughReplicas` rather than silently degrading.

You can demonstrate all three commit-placement outcomes (loss, duplicates, correct) by moving `commit()` before or after processing and SIGKILLing the consumer between them, then explain each outcome from the numbers in `rpk group describe` or `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe`.

You can run a consumer whose handler takes 90 seconds per record without it being evicted from the group, by pausing partitions and bounding work per poll, and show the rebalance log lines before and after the fix.

36.topic: Temporal at depth: signals, queries, versioning, sagas, worker tuning
outcomes: You can deploy a patched Kaupex worker (`workflow.patched('compile-v2')`) while at least ten compile workflows are mid-activity, show with `temporal workflow show` that old runs finish on the old branch and new runs record the patch marker, and later remove the old branch only after a query for pre-deploy Running executions returns zero.

You can run a replay job in CI that pulls the last seven days of `CompileTask` histories, replays them through the candidate image, and fails the pipeline on the first `NondeterminismError`; you can demonstrate it catching a deliberately reordered activity.

You can force a non-retryable failure in the third step of the Kaupex publish saga and show the compensations execute in reverse order with idempotent retries, the execution ends Failed with `compensated`, and repeating the failure with a worker kill mid-compensation produces no duplicate HubSpot records.

37.topic: Entity resolution and record linkage: blocking, fuzzy and probabilistic matching, survivorship
outcomes: You can take three dirty exports of the same ~50k customers and produce, in one command, a candidate pair set under 1e7 pairs with measured pairs completeness above 99 percent, and state the reduction ratio versus the 11.25 billion all-pairs baseline.

You can justify each field's comparator and threshold in one sentence apiece (why Jaro-Winkler on surname, why trigram Jaccard on company name, why a day-difference band on date of birth) and show what breaks when the wrong one is used.

You can explain a single pair's score field by field from a match-weight waterfall - prior, per-field log2(m/u), term-frequency adjustment - to a non-statistical customer stakeholder in under three minutes.

38.topic: Landing in a codebase you did not write: orientation, reproduction, isolation, minimal fix
outcomes: You can land in a repo you have never opened and, within 10 minutes, name its entrypoints, the exact test command, its config and state surface, and the three files most likely to contain the bug - checked against the six recorded sessions.
You can turn a one-paragraph bug report into a committed failing test that runs in under 10 seconds on a clean clone and fails for the reported reason rather than a proxy for it.

You can write a repro.sh with correct 0/1/125 exit semantics and drive `git bisect run` to a first-bad-commit across a 500-commit range containing dependency bumps and broken commits, ending with a bisect.log you can paste into the ticket.

39.topic: Testing and contracts: pytest, property tests, OpenAPI contract tests
outcomes: You can run `pytest -m unit` on the Kaupex Task Compiler in under five seconds and the full suite (unit, integration against a testcontainers Postgres, API, contract) in CI, with `--strict-markers --strict-config`, `filterwarnings = error` and `xfail_strict = true` enforced and every marker registered.

You can write a Hypothesis `RuleBasedStateMachine` for the Task lifecycle that, when a deliberately planted bug allows cancel after complete, prints a minimal three-step counterexample which you turn into a pinned regression test with `@reproduce_failure` or `@example`.

You can make a full `schemathesis run` against the Kaupex `/openapi.json` pass with all default checks enabled and at least one OpenAPI link exercised in the stateful phase, and explain from the failure output which handler or schema field was wrong for any check you had to fix along the way.

40.topic: Warehouse layer: dbt, DuckDB, dimensional modelling
outcomes: You can write the grain of each fact table as a single sentence, encode it as a unique_combination_of_columns test, and demonstrate the build failing when a duplicated extract is loaded.

You can run dbt build on a fresh clone with only a Postgres DSN and end with fct_llm_calls, fct_tenant_daily, dim_tenant (SCD2), dim_model and dim_date materialised in DuckDB, every test passing, and dbt docs generate producing a lineage graph that terminates at the defendermate_weekly_email exposure.
You can change a tenant's plan tier in Postgres, run dbt snapshot, and show two versions in dim_tenant with correct dbt_valid_from/dbt_valid_to while historic calls remain attributed to the old tier.

41.topic: React and Next.js for FDE demos and internal tools
outcomes: You can scaffold a Next 16 App Router app and, in under two hours, ship a typed list/detail UI over an existing FastAPI service with server-side fetching, a `loading.tsx` skeleton and an `error.tsx` boundary, with `next build` passing type-check and showing each route's static/dynamic marker.

You can draw the server/client boundary for a given screen on a whiteboard, naming which components are Server Components, which are `'use client'`, exactly what crosses the boundary as props, and where the secret-bearing fetch runs, and justify each choice in one sentence.

You can stream Claude output from DefenderMate through a Route Handler to a Client Component with a working Stop button, show in FastAPI logs that the upstream generation stops within one second of abort, and demonstrate it working behind a default-config Nginx after adding the documented headers.

42.topic: PySpark (optional: Databricks- or Palantir-style roles only)
outcomes: You can rewrite DefenderMate's per-tenant, per-day usage aggregation (calls, tokens, cost, distinct users, p95 latency) as a PySpark job, run it with `spark-submit --master local[4]` over Parquet exports, and show with `assertDataFrameEqual` that it matches the Postgres query row for row, including on days with nulls and time zone edges.

You can draw the driver, executor and cluster-manager diagram from memory, place the Python process, the JVM, Py4J and the Python UDF workers on it, and state which process dies and with what error for `collect()`, an oversized broadcast, an `applyInPandas` group, and a large shuffle.

You can read `explain(mode="formatted")` for an unfamiliar job and identify every Exchange and its cause, the join strategy chosen, whether filters reached the Parquet scan, and where a Python UDF broke codegen, and predict the number of stages before running it.

43.topic: Designing Data-Intensive Applications and Kleppmann's lectures
43.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
outcomes: You can draw PostgreSQL single-leader replication on a whiteboard and, for each synchronous_commit setting (off, local, remote_write, on, remote_apply), state exactly which failure loses acknowledged writes and how a client would observe it.

You can take a user story such as 'saved my profile, refreshed, saw the old one', name the missing guarantee (read-your-writes), and describe two implementations, one of them the LSN-tracking approach using pg_current_wal_lsn() and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn().

You can take five concurrent-transaction scenarios, predict which anomaly occurs under READ COMMITTED and under REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL, and prove it in two psql sessions, then show the SERIALIZABLE retry loop or explicit lock that removes it.

44.topic: MIT 6.824 selected lectures: Raft, linearizability, transactions
44.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
outcomes: You can draw a 5-node Raft cluster on a whiteboard and narrate election, replication and commit with the correct RPC fields and persistence points, including the Figure 8 case, in under 15 minutes with no notes and survive interruptions at any step

You can take any Figure 7-style log configuration and state, per server, whether it can win an election, what prevLogIndex the leader will settle on for each follower, and which entries will be truncated
You can decide by hand whether a short history of concurrent reads and writes is linearizable, and confirm it by feeding the same history to Porcupine with a register model

45.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
outcomes: You can run `make RUN="-run 3A" raft1` through `-run 3D` and pass all of 3A, 3B, 3C and 3D with `-race`, repeated with `-count 10`, with the whole suite under the 600-second grading limit and no individual test over 120 seconds

You can point at the specific line in your raft.go that implements each numbered rule in Figure 2, including the two easily-skipped ones (step down on a higher term seen in a reply; apply while commitIndex > lastApplied)
You can reproduce the Figure 8 scenario on a whiteboard in under five minutes and state exactly which line of your commit-advance code prevents it

46.topic: System design playbook: load balancing, caching, sharding, queues, rate limits, IDs, search
46.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
outcomes: You can run a 45-minute design of a stated system (DefenderMate at 500 tenants, or an unfamiliar prompt) against a visible clock and leave behind written requirements, a numbers table, a component diagram, two deep dives and a failure story without being prompted for any of them.

You can produce a capacity estimate in under five minutes from stated assumptions (average and peak QPS, storage per year, bandwidth, cache size for a target hit ratio, worker count from Little's Law) and name the component that saturates first with the number that proves it.

You can choose a load-balancing algorithm and connection-reuse configuration for a stated workload (short JSON calls vs long SSE streams) and write the Nginx upstream block or ALB target-group settings, including health-check thresholds and a deregistration delay that matches the pod's grace period.

47.topic: LLM-era system design: serving, caching, batching, rate limits, retries, latency budgets
47.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
outcomes: You can write a per-hop latency budget for an LLM feature that sums to a stated p95, set every hop timeout from it, propagate a deadline down the chain, and show the `histogram_quantile()` query that proves the budget is being met in Grafana.

You can state cost per request as a formula with named token terms, name the four multipliers that inflate it (retries, agent loops, tool round-trips, judge models), and produce a per-tenant per-feature monthly cost number from a `llm_calls` table you designed.

You can restructure a prompt so the stable prefix is cacheable, place `cache_control` correctly, and demonstrate a measured cache hit ratio with `cache_read_input_tokens` before and after, including the cost break-even point where caching starts paying.

48.track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
outcomes: You can run a 45-minute design mock in which the recording shows each phase transition (requirements, estimation, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, close) within two minutes of the planned budget, with no phase skipped.

You can, for any of the six archetypes, state three core functional requirements, an explicit out-of-scope list, and non-functional requirements with numbers (availability, p99 latency, peak QPS, retention, consistency per operation) inside five minutes without prompting.
You can derive QPS, storage and bandwidth in powers of ten in under three minutes and, for each number, say which design decision it changes (shard or not, in-memory or not, one primary or many).

49.topic: LLM fundamentals: tokens, attention, pretraining, RLHF, scaling, limits
outcomes: You can take a customer's real document, tokenize it with two different tokenizers, and state tokens-per-KB and the resulting per-1000-document cost within 10% of the actual billed amount.

You can draw scaled dot-product attention on a whiteboard from memory — Q/K/V projections, sqrt(d_k), softmax over keys, causal mask — and derive from the drawing why context is O(n^2) and why a KV cache exists.

You can size a self-hosted deployment on the spot: given parameter count, precision, concurrency and context length, you produce weight memory and KV-cache memory and say whether it fits the customer's GPUs.

50.topic: Prompt engineering as code: versioning, regression sets, structured outputs
outcomes: You can take any row in DefenderMate's llm_calls table and recover the exact prompt text, model snapshot and output schema that produced it, from Git, using only the logged prompt_id, prompt_version and prompt_hash.

You can run the smoke suite on a prompt change in under two minutes and get a per-tag score table with the delta against a committed baseline and the id of every case that flipped in either direction.

You can open a pull request that edits a prompt and have CI block the merge on a regression larger than two sigma, with the three worst-regressed case IDs named in the failure output and a sticky score comment on the PR.

51.topic: Tool use, structured outputs and MCP servers
outcomes: You can draw the MCP trust boundary for a customer deployment on a whiteboard - user, host, client, server, upstream - and for each arrow name what crosses it, who authenticates it, and one concrete attack it enables if unprotected.

You can hand-write a valid tools/call JSON-RPC request and its two possible failure responses (a -32602 protocol error object versus a result with isError: true) without an SDK, and say which one the model is meant to recover from.

You can build a Streamable HTTP MCP server that validates Origin, publishes RFC 9728 protected resource metadata, returns 401 with a correct WWW-Authenticate header, and rejects a token whose audience is not your canonical server URI - demonstrated by a test that passes a valid token and one issued for another resource.

52.topic: Agents: workflows vs agents, planning, memory, multi-agent, human-in-the-loop
outcomes: You can take a customer process described in prose and return a per-step table classifying every step as deterministic code, a single LLM call, a named workflow pattern, or an agent, with the specific decision criterion written next to each agent classification.

You can implement the client-side agent loop against the Messages API from scratch - looping while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, returning `tool_result` blocks with `is_error` on failure - with an iteration cap, a wall-clock deadline and a cumulative token budget that fails closed to a human and attaches the partial trace.

You can predict an agent run's cost in tokens and dollars before writing it, then show measured `cache_read_input_tokens` versus `cache_creation_input_tokens` proving prompt caching moved it by the amount you predicted.

53.topic: RAG at depth: chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, reranking, contextual retrieval, caching
outcomes: You can re-run the full retrieval eval on the held-out set with a single command and produce a table showing recall@5, recall@20, nDCG@10, answer accuracy, p95 latency and cost per 1k queries for every variant, with one variable changed per row.

You can beat your frozen naive baseline by a stated margin (target: at least +15 points recall@5 or a halving of top-20 retrieval failures) and name which specific change produced which part of the gain.

You can write the hybrid SQL from memory - a pgvector ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 arm and a websearch_to_tsquery/ts_rank_cd arm, each to depth 50, fused with RRF at k=60 - and explain why fusing raw scores instead would be wrong.

54.topic: Fine-tuning vs prompting: LoRA, PEFT, when not to
outcomes: You can run the fine-tune-versus-prompt gate live in a scoping call and produce, within ten minutes, a written recommendation plus the specific measurement that would reverse it.

You can execute a QLoRA supervised fine-tune of a 7B-class model on a single free-tier GPU end to end — chat-template formatting, completion-only loss masking, SFTConfig, checkpoint selection — and reload the adapter in a fresh process to reproduce your eval scores exactly.

You can read a LoraConfig and state its trainable-parameter percentage, approximate memory footprint, and overfitting risk, and explain what changing r without changing lora_alpha does to the effective update.

You can produce, in under an hour for a new customer system, a written threat model that maps every untrusted-content entry point, private-data reachability and egress channel to an OWASP LLM Top 10 ID with a named mitigation and a stated residual risk.
You can clear every Gandalf level and explain, for each one, which defence layer you defeated and what the equivalent defence would be in a production system.

You can demonstrate a working end-to-end indirect injection against a deliberately vulnerable demo - payload hidden in a retrieved document that causes an unauthorised tool call - and then show it blocked by a specific control you added.

You can take a bare Hetzner instance to a responding Hermes gateway in under 60 minutes with key-only SSH, a cloud firewall permitting only 22/tcp inbound, no public bind on the dashboard or API server, a pinned image tag, and hermes doctor clean.

You can register your HubSpot MCP server in config.yaml, prove with hermes mcp test that exactly the intended tools appear as mcp_hubspot_*, and demonstrate that an excluded write tool is genuinely absent from the model's tool list rather than merely discouraged in a prompt.

You can show from the config and a live terminal call that the HubSpot token reaches the MCP subprocess and nothing else - that execute_code and terminal cannot read it because of the name-based env filter and the MCP env allowlist.

57.topic: Permission-aware retrieval: mirroring customer ACLs into RAG and agent tools
outcomes: You can choose early binding, late binding or a hybrid per corpus and defend it in front of a security architect with four numbers: permission churn rate, principals per document, corpus size and the agreed staleness budget.
You can model a customer's nested-group ACLs as a relationship schema in SpiceDB or OpenFGA, and explain when your retriever calls Check, BatchCheck or ListObjects and what each one costs at p95.

You can flatten a two-hop nested group membership from a directory (Graph transitiveMemberOf or LDAP in-chain matching) and prove a user gains access through the nested path and loses it when the inner membership is removed.

58.topic: Evals as infrastructure: eval sets, LLM-as-judge, human review, CI gates
outcomes: You can produce a 200-case labelled set for DefenderMate with a written sampling frame, at least 20% double-labelled, a reported Cohen's kappa, and every case carrying source, labeller and labelled_at provenance.

You can report per-class precision, recall and F1 with support and 95% Wilson intervals plus a confusion matrix, and can explain in one sentence why you refuse to answer 'what's the accuracy?' with a single number.

You can state whether the difference between two prompt or model versions is real: paired run over identical cases, McNemar or paired bootstrap, an interval on the delta, and the sample size that would be needed to detect the effect the customer cares about.

59.topic: LLM observability: traces, cost, latency, datasets
outcomes: You can take a single request id from a Kaupex API response and open one trace that shows the HTTP span, retrieval span, every model generation with its prompt version, token usage, USD cost and TTFT, and the tool calls in between - with no gap where the LLM call is an opaque 8-second block.
You can state cost per tenant per day and cost per successful answer for a deployment, pulled from the Metrics API rather than a provider invoice, and explain the difference between the two numbers.
You can show p50/p95/p99 latency broken down into time-to-first-token, provider time and your own orchestration self-time, and name which of the three you would attack first for a given complaint.

You can stand up a LiteLLM proxy in front of at least three providers where one `model_name` alias resolves to multiple deployments, and point an unmodified `openai` Python client at it with no application code change beyond `base_url`.

You can send 10% of traffic to a candidate model using a deterministic, session-sticky bucketing function plus tag routing, and prove from `x-litellm-model-id` on 10,000 requests that the realised split is within one percentage point of the target.

You can write the PromQL that produces a per-arm comparison table - request count, error rate, p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, p95 TTFT, fallback count and cost per successful request - each series broken down by `model_id`, and explain why averaging two arms' p95 values is meaningless.

61.topic: Serving at scale: vLLM, quantisation, KV cache, batching, GPU maths
outcomes: You can compute, on a whiteboard in under three minutes and without a calculator, KV cache bytes per token for a named model and the maximum concurrent sequences it supports at a named context length on a named GPU, then state which of --max-model-len, --max-num-seqs or --gpu-memory-utilization you would move first and what it costs.

You can derive the roofline ridge point for a given GPU from its HBM bandwidth and bf16 TFLOP/s, state the batch size at which decode stops being memory-bound, and use it to predict which optimisations will and will not help before running them.

You can produce a benchmark table with at least five configurations (bf16 baseline, FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache, chunked prefill on/off, TP1 replicas vs TP2) reporting p50/p95 TTFT, p95 TPOT, output tokens/s per GPU and goodput at a stated SLO, where every row is reproducible from a recorded server and client command line.

You can run one scheduled job that compares a frozen reference window to the current window and emits a machine-readable snapshot with named metrics, explicit thresholds, per-segment breakdowns and a minimum-n gate - not a notebook HTML file.
You can classify an observed change as input, prediction, label or concept drift and defend the classification with the specific evidence that distinguishes them.

You can show per-class precision and recall for the classifier with confidence intervals computed from a stratified random audit sample, and explain why the same numbers computed from the complaint queue would be wrong.

63.topic: Experiment tracking and prompt versioning as CI
outcomes: You can stand up a prompt registry with immutable versions and environment labels, and show the same prompt served to staging and production from two different versions with zero code differences between the two deployments.

You can make a pull request fail on an eval regression using langfuse/experiment-action, with the PR comment showing the score, the baseline it was compared against, and the result JSON attached as an artifact.
You can produce, from a run id alone, the prompt version, model snapshot, decoding params, dataset hash, judge version and git SHA that produced any number you have ever reported.

64.topic: Cost and latency engineering: prompt caching, batching, smaller models
outcomes: You can produce a per-feature cost breakdown for a running system from your own `llm_calls` ledger and reconcile it to within 2% of the Usage and Cost Admin API figures for the same period.

You can raise the prompt cache hit rate on a real workload above 80% and prove it from `cache_read_input_tokens / (cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens)`, not from an assumption that caching is on.

You can state the caching break-even from memory (1.25x write, 0.1x read, so roughly 1.2 reuses within the 5-minute TTL; 2x write, so roughly 2.2 reuses at 1h) and decide whether a given call site should be cached at all.

65.topic: Platform fluency for take-homes: Anthropic and OpenAI APIs side by side
outcomes: You can open a blank file with no documentation and write a working multi-turn tool-calling loop on the Anthropic Messages API and on the OpenAI Responses API in under twenty minutes each, including correct `tool_result` and `function_call_output` plumbing and a `max_iterations` guard.

You can recite the field-level diffs on demand — `input_schema` vs `parameters`, top-level `system` vs `instructions`, `max_tokens` required vs `max_output_tokens` optional, parsed `input` object vs `arguments` JSON string — and correct a colleague's code by reading it, without running it.

You can enforce a JSON contract three ways (OpenAI `text.format` with `strict: true`, Anthropic `output_config.format`, and the forced-tool fallback) and justify which one you would deploy on a customer's Bedrock estate and why.

You can complete the PortSwigger apprentice and practitioner labs across access control, authentication, JWT, OAuth, SQL injection, XSS, SSRF, CSRF, XXE and business logic, and produce a lab completion list as evidence.

You can take an unfamiliar API's OpenAPI spec and, within an hour, produce an authorization matrix of endpoint x role x tenant with the identity-swap test result in every cell, and name the highest-risk three routes.
You can exploit and then correctly fix a cross-tenant IDOR in your own code, and ship a pytest regression test that fails on the vulnerable commit and passes on the patched one.

You can produce a level-1 DFD of DefenderMate with numbered trust boundaries and a STRIDE-per-interaction table in under 90 minutes, where every row carries an existing control, a gap, a severity with a written justification, an owner and a status.

You can list every secret in a running system from a repo scan plus an infrastructure scan, and state for each one its blast radius, its current TTL, who reads it, and how many minutes a rotation takes.
You can rotate a live Postgres credential used by a running service under continuous load and show a request log with zero 5xx and zero authentication errors across the cutover.

68.topic: Enterprise SSO and directory integration: SAML 2.0 SP setup, SCIM provisioning, group mapping
outcomes: You can take a raw SAMLResponse from either binding, decode it (base64 plus raw DEFLATE) and, within five minutes and without a reference open, name which of Issuer, signature, Status, Destination, Recipient, InResponseTo, NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter, Audience or replay caused the login to fail.

You can stand up a FastAPI SP that publishes valid SP metadata, completes an SP-initiated and an IdP-initiated login against a live Okta org, and enforces signed assertions, audience, recipient, skew-bounded time windows and a Redis-backed replay cache.

You can ship a SCIM 2.0 /Users and /Groups service that passes Okta's Test Connector Configuration and survives an Entra initial plus incremental cycle: create, profile update, group add and remove, and deactivate.

You can execute the full SSRF-to-IMDS-to-credentials chain in flaws2.cloud, load the stolen role, run aws sts get-caller-identity, and then name the three independent controls (app-level URL validation, least-privilege role, IMDSv2 with hop limit 1) that each break the chain.
You can reconstruct that same attack from CloudTrail in Athena, point to the exact fields that reveal instance-credential exfiltration, and say which GuardDuty finding would have fired.
You can escape a privileged Pod to root on the node in Kubernetes Goat and then write the securityContext plus Pod Security restricted profile that makes the escape impossible.

70.topic: Compliance: SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI, what FDEs actually do
outcomes: You can produce a control map for DefenderMate with at least 30 rows, each carrying framework references, a named implementation mechanism, a retrievable evidence artifact, an owner and a test frequency, and a written justification for every 'not applicable'.

You can read a vendor SOC 2 Type II report and, in ten minutes, state the audit period, the criteria categories in scope, any exceptions, the carve-outs, and the complementary user entity controls that now belong to you.

You can draw DefenderMate's regulated data flow end to end - browser, webhook, Redis, Postgres, model provider, S3, CRM, email, logs and traces - and name every processor and subprocessor that touches personal data.

You can declare an incident against a written threshold, assign a severity from a scale that names observable conditions, and state the customer notification obligation that severity triggers, in under two minutes from first signal.

You can act as incident commander on a live bridge with a customer executive present: assigning single owners with deadlines, enforcing one conversation, maintaining a timestamped decision log, and refusing to speculate about root cause.

You can design a tabletop exercise for a specific customer architecture with written objectives, at least four timed injects that each force a decision, evaluation criteria, and a data-collection plan - and facilitate it for 45-60 minutes without rescuing the participants.

You can run a 45-minute discovery session end to end from your own script - consent, context, past-behaviour walkthrough, screen-share observation, constraints, closing ask - and finish on time with the transcript, the scorecard and the write-up committed the same day.
You can show a talk-ratio under 30 percent and a leading-question count that falls measurably from interview one to interview five, evidenced by the tagged transcripts, not by your recollection.

You can take any stated request ('we need a dashboard', 'we need an agent') and ladder it in under ten minutes to the decision it supports, the person who makes that decision, and one number in money, time or risk.

73.topic: Engagement documents: site survey, PRD-lite, SOW, ADRs, design docs, runbooks
outcomes: You can complete a site survey of an unfamiliar customer environment in under two working days and hand back a blockers table where every row has a named human, a needed-by date and a schedule impact stated in days.

You can turn a vague sponsor request into a one-page PRD-lite whose success metric names the exact fields and source system it is computed from, and whose non-goals list has at least three concrete entries.

You can draft the SOW section set - deliverables, customer obligations, assumptions, exclusions, acceptance, change control - and explain for any single line which delivery failure it exists to prevent.

You can deliver a ten-minute demo with no notes and hit measured targets on the tape: first visible value under 90 seconds, under 15 seconds of total dead air, and fewer than three filler words per minute.

You can stand the whole demo up from a clean clone on a machine you have never used in under five minutes, with digest-pinned images and seeded synthetic data, and reproduce the identical run six weeks later from a git tag.

You can answer 'what does this cost us at a million requests a month' with a number, the marginal-versus-fixed split, and a sensitivity row, straight off a one-page unit-economics sheet you built yourself.

You can take a 2000-word draft and cut it 30% in one editing pass without losing a claim, showing the before/after word count and a list of the passive constructions, nominalisations and vague quantifiers you replaced.
You can state, for any page you write, which Diataxis mode it is and what belongs on a different page - and you can point at content you actually moved out.

You can write an incident write-up with impact in customer terms, a timestamped timeline with timezone, root cause separated from trigger, a stated detection gap, and action items that each have an owner, a date and a prevent/detect/mitigate label.

You can state, for each of your top ten target companies, a sourced band (P25/P50/P75 split into base, annualised equity and total), a target, a stretch and a walk-away number, with the arithmetic behind the walk-away written down.

You can deflect the compensation-expectations question three consecutive times on a recorded call without naming a number, without lying about current pay, and without sounding evasive - and then give a defended range if pressed a fourth time.

You can convert any option grant into a three-scenario expected-value range given strike, 409A FMV, last preferred price, fully diluted share count, preference stack and vesting shape, and name the inputs you would have to request to do it.

77.topic: Domain fluency: fintech ops, healthcare intake, procurement, logistics
outcomes: You can sketch from memory, for any of the four domains, three end-to-end workflows with actors, systems of record and the two points where the process actually stalls, and name the exception queue that is the real automation target.

You can state per domain which data must never enter a prompt, a log, a span attribute or an eval fixture, and cite the specific rule that forbids it - PCI's prohibition on storing sensitive authentication data, HIPAA's eighteen Safe Harbor identifiers, GDPR Article 9, ITAR technical data, contract pricing under NDA.

You can name the human who signs each decision class and the threshold that pulls them in - BSA officer, Privacy Officer, controller under dual control, category manager against a delegation-of-authority table, licensed customs broker, dispatcher - and say what evidence their approval must leave behind.

78.topic: Releasing to a fleet of customer installs: support and skew policy, preflight gates, cohort rollout
outcomes: You can take any install's current version and, from your own written policy, state in under a minute whether it is in the support window, what the supported upgrade path to current is (including required stopovers), and what the customer has to do if it is out of window.

You can write a RELEASES.md that a customer's change board accepts: SemVer definition of breaking for your product, dated EOL table, N-2 skew rules with the required component upgrade order, backport bar by severity, and a deprecation notice period.

You can write and run a preflight spec that hard-fails an unsupported version jump, a too-old Kubernetes or Postgres, and an under-resourced node pool, exits non-zero in the customer's pipeline, and prints a message plus runbook URI an engineer who has never met you can act on.

79.topic: Async engagement communication: weekly status update, escalation and slip notes, decision memo
outcomes: You can write a weekly engagement update in under 20 minutes that three readers who have never seen the project can each answer 'what is the status, what is needed from me, by when' from in 30 seconds, verified by a timed blind-read test with the results recorded.
You can state your GREEN/AMBER/RED threshold rules in one sentence each, apply them to four consecutive weeks of a real project, and defend an amber that your own manager wanted reported as green.

You can send a slip note the day the evidence appears rather than the day the milestone is missed, with a new date justified by remaining scopes plus measured completion rate plus an explicit optimism-bias uplift, and two or three costed replan options with a recommendation.

80.topic: Narrative: why FDE, why this company, travel, comp
outcomes: You can deliver a 'why FDE' answer in 55-65 seconds, on the first take, that contains a dated specific moment, one verifiable metric, and an explicit acknowledgement of the cost of the role.

You can deliver a company-specific 'why this company' answer that states one falsifiable claim about their delivery problem, sourced from a primary document you can name, and that would be false if said about their nearest competitor.
You can state your travel availability as a percentage, a trip shape and a hard limit, and defend the arithmetic behind it when asked 'what if we needed more?'.

You can state, for any metric on your resume, the numerator, the denominator, the measurement window, the instrument that produced it and the sample size, without hedging and without looking anything up.
You can name what else changed during each improvement window and say explicitly whether you isolated the cause, including saying 'I could not isolate it' when that is the truth.

You can go three levels deep on every technical bullet - stages, then concurrency/retry/schema mechanics with real config values, then the failure conditions - and stop where your knowledge actually ends.

82.topic: Take-home rehearsals (four, five hours each, recorded walkthrough)
outcomes: You can take an ambiguous take-home prompt and produce, within twenty minutes, a written scope contract naming three in-scope capabilities, an explicit out-of-scope list, and the assumption whose falsity would change the design.
You can go from empty directory to a green CI run on your own scaffold in under ten minutes, timed and repeatable, without copying from a previous project.
You can ship four public repos that each run end to end on a clean machine from a single documented command, verified by cloning into a fresh directory and following your own README literally.

You can run a 30-minute decomposition cold on an unseen prompt: five minutes of clarifying questions, a restated problem you get explicit agreement on, five to seven MECE workstreams with owners, sized ranges, a sequenced phase plan and stated risks - holding the time budget to within two minutes, on video.
You can turn any vague ask into one sentence containing a metric, a baseline, a target, a population, a date and the instrument that measures it, and name the non-ML baseline you would ship first.

You can enumerate the customer-side access path (network route, identity and role, egress policy, security review, DPA or BAA) unprompted, size it in calendar weeks, and attach a named owner to each item.

You can take an underspecified LLM prompt to a written set of requirements in six minutes that includes a measurable quality bar with a target and a measurement method, a latency target expressed as TTFT and total, a cost ceiling per request, and an explicit statement of where customer data is allowed to go.

You can compute, in under four minutes and out loud, tokens in and out per request, tokens per minute against provider ITPM and OTPM limits, cost per request and per month, and - for self-hosted - concurrent sequences from KV cache maths, naming for each number the design decision it changes.

You can draw an evaluation and observability subsystem as boxes on the diagram before minute 40 in every mock, including golden set in CI with a gate value, online sampling and scoring, a human review queue feeding labels back, and judge agreement against human labels.

85.topic: Coding drills: data manipulation and AI-assisted production builds
outcomes: You can profile an unfamiliar dirty dataset and state its row count, null profile, duplicate count and the two dtype problems that will bite you, out loud, within the first three minutes of a timed drill.
You can produce a correct grouped, joined and time-bucketed answer in pandas within 25 minutes on a dataset you have never seen, and reconcile the output total against the cleaned input in code.
You can write ROW_NUMBER, LAG, a ROWS-framed rolling aggregate, an as-of join and a gaps-and-islands query in SQL without a reference open, and explain the ROWS-versus-RANGE difference on demand.

You can run a 45-minute client simulation that ends with a restated problem, a dated thin slice, three named asks with owners, and explicit non-goals - without ever proposing a solution in the first eight minutes.
You can name which hostile archetype you are facing within five minutes, cite the tell that told you, and adapt the conversation accordingly on tape.
You can take a direct attack on your design and respond with acknowledge-specify-bound in under 20 seconds of dead air, verified by transcript timing across four recordings.

87.topic: STAR stories (ten) and two full-loop simulations
outcomes: You can name any of the ten slots cold and deliver that story in 3:00 +/- 20 seconds, with no notes, on camera, hitting a 15/15/50/20 STAR split.
Every story's Result contains a baseline, a post value, a measurement window and the instrument that produced both - and you can survive two consecutive 'how do you know that number?' probes on each.
You can give a second, non-overlapping example for at least six of the ten slots when the interviewer says 'that one doesn't count, give me another'.

88.topic: Public proof: three case studies and repos
outcomes: You can hand any of the three case study pages to a senior engineer who has 90 seconds and have them correctly state what the system does, what the hard constraint was, and what broke — verified with three readers, not assumed.

You can point a stranger at each repo and have them go from `git clone` to a working, seeded local stack with one documented command, on a machine that has never run your code, in the time your README claims.
You can defend every number on every page by naming the metric, the window, the measurement point and the artifact it came from, and you have deleted every claim that failed that test.
You can state in one sentence the claim the write-up makes and name the kind of engineer who would plausibly disagree with it.
You can defend every number in the piece - baseline, method, window, sample size, percentile - and point at the log line, command or dashboard each one came from.

You can describe the agent's blast radius in under two minutes: what it may execute, what the approvals policy and tool allowlist block, what authenticates the gateway, and what a prompt injection arriving through a CRM note would still reach.

90.topic: Target list: 40 companies, referrals, warm intros
outcomes: You can produce forty live rows where every row has a req_url, req_id, posted_date, a stored JD snapshot, an explicit eligibility verdict with the evidence behind it, and a comp band tagged as a US band or an India band with two independent sources.

You can refresh the live/closed status of all forty rows in under ten minutes by running one command against the public ATS endpoints, and produce a diff listing closed reqs, reposts and newly opened reqs at existing targets.
You can point at twenty rows that each name a specific human, your actual relationship to them, the exact ask you will make, and the date you last touched them.

91.topic: Application pipeline: apply in waves, run three or four loops in parallel
outcomes: You can state your six funnel conversion rates from your own tracker, broken out by channel and by wave, and back-solve the size of the next wave from a target of two offers in one two-week window.
You can show a tracker in which every open row has an owner, a next action and a due date, and no row has gone untouched for more than seven days across a full four-week stretch.
You can sustain three to four loops simultaneously for a month without missing or double-booking a round, with a scheduled prep block before and a written debrief after every technical interview.

92.topic: Timed algorithmic screens: core data structures, complexity out loud, easy-medium volume
outcomes: You can name the pattern and state time and space complexity out loud before writing a line, evidenced across 60 logged problems, with your pre-coding complexity matching the shipped solution on at least 90 percent of entries.
You can land a working, self-tested easy-medium solution on an unseen problem in under 20 minutes, verified by log timestamps and by three recorded screens rather than by recollection.

You can type from memory, with no reference open, the half-open binary search, BFS on a grid with visited marked at enqueue, iterative inorder traversal, Kahn's topological sort, union-find with path compression, and a monotonic stack.

93.topic: Linear algebra for ML: vectors, matrices, eigendecomposition, SVD
outcomes: You can hand-derive the SVD of an arbitrary 2x2 matrix at a whiteboard in under ten minutes - A^T A, eigenvalues, V, Sigma, U - and multiply back to verify, with no notes.

You can implement power iteration, Householder QR plus the QR algorithm, and one-sided Jacobi SVD in NumPy only, each with a test asserting agreement with numpy.linalg to 1e-8 on well-conditioned, rank-deficient, defective and Hilbert fixtures.

You can take any real design matrix and produce a one-page diagnostic - log-scale singular-value spectrum, numerical rank at a stated tolerance, kappa_2, the offending columns from pivoted QR and VIF - and say whether an OLS fit is trustworthy and what to do if it is not.

94.topic: Calculus and optimisation: gradients, chain rule, convexity, gradient descent variants
outcomes: You can derive, closed-book on a whiteboard in under 15 minutes, dL/dz = p - y for softmax + cross-entropy and then backpropagate through a two-layer MLP with every tensor shape stated, explaining why frameworks fuse the softmax into the loss.

You can implement a scalar reverse-mode autodiff engine (Value, topological sort, accumulate with +=) from an empty file and gradient-check it against central differences in float64 to relative error below 1e-7.
You can write down, from memory, the update rules for SGD, momentum, Nesterov, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam and AdamW, derive Adam's bias correction, and state what Adam's very first step equals and why.

95.topic: Probability: distributions, Bayes, conditional independence, the CLT
outcomes: You can derive Bayes' theorem from the definition of conditional probability, expand the denominator with the law of total probability, and compute a positive predictive value for a 1-percent-prevalence screening problem in your head to the nearest five points.

You can generate exact samples from five named distributions using nothing but rng.random() - at least two by closed-form inverse transform and one by rejection sampling - and verify each against scipy's CDF with a KS test and a QQ-plot.

You can derive the Beta-Binomial posterior by hand, state the posterior mean as a shrinkage of the raw rate toward the prior, and reproduce it in NumPy so the analytic and Monte Carlo quantiles agree to within a few MC standard errors.

96.topic: Statistical inference: estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, ANOVA
outcomes: You can implement, in pure NumPy and from the formulas, Welch's t (with Satterthwaite df), the one-way ANOVA F from the SS decomposition, and percentile/basic/BCa bootstrap intervals, and show a pytest suite asserting agreement with scipy.stats.ttest_ind, f_oneway and bootstrap to 1e-6 on three real datasets.

You can produce a confidence interval for a difference in means two ways - analytically by inverting the Welch statistic and empirically by bootstrap - and explain in one sentence why they agree here and where they would diverge (skew, small n, a non-smooth statistic).

You can state, for any test you run, the exact null hypothesis, the reference distribution, and the specific assumption you are leaning on, and name the diagnostic (QQ plot, Levene, group-wise n and s table) you used to decide it was tenable.

97.topic: Experimentation and causality: A/B design, power, sequential testing, confounding
outcomes: You can derive n = 2σ²(z_{1-α/2}+z_{1-β})²/Δ² on a whiteboard from the rejection rule, apply it to a 3% baseline conversion with a 5% relative MDE, and match statsmodels TTestIndPower to within 1%, then produce the MDE-vs-N curve and translate it into whole-week runtime for a stated daily traffic.

You can run a 10,000-replicate Monte Carlo A/A study showing the false-positive rate of a daily-peeked fixed-horizon t-test rising well past 5%, and show an always-valid confidence sequence on the same simulated streams holding at 5% while quantifying how much wider its interval is at the planned N.

You can implement CUPED from the pre-period covariate up (θ* = Cov(Y,X)/Var(X)), report the realised variance reduction against the predicted 1-ρ², and prove correctness by rerunning the A/A suite with adjustment on and showing uniform p-values.

98.topic: Information theory and loss functions: entropy, KL, cross-entropy, maximum likelihood
outcomes: You can derive cross-entropy loss from maximum likelihood on a whiteboard, closed book, in under five minutes - i.i.d. log-likelihood, division by N, empirical distribution, CE(P_hat, Q_theta) = H(P_hat) + KL(P_hat || Q_theta) - and state which assumptions you used and which you did not.

You can hand-compute H, KL and CE for two small discrete distributions in both bits and nats, confirm CE(P,Q) = H(P) + KL(P||Q) to 1e-12 in NumPy, and convert any of those numbers to perplexity and back.

You can look at any objective put in front of you - MLE, an ELBO, a GAN loss, a distillation term, an RLHF KL penalty - and name the divergence, the direction, and the bias it will produce (mode-covering over-smoothing or mode-seeking collapse).

99.topic: Numerical computing: NumPy vectorisation, floating point, numerical stability
