outcomes: You can look at a nan, an inf or a silently-wrong number in a training loop and name the cause and the fix on the spot - subtract-the-max in logsumexp, log_softmax instead of log(softmax(z)), log1p instead of log(1+x), Welford instead of E[x^2]-E[x]^2, a float64 accumulator instead of float32 - and say whether the evidence points at the forward pass, the backward pass or the data loader.

You can rewrite any Python loop over an array as a broadcast NumPy expression, and before running it state the expected speedup to an order of magnitude and the peak memory of the temporaries to within a factor of two, then confirm both with timeit.repeat and tracemalloc.

You can implement stable logsumexp, softmax and cross-entropy in NumPy, prove they agree with scipy.special.logsumexp and torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy to 1e-6, and produce a test where the naive version returns inf or nan in float32 while yours does not.

100.topic: Supervised learning I: linear and logistic regression, regularisation, the bias-variance trade-off
outcomes: You can derive the normal equations both by calculus and by orthogonal projection, closed-book in under five minutes, and state exactly when (X'X)^-1 does not exist and what np.linalg.lstsq returns instead.

You can implement OLS (closed-form and gradient descent), ridge, lasso by cyclic coordinate descent with soft-thresholding, and logistic regression by gradient descent and by IRLS, in NumPy, and show every one agreeing with scikit-learn's coefficients to 1e-6 on a fixed dataset.

You can write the bias-variance decomposition from memory, say what each term is an expectation over, estimate bias and variance by bootstrap on a simulated problem where the truth is known, and commit the stacked bias-variance-total figure.

101.topic: Supervised learning II: decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting with XGBoost and LightGBM
outcomes: You can derive the gradient-boosting update on a whiteboard, closed book, in under ten minutes for both squared error (g = F - y, so pseudo-residuals are literal residuals and the leaf value is their mean) and log loss (g = p - y, k = p(1-p), leaf value -sum(g)/(sum(k) + lambda), F_0 = the base logit).

You can write the XGBoost structure score and split-gain formula from memory, and use it to explain in one sentence what gamma does, what lambda does, and why min_child_weight means a row count under squared error but an uncertainty budget under log loss.

You can ship a NumPy-only gradient-boosted regression tree with vectorised cumsum split-finding, shrinkage, row and column subsampling and early stopping, match sklearn's GradientBoostingRegressor to within float noise at matched settings, and name every remaining source of divergence against XGBoost and LightGBM.

102.topic: SVM, k-NN and Naive Bayes: margins, kernels, and when each still wins
outcomes: You can derive the soft-margin SVM closed-book in under ten minutes in all three forms - constrained primal with slacks, the equivalent unconstrained hinge-plus-L2 objective, and the dual with its 0 <= alpha_i <= C box and sum_i alpha_i y_i = 0 equality - and classify any training point into its KKT case from its alpha.

You can implement a soft-margin kernel SVM, k-NN and multinomial Naive Bayes in NumPy from the equations alone, match scikit-learn's accuracy to within 1 percent on the same split, and show the NB joint log-likelihoods agreeing to 1e-10.

You can predict, before running anything, which way the decision boundary and the support-vector count move when C or gamma is changed, and read a (C, gamma) validation heatmap to point at the overfitting corner, the underfitting corner and the usable ridge.

103.topic: Model evaluation: cross-validation, data leakage, metric choice, calibration
outcomes: You can look at any dataset and pick the split in under five minutes - random, stratified, grouped, time-ordered, or grouped-and-time-ordered - by naming the unit of independence and the deployment cadence out loud, and justify it to a customer's data scientist who wanted a random 80/20.

You can find a planted leak in someone else's notebook by running a per-column out-of-fold single-feature AUC screen plus a timestamp audit, name which of the six leakage types it is, point to the exact line where it enters, and quantify the score inflation by re-running with it removed.

You can derive the cost-optimal threshold t* = C_fp/(C_fp + C_fn) from expected cost, build the cost matrix with a customer in their own units, and produce the tuned threshold out-of-fold with its expected weekly cost and alert volume.

104.topic: Feature engineering, selection, and imbalanced data: SMOTE, class weights, target encoding
outcomes: You can take a raw table with a 1 percent positive target and build a single leakage-free imblearn Pipeline - ColumnTransformer with out-of-fold target encoding, scaler, sampler, estimator - that passes cross_validate with no step ever seeing validation rows, and you can point at the line that guarantees each property.

You can derive on a whiteboard the m-estimate target encoding (n_c*ybar_c + m*ybar)/(n_c + m) from a Beta-Binomial posterior, state what m means in rows, and say what a single-row category must encode to and why.

You can implement SMOTE in under 30 lines of vectorised NumPy, reproduce imblearn's class counts on the same seed, and name the three assumptions it makes about the minority class and the feature space.

105.topic: Hyperparameter optimisation: grid, random, Bayesian search with Optuna
outcomes: You can pick between grid, random, successive halving and TPE for a given search space and a fixed trial budget, and defend the choice from the space dimensionality, the cost per evaluation and the fold-to-fold noise rather than from what is fashionable.

You can derive the random-search coverage bound 1-(1-p)^n at a whiteboard, use it to say why 60 trials is the usual floor, and explain why the bound only holds under the sampling distribution you chose (so learning_rate must be log-uniform).

You can write, from memory, an Optuna objective that builds a sklearn Pipeline inside the trial, cross-validates it, reports intermediate values for pruning, records per-fold scores and best_iteration as user attributes, and returns a single scalar - and prove no transform was fitted outside a fold.

106.topic: Unsupervised learning: k-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, PCA, t-SNE, UMAP
outcomes: You can implement k-means++ with Lloyd, DBSCAN, agglomerative clustering with single/complete/Ward linkage, and PCA via SVD in vectorised NumPy, and reproduce scikit-learn's partition at ARI >= 0.95 and its components to rtol=1e-10 after fixing the per-component sign convention.

You can derive both k-means update rules by coordinate descent, prove the objective decreases monotonically, and explain from that derivation alone why the method is bound to squared Euclidean distance and the arithmetic mean.

You can choose k on an unlabelled customer table and defend it with a table of inertia, per-cluster silhouette (not just the mean), gap statistic, Calinski-Harabasz and a bootstrap-ARI stability score, and say which k the customer can actually operationalise.

107.topic: Explainability: SHAP, LIME, permutation importance, partial dependence
outcomes: You can implement permutation importance, PDP + ICE and KernelSHAP in NumPy straight from their definitions and reconcile each against sklearn.inspection and the shap library to a stated tolerance, explaining every remaining difference (RNG stream, background sample, brute vs recursion, log-odds vs probability).

You can compute Shapley values by hand for a three-feature model over all eight coalitions, verify sum(phi) = f(x) - E[f(X)] numerically, and derive the Shapley kernel as the weighting that makes a weighted least-squares fit return those same values.

You can demonstrate with numbers on one dataset that MDI ranks an injected random column near the top, permutation importance on the test fold does not, and joint permutation of a correlated cluster recovers importance that both single-column permutations reported as zero.

108.topic: Time series forecasting: decomposition, ARIMA, Prophet, and honest backtesting
outcomes: You can take an unseen daily business series, produce in under 30 minutes a defended preprocessing decision - transform (with the Box-Cox lambda and how you chose it), d and D (with the seasonal strength F_S and the KPSS output), and candidate (p,q,P,Q) read off the ACF/PACF - and state which of those choices AICc is and is not allowed to arbitrate.

You can implement STL from scratch (inner loop with cycle-subseries loess and low-pass filter, outer loop with bisquare robustness weights) and show your components matching statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL to within float tolerance, plus a reconstruction assertion that seasonal + trend + resid equals the observation.

You can write a rolling-origin backtest harness from scratch supporting both expanding and sliding windows, an embargo gap sized to the widest rolling feature, per-horizon error matrices, and a configurable refit cadence, and draw its cut points on a timeline for a customer.

109.topic: Recommenders and anomaly detection: collaborative filtering, matrix factorisation, isolation forests
outcomes: You can derive the biased matrix-factorisation objective and its SGD update rule on paper, implement it in NumPy only, and beat the mu + b_u + b_i baseline on MovieLens-100K held-out RMSE.

You can implement one ALS sweep as a per-user ridge solve with np.linalg.solve, show the training loss is monotone non-increasing across sweeps, and state the conditions under which you would ship ALS rather than SGD.

You can produce one table for MovieLens showing held-out RMSE, recall@10, NDCG@10 and catalogue coverage for popularity, item-item kNN, SGD-MF and BPR-MF under the same temporal split, and explain every row where RMSE and recall@10 disagree.

110.topic: Neural network foundations: backpropagation, activations, initialisation, regularisation
outcomes: You can derive, on a whiteboard and without notes, delta^L = grad_a J (*) phi'(z^L), delta^l = ((W^{l+1})^T delta^{l+1}) (*) phi'(z^l), dJ/dW^l = delta^l (a^{l-1})^T, and restate all of it in batched row-major NumPy shapes including where the 1/B belongs.

You can implement a reverse-mode autograd engine from scratch (topological order, VJP per primitive, gradient accumulation on fan-out, broadcast-aware reductions) and train a multi-layer MLP with it, no framework in the training path.

You can write a centred finite-difference gradient check with a relative-error criterion that passes at ~1e-7 in float64 for weights, biases and the regularisation term, explain why ReLU kinks cause false failures, and have it run as a pytest test in CI.

111.topic: Training deep networks: optimisers, batch norm, schedules, mixed precision, debugging a bad loss curve
outcomes: You can implement SGD-with-momentum (including dampening and Nesterov) and Adam (including bias correction and PyTorch's eps placement) from scratch and show a pytest assertion that parameters match torch.optim to within 1e-6 over 100 float64 steps across a grid of hyperparameters.

You can derive, on a whiteboard and without notes, that gradient descent on a quadratic requires eta < 2/lambda_max, state the optimal step size and the rate in terms of the condition number, and use it to explain a specific diverging run.

You can write a warmup+cosine schedule as a closed-form function of the global step, assert it against SequentialLR/CosineAnnealingLR to 1e-9, and name the four ways a schedule silently breaks (per-epoch stepping, step ordering, missing scheduler state on resume, AMP-skipped steps).

112.topic: PyTorch at depth: tensors, autograd, Dataset and DataLoader, the training loop, profiling
outcomes: You can hand-derive the backward for a fused softmax-cross-entropy and for SiLU, implement each as a `torch.autograd.Function` with `save_for_backward` and `needs_input_grad`, and have `torch.autograd.gradcheck` pass in float64 at default tolerances without loosening `atol`.

You can build a ~300-line NumPy-backed autograd engine with broadcasting-aware backward (add, mul, matmul, sum/mean, relu, exp/log, softmax-CE, reshape, transpose) whose gradients match PyTorch to 1e-6 on a 2-layer MLP for non-square, broadcasting shapes, asserted in pytest.
You can predict `size()`, `stride()` and `storage_offset()` after a chain of slice/transpose/expand operations, say in advance whether `view()` will raise, and explain in stride terms why it does.

113.topic: Computer vision: CNNs, ResNet and EfficientNet, transfer learning, augmentation, detection
outcomes: You can hand-compute, on a whiteboard in under two minutes with no library, the output H x W, parameter count and theoretical receptive field at every stage of ResNet-18 for a given input size, and say which stage first stops resolving a 16-pixel object.

You can implement conv2d and max-pool forward and backward in NumPy and have torch.autograd.gradcheck agree with your analytic gradients on float64 with eps=1e-6, including stride 2, padding 1 and a non-square batch.

You can build ResNet-18 from nn.Conv2d/nn.BatchNorm2d/nn.Linear with no torchvision.models, train it past 90% CIFAR-10 test accuracy, and justify every recipe choice (3x3 stride-1 stem, He init, no weight decay on BN and bias, warmup plus cosine, random crop and flip) with the measured cost of removing each.

114.topic: Sequence models: RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs, seq2seq and the road to attention
outcomes: You can derive backpropagation through time on a whiteboard for a vanilla RNN - dL/dh_t recursion, dL/dW_hh as a sum over t, and the explicit product prod_k W_hh^T diag(1 - h_k^2) - and point at the exact factor that vanishes.

You can write the LSTM's six equations and the GRU's four from memory, and show that dc_t/dc_{t-1} = diag(f_t) for the LSTM and that h_t = z_t h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t) h~_t gives an identity Jacobian at z_t = 1, naming these as the specific fixes for the specific factor above.

You can implement LSTMCell and GRUCell from tensor ops only (fused matmul, chunked gates, forget-gate bias 1.0) and have them pass both torch.autograd.gradcheck in float64 and an allclose comparison against torch.nn.LSTMCell with copied weights, as a pytest test in CI.

115.topic: Transformers from scratch: attention maths, positional encoding, build a small GPT
outcomes: You can derive scaled dot-product attention on a whiteboard from the query/key/value story, state every tensor shape, and prove the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor from the variance of a d_k-term dot product plus the softmax Jacobian diag(a) - a a^T.

You can write a working multi-head causal self-attention module from memory in under 30 minutes without nn.MultiheadAttention, and show it agrees with F.scaled_dot_product_attention(is_causal=True) to within 1e-4.

You can prove your causal mask is airtight by perturbing token t and asserting that logits at every position before t are bitwise unchanged, and you can explain why a suspiciously low val loss is the expected symptom of failing that test.

116.topic: Fine-tuning at depth: full fine-tune vs LoRA, QLoRA and PEFT, DPO, and evaluating the result
outcomes: You can write h = W0x + (alpha/r)BAx from memory, state that A is Gaussian-initialised and B is zero so delta_W starts at zero, compute the trainable parameter count for a given r and target_modules, and derive dL/dA and dL/dB.

You can produce, before launching, a written per-parameter memory ledger for full fine-tune, LoRA and QLoRA on a named model and GPU, predict peak VRAM within about 20%, and confirm it with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated().

You can implement LoRALinear as a plain nn.Module with no peft dependency, inject it by walking named_modules, train it to the same eval loss as the peft implementation, merge it, and assert the max absolute logit difference between merged and unmerged is under 1e-4.

117.topic: Multimodal learning: CLIP, vision-language models, shared embedding spaces
outcomes: You can write the symmetric InfoNCE loss from memory and implement it in about fifteen lines of PyTorch (F.normalize, logit_scale.exp(), a single I @ T.t(), labels = arange(N), 0.5 times the mean of the two cross-entropies), with a pytest that asserts the loss on a random batch equals log N to three decimal places and that permuting the text rows raises it.

You can derive dL/ds_ij = (p_ij - 1[i=j])/N on a whiteboard, state analytically where the gradient mass goes as tau -> 0 and as tau -> infinity, and back it with a measured temperature sweep plotting loss and the share of gradient norm carried by the single hardest negative.

You can train a dual encoder on Flickr8k and report text-to-image and image-to-text R@1/R@5/R@10 next to a pretrained ViT-B/32 baseline, stating the gallery size, the caption-sampling rule and the any-of-five hit convention explicitly, with a leakage assertion that no test image appears in the training pairs.

118.topic: Graph neural networks: message passing, GCN/GAT, and enterprise graph use cases
outcomes: You can derive the GCN propagation rule from the first-order Chebyshev approximation on a whiteboard, write the per-node form h_i' = sigma(sum_j 1/sqrt(d~_i d~_j) W h_j), and justify symmetric normalisation over unnormalised sum and over row-stochastic mean in terms of activation scale, symmetry and the spectrum of the propagation operator.

You can implement GCN and GAT layers from a raw (2, E) edge_index using gather plus index_add_ with a segmented, max-shifted neighbourhood softmax, match torch_geometric.nn.GCNConv and GATConv within atol=1e-6, and pass torch.autograd.gradcheck in float64 on a toy graph.

You can produce a depth-versus-accuracy curve on Cora alongside a measured smoothing statistic, and state from those two plots whether a failing 8-layer model is suffering over-smoothing, over-squashing, vanishing gradients or ordinary overfitting - and name the fix for each.

prompts.p: Walk me through exactly what `set -euo pipefail` does, then give me three concrete cases where `set -e` will not stop the script. How would you structure a script so it is correct even if -e were removed?

Design: you need a nightly job on a customer's bastion that pulls 50k records from a paginated REST API, transforms them, and loads them into Postgres. Only bash, curl, jq and psql are available. How do you make it idempotent, restartable after a crash, observable, and safe if cron fires it twice concurrently?

Debug: a cron job's log says 'done' every night but the target table has not updated in three weeks. The script is 300 lines of bash written by someone who has left. Where do you look first, what tools do you use and in what order, and how do you avoid making it worse while you investigate?

A script has a `trap cleanup EXIT` and three background `curl` jobs. The user presses Ctrl-C. Which processes receive SIGINT, which do not, what does the EXIT trap see in `$?`, and how do you guarantee the children die with the parent?

When do you refuse to write something in bash and reach for Python? Name the specific signals in the requirements that trip that decision, and how you would explain the trade-off to a customer engineer who insists on 'just a shell script'.

How do you test a bash script that calls curl, psql and the aws CLI without touching real services? Describe the test structure, how you fake the external commands, how you exercise the retry and failure paths, and what runs in CI.

Your script works on your MacBook and fails on the customer's Ubuntu host - or the other way around. Explain the portability landscape (bash 3.2 vs 5, GNU vs BSD coreutils, sh as dash, busybox) and what policy you would set for scripts shipped to customers.

The nightly loader has `set -e` but its critical step is `extract | tee extract.log`; without pipefail the pipeline exits 0 when extract fails, the empty file loads cleanly, and cron reports success for three weeks before the customer notices stale dashboards.

A cleanup trap runs `rm -rf "$WORKDIR/"` and WORKDIR is unset because the config file failed to source earlier; without `set -u` or `${WORKDIR:?}` the expansion becomes `/` and the script wipes the host it is running on.

A script developed against tidy test data uses `for f in $(find $dir -name '*.csv')`; the customer's export directory has filenames with spaces, so half the files are split into non-existent paths and skipped silently while the summary line still says 'processed N files'.

A 5-minute cron job has no flock and no timeout; one run stalls on a hung upstream API, the next twelve runs stack up, and the customer's database connection pool is exhausted by your script rather than their application.

A script written on a Mac uses `mapfile`, `declare -A` and `sed -i ''`; it fails with 'command not found' on the customer's RHEL bastion, or the reverse - `sed -i ''` on GNU sed treats the empty string as a filename and edits nothing.

The bearer token is passed as `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"` while `set -x` is on for debugging; the token lands in the trace log, which is shipped to the customer's central log store and read by everyone with Kibana access.

`psql ... | while read -r id; do count=$((count+1)); done` runs the loop in a subshell, so the final report says '0 rows migrated' and the on-call engineer rolls back a migration that actually succeeded.

Walk me through everything that happens between the moment a Hetzner VM is powered on and the moment a systemd-managed Python service accepts its first TCP connection. Where in that chain would a missing initramfs driver, a bad fstab entry, and a wrong ExecStart path each fail, and how would the symptoms differ?

A customer says their inference service is 'hung'. You have SSH as a non-root user with sudo, no APM, and one PID. Show me, command by command, how you decide within five minutes whether it is deadlocked in userspace, blocked in the kernel, out of file descriptors, or being CPU-throttled by its cgroup.

Design the systemd unit for a FastAPI service that needs to bind port 443, write to /var/lib/app, read a secret API key, and restart on crashes but not mask a config error. Justify every directive, and tell me which ones you would remove on a customer host running an older systemd.

df reports the root filesystem at 100% but du of / sums to 60%. Explain the mechanism, find the culprit without rebooting, and free the space without losing the process. What would you change in the deployment so it does not recur?

Explain the difference between the kernel OOM killer and a cgroup memory.max kill, how you would prove which one fired from logs and sysfs, and how OOMScoreAdjust, MemoryHigh and OOMPolicy each change the outcome for a multi-worker gunicorn service.

A deploy script that works when run by hand hangs forever when run from CI over SSH on a customer box. List the most likely causes in the apt/dpkg layer and in the environment differences, and describe how you would make the script idempotent and non-interactive.

You need to hand a customer's platform team a service they can operate without you. What do you put in the unit file, the journal configuration, and the sudoers rules so that a junior engineer can restart, read logs, and roll back safely without being able to become root?

A service is deployed with Restart=always and MemoryMax=; it OOMs every 40 seconds and restarts, so health checks flap green and nobody notices for a week until memory.events shows oom_kill in the thousands.

ExecStart wraps the app in `/bin/sh -c`, so on `systemctl stop` SIGTERM reaches sh and is never forwarded; after TimeoutStopSec the whole cgroup gets SIGKILL and in-flight customer requests are dropped on every deploy.

Logs are rotated with rm plus a new file; the process keeps the deleted inode open, /var fills to 100%, df and du disagree by 40 GB, and the on-call engineer expands the volume instead of truncating the fd.
A vendor repo (NVIDIA, Docker, a database) is added with no pin; `apt upgrade` pulls a newer libssl or systemd from it, and the customer's compliance-scanned baseline drifts with no change record.

The unit says After=network.target but not network-online.target, so on cold boot the app starts before DHCP finishes, fails DNS on its first outbound call, exits 1, and the start-rate limiter leaves it dead until someone runs `systemctl reset-failed`.

TLS key is 0600 root:root and the service runs as User=app; it worked in testing because the engineer ran it with sudo. On the first real reboot the service fails with EACCES and the cert path looks correct to everyone reading the config.

A process on a customer host is in D state on a hung NFS mount; the team spends two hours running kill -9 and restarting the service before checking /proc/PID/wchan, which would have pointed at the storage team in thirty seconds.

Walk me through everything that happens between a customer typing https://app.example.com and the first byte rendering. At each step, name the tool you would use to prove it happened and one way it fails in a corporate network.

A customer says our webhooks stopped arriving on Tuesday; nothing changed on their side and nothing changed on ours. Without access to their network, how do you isolate this, what exactly do you ask them to run, and what do you run yourself?

Design the ingress path for a multi-tenant API that serves streaming LLM responses lasting up to five minutes on AWS: which load balancer, which timeouts, HTTP/2 or not, where TLS terminates, and how you preserve the client IP for per-tenant rate limiting without trusting a spoofable header.

Explain the TLS 1.3 handshake versus TLS 1.2, and what SNI and ALPN are each for. Then: the customer's security team mandates mTLS for the webhook receiver. What changes on each side, and what is the operational cost over twelve months?

You see intermittent 502s at the load balancer with no corresponding error in application logs. Give me the three most likely causes and the specific evidence (command and output line) that confirms or rules out each.
Here is ss -ti output for a slow connection showing rto, rtt, cwnd, retrans, unacked and lastsnd. Tell me whether the bottleneck is the network, the sender or the receiver, and what you would change.

A security group allows inbound 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and the subnet's NACL allows inbound 443 only; nothing works. Why, and what is the minimal fix? Follow-up: which of these is stateful, and what does that imply for connection tracking under load?

Backend keepalive shorter than the load balancer idle timeout (gunicorn keep-alive 2 s behind an ALB at 60 s): the backend closes an idle connection, the LB reuses it, and customers see intermittent 502s that appear in no application log, so the team blames the network for a week.

A certificate renewal deploys cert.pem instead of fullchain.pem; browsers still work because they fetch the missing intermediate via AIA, but the webhook sender's Python or Java client fails with 'unable to get local issuer certificate' and deliveries silently stop until the retry window expires.

A 90-second non-streaming model call is cut at 60 s by the ALB idle timeout: the backend finishes, logs a 200 and bills the tokens while the client receives a 504 and retries, doubling cost and creating duplicate side effects.

The NAT gateway or Kubernetes node hits nf_conntrack_max under a traffic spike; dmesg shows 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet', new connections time out while established ones are fine, and it gets misdiagnosed as a flaky upstream API.

A DNS record is created after the first failed lookup, so the customer's resolver holds NXDOMAIN for the SOA negative-cache TTL; you cannot reproduce it from your laptop on a different resolver and 'DNS is fixed' is true everywhere except where it matters.

The customer's TLS-intercepting proxy re-signs every certificate with a private CA; your container image lacks it, requests fails with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED only inside their network, and someone ships verify=False to make the demo work.

A WireGuard or VXLAN overlay lowers the path MTU and ICMP fragmentation-needed is filtered: health checks and small requests pass, but any JSON payload over roughly 1400 bytes hangs forever with retransmissions visible only in tcpdump.
Load average is 60 on an 8-vCPU customer host, CPU is 10% busy and iostat %util is 5%. Walk me through your first three minutes, the exact commands, and what you expect to find.

A customer's FastAPI pod has a 500m CPU limit and its p99 tripled after a traffic increase; node metrics show 70% idle. Diagnose it, show me the evidence you would collect, and explain why raising the limit is not the whole fix.
Explain what iostat -xz 1 tells you and what does not. Which fields let you say a device is saturated, and give me a case where %util is 100% and the disk is fine.
You need to look inside a stuck worker in production. When do you reach for strace, when for perf, when for py-spy, when for bcc, and what is the cost and blast radius of each?

A box has 200 MB free out of 64 GB and the customer wants to buy RAM. How do you decide whether there is a memory problem at all? Name the exact numbers you would read and the threshold that changes your answer.
The OOM killer just killed the database instead of the leaking Python worker. Explain how the victim is chosen and how you would prevent a recurrence without adding memory.

Design what you would leave behind on a single customer VM with no Kubernetes and no cloud metrics so that next time it slows down they can hand you a diagnosis instead of a complaint. What do you sample, at what cadence, where does it go, and what is the one alert you would set?

A rotated log is deleted while a service still holds the fd: df reports 100%, du reports 40%, the API returns ENOSPC on every write and the on-call deletes unrelated files for an hour before anyone runs lsof +L1.
Inode exhaustion from millions of small session or cache files: df -h shows 30% used, writes fail with 'No space left on device', and the team resizes the disk twice before someone runs df -i.

Kubernetes CPU limits set equal to requests: the Python worker is CFS-throttled every 100 ms period, p99 latency goes 10x under a traffic bump, the node dashboard shows 70% idle, and the customer concludes the model is slow.

One core pinned at 100% by a GIL-bound worker or a single NIC RX queue while fifteen cores idle: top's summary line says 7% CPU, the team adds more replicas on the same box, and only mpstat -P ALL shows the hot core.

Memory pressure with no single culprit: MemAvailable near zero, si/so non-zero, major faults climbing, everything 'randomly slow', then the OOM killer takes Postgres instead of the leaking worker because nobody set OOMScoreAdjust.

strace left attached to a production process without -o, or attached without -f to a multi-threaded server so it shows nothing, or the tracer is killed with -9 and the worker stays in T state until someone notices it stopped serving.

nf_conntrack table full or ephemeral port exhaustion on a webhook-heavy box: intermittent connection failures only under load, retries make it worse, and the one line in dmesg that names the cause is never read.

A customer's on-call engineer says a nightly job started failing 'sometime in the last three weeks' and there are about 900 commits on main. Walk me through exactly how you find the culprit, including how you handle commits that do not build.
Explain what `git reset --hard HEAD~3` actually does to HEAD, the index, and the working tree, and then tell me how you would recover if you ran it by mistake on a branch that was never pushed.
During a rebase you see a conflict hunk and decide to keep 'your' change. Which of `--ours` and `--theirs` do you use and why is that the opposite of what you would use during a merge?
Design the Git-side guardrails for a 40-engineer monorepo: what goes in client hooks, what goes in CI, what goes in branch protection, and how do you keep the hooks from being bypassed?
A production API key was committed to a repo with 30 forks and a 2-year history. What do you do in the first 10 minutes, what do you do in the first day, and what can you never fully undo?
Why does `--force-with-lease` still lose data in some setups, and what flag closes that gap? Describe the exact sequence of events that produces the data loss.
A customer's CI clones a 15 GB monorepo from scratch on every run and it takes 9 minutes before tests start. Which clone and checkout flags do you reach for, and what does each one trade away?
A teammate runs `git push --force` on a shared feature branch after an IDE auto-fetched, silently dropping two days of a colleague's commits; nobody notices until the demo build lacks the feature.
The pre-commit hook grows to run the full 4-minute test suite, so the team commits with `--no-verify` by habit and the hook becomes theatre while CI stays red half the day.

A `.env` with production database credentials is committed and then 'deleted' in the next commit; six months later a contractor's clone is compromised and the still-valid credential in history is used.
A CI pipeline clones with `--depth 1`, then a release script runs `git describe --tags` and produces garbage versions because the tag is outside the shallow history.
Submodules pinned to a SHA that was force-pushed away on the upstream repo; `git submodule update` fails with 'fatal: reference is not a tree' on every fresh clone and blocks all deploys.
Windows contributors commit CRLF files with no `.gitattributes`, so every rebase touching those files shows the whole file as a conflict and a 3-line change becomes an unreadable 800-line diff.

Someone bisects on a merge-heavy main without `--first-parent`, lands on a mid-feature-branch commit that never built on its own, and reports a false culprit that sends the team investigating the wrong service for a day.

A customer CTO says 'containers are lightweight VMs, so our tenants are isolated from each other on the node.' Correct them precisely: what is shared, what is isolated, and what would you change in the run configuration before agreeing to run their untrusted plugin code in a container?

Walk me through everything that happens from docker run -p 8080:80 nginx to the first HTTP response arriving at a browser on the host. Name the processes, syscalls, filesystem mounts and iptables rules involved, in order.

This Dockerfile takes nine minutes to rebuild after a one-line code change: it copies the whole repo, then runs pip install, then sets CMD. Draw the layer stack, tell me exactly which layers are invalidated and why, then rewrite it so the rebuild takes under ten seconds and the final image is under 200 MB.

A container in the customer's environment exits with code 137 every few hours. Give me your diagnostic sequence, the two distinct root causes that produce 137, and how you would tell them apart from the host in under five minutes.

The app container can curl the Postgres container by service name in Compose on your laptop, but on the customer's VM it intermittently fails with 'could not translate host name'. What is 127.0.0.11, how does it forward queries, and what would you check on the host?

Two services must talk to each other over Docker networking on one host; the security team requires that neither is reachable from the host's public interface and that the database is reachable from nothing except the app. Design the networks, port bindings and DOCKER-USER rules, and show how you would prove the properties with iptables and ss.
You deleted a 400 MB dataset in a later RUN step and the image got larger. Explain what overlayfs did on disk, and how you would fix it both with and without a multi-stage build.

A JVM or Node service is OOM-killed (exit 137) under a 2 GB --memory limit because the runtime sized its heap from the host's 64 GB visible in /proc/meminfo; the fix is -XX:MaxRAMPercentage or --max-old-space-size, not a bigger limit.

docker stop on the customer's app always takes the full 10 seconds and returns 137 because the entrypoint is sh -c 'python app.py', so SIGTERM stops the shell and never reaches Python; in-flight writes are killed mid-transaction on every deploy.
A single-node Docker host stops scheduling containers and Postgres crashes with 'No space left on device' because json-file logs for a chatty service grew to 200 GB with no max-size configured.

After the client VPN connects, the container can no longer reach the client's on-prem SQL Server at 172.18.4.20 because Compose created a 172.18.0.0/16 network and the host now routes that CIDR to the bridge.

A published port that works in dev returns connection refused at the customer site because the app binds to 127.0.0.1 when HOST is unset, and DNAT delivers packets to the container's eth0 where nothing is listening.

A nightly docker system prune -a --volumes cron deletes the customer's Postgres data because the image's VOLUME instruction created an anonymous volume instead of the named volume everyone assumed Compose had declared.

A CIS benchmark hardening script sets net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 on the customer host; containers start and docker ps looks healthy but nothing has outbound connectivity, and two hours go to DNS theories before anyone checks sysctl.

A customer's security team sends you a 312-row CVE export from their scanner and says nothing deploys until it is zero, and go-live is Thursday. Walk me through your first hour, what you would actually change in the image, what you would push back on, and what the document you hand them on Wednesday night looks like.

Explain exactly what happens between `cosign sign` starting in a GitHub Actions job and `cosign verify` succeeding on a customer's laptop: which services are contacted, what is stored where, and what would an attacker need to control to produce a signature that passes your verify command?

Design the image supply chain for a customer whose production cluster is air-gapped: how do images, SBOMs, signatures, the Trivy database and trust roots get across the boundary, how does the cluster verify without reaching public Sigstore, and where does your CI's SLSA level stop meaning anything?

A pod goes into CrashLoopBackOff right after you switch the image to non-root and enable `readOnlyRootFilesystem`; logs show `PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/app/.cache'`. List the possible causes, the fix you would pick for each, and how you would have caught this before it reached the customer's cluster.

Why is `--ignore-unfixed` both necessary and dangerous in a CI vulnerability gate? Describe a gate design that stays green for months without anyone adding `continue-on-error`, including how suppressions expire and how new disclosures on already-deployed digests get caught.

What is the difference between an SBOM, a SLSA provenance attestation and a cosign signature? For each, tell me which customer question it answers, how it is stored in the registry relative to the image, and one way each can be technically valid yet misleading.

Write, at the whiteboard, a multi-stage Dockerfile for a FastAPI service that depends on psycopg with C extensions, such that the runtime stage has no compiler and runs as a numeric non-root user. Then tell me how you would prove the runtime stage still has every shared library it needs before the first customer request hits it.

A team ships `FROM python:3.12` with gcc, perl and 1.1 GB of Debian, the customer's Wiz scan on go-live morning reports 400 CVEs, and the change window closes while everyone argues about which of them are real.

Switching to Alpine to 'fix' image size makes a Python wheel with no musllinux build compile from source for 18 minutes on every CI run, and later the musl resolver's handling of Kubernetes search domains produces intermittent NXDOMAIN under load that nobody connects to the base-image change.

The Dockerfile says `USER appuser` and the pod spec says `runAsNonRoot: true`; the pod sits in CreateContainerConfigError with 'cannot verify user is non-root' because the kubelet cannot resolve a named user without reading /etc/passwd from the image.

`CMD npm start` makes `sh` PID 1, SIGTERM is never delivered to Node, every pod takes the full 30-second grace period and then is SIGKILLed mid-request, so a 20-pod rolling deploy takes 10 minutes and drops traffic the whole time.

A private registry token is passed as `ARG NPM_TOKEN` and the image is pushed to a shared registry; six weeks later someone runs `docker history` on it and the still-valid token is in the layer metadata for everyone with pull access.

The Trivy gate runs with `--exit-code 1` and without `--ignore-unfixed` on a Debian base, goes red every other day on CVEs with no upstream fix, and within a month the job has `continue-on-error: true` and the gate is theatre.

Cosign signs the tag instead of the digest; a later build moves the tag, verification of `repo:v1.2` still passes because the signature was looked up by whatever digest the tag now points at, and the customer's audit trail no longer says what actually ran.

Walk me through, component by component, everything that happens between kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml and the first HTTP 200 through an Ingress: which controllers act, in what order, what they write, and what you would check if the process stalled at each stage.

A customer reports 503s for about 30 seconds after every deploy and says the platform is fine. What do you look at first, what are the three most likely causes, and what changes to the Deployment and Pod spec would you make to eliminate them?

How does a ClusterIP work when no network interface has that address? Explain kube-proxy in iptables mode, why ICMP to a ClusterIP fails, what changes with IPVS, and what disappears entirely when the cluster runs Cilium with kube-proxy replacement.

Design the config and secrets story for a service that must pick up feature-flag changes without a redeploy but rotate database credentials with zero downtime. What do you mount how, what are the update semantics of each path, and where does it break?
A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, kubectl logs is empty and kubectl logs --previous prints nothing. Describe your next five commands and what each exit code (1, 127, 137, 139, 143) would tell you.

A security lead says 'Kubernetes Secrets are base64, so they are plaintext; we will not use them.' What is accurate in that statement, what would you tell them about etcd encryption at rest, RBAC exposure and env versus volume injection, and what would you actually deploy on their cluster?

Explain what happens when a pod in namespace dokeo resolves the name postgres, and then api.stripe.com: how many DNS queries does CoreDNS see for each, why, and how would you fix the second case for a latency-sensitive path? When would you choose a headless Service instead?

A ConfigMap is mounted with subPath so the customer's config edits never reach the running process; the team concludes the app ignores configuration and hand-edits the container, and the fix (drop subPath, or roll pods via a checksum annotation) is discovered weeks later.

Two Deployments in one namespace share the label app: api; the second ReplicaSet adopts the first one's pods, both controllers fight to reach their replica counts, and the platform team sees a rollout that never converges and pods being killed with no obvious owner.

The readiness probe calls an endpoint that queries the database; a 20-second database failover marks every pod NotReady, the Service has zero endpoints, and a transient dependency blip becomes a full outage, made worse by a liveness probe that also hits the database and triggers a restart storm.

targetPort is set to the Service port (80) instead of the container port (8080); endpoints exist and describe looks healthy, but the ingress controller returns 502 for every request to the new pods only, so the rollout looks fine in kubectl and broken to users.

A database password is rotated in the Secret but the app still uses the old one because it was injected as an env var; nobody runs kubectl rollout restart, the old credential is revoked on schedule, and the customer's first symptom is connection-refused at 3am.

An Ingress is applied without ingressClassName on a cluster that runs both the customer's ingress-nginx and k3s Traefik; neither controller claims it, kubectl get ingress shows an empty ADDRESS, and the deploy is 'done' while the URL returns nothing.

cert-manager's HTTP-01 challenge fails because a controller-level HTTPS redirect (or a Hetzner firewall rule blocking port 80) swallows /.well-known/acme-challenge, and repeated retries against the production ACME endpoint exhaust the duplicate-certificate rate limit so the real fix cannot be validated for a week.

A customer pages you: the new version will not start and pods keep restarting. You have kubectl and ten minutes. Walk me through exactly what you run, in what order, and what each output rules in or out.

Explain how requests and limits flow from the manifest through the scheduler and the kubelet into cgroups. Now a service shows p99 latency doubling under load with no errors and CPU at 60% in kubectl top; what do you check and why?

Design the probes, resources, HPA and PDB for a FastAPI service with a Postgres backend on a customer's EKS cluster where the platform team enforces ResourceQuota and Pod Security restricted. Give actual numbers and defend each one.

A NetworkPolicy is applied and `kubectl get netpol` shows it, but the API can still reach a database it should not. Give three distinct root causes and how you would distinguish them in under five minutes.

Your `kubectl rollout undo` succeeded and every pod is Ready, but the application is still broken. What kinds of change does undo not revert, and how do you structure deploys so a rollback is actually atomic?

The customer's security team wants read-only access for their auditors. Describe the Role, the binding, the token lifetime and how you prove to them what the identity can and cannot do, including Secrets and pods/exec.

Walk through everything that happens between `kubectl delete pod` and the container exiting, including the race that produces 502s during a rolling update and how you eliminate it without slowing deploys.

A liveness probe on /health that also pings Postgres: a 30-second RDS failover restarts every API pod at once, and the reconnect storm turns a blip into a ten-minute outage that the customer blames on your product.

timeoutSeconds left at the default 1s on a Python service that pauses for GC under load: probes time out, the kubelet restarts healthy pods, restarts add load, and the fleet enters CrashLoopBackOff while the customer reports that Kubernetes keeps killing the app.

A CPU limit set equal to a low request on a Go or Java service: CFS throttling adds 100-300ms of tail latency with zero errors and a calm `kubectl top`; only container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total reveals it, weeks later.

HPA scales the API to 40 replicas during the customer's load test, each opening a 20-connection pool, exhausting Postgres max_connections at 100 and taking down the very database the autoscaler was meant to protect.

The platform team adds a ResourceQuota to the client namespace; the next CronJob without requests fails admission at 02:00 as a ReplicaSet FailedCreate event nobody watches, and the nightly report silently stops for a week.

A NetworkPolicy is signed off in the security review on a cluster whose CNI does not enforce policy (kindnet in staging, AWS VPC CNI without network policy enabled in prod); a pentest six months later finds the DB reachable from every pod.

A managed cluster upgrade hangs for hours because a single-replica Deployment has a PDB with minAvailable 1; the drain never completes, someone force-deletes the pod, and in-flight requests are lost during the customer's business hours.

An RWO EBS volume's pod is rescheduled to a different AZ after a node failure and sits Pending on a zone mismatch or Multi-Attach error while the customer's database is down, because the StorageClass used Immediate binding.

Walk me through everything that happens between a git push to the config repo and a pod running the new image. Name each Argo CD component involved, where the latency comes from, and what you would change to make it both faster and safer.

Argo CD renders Helm with helm template instead of helm install. What are the concrete consequences for hooks, lookup, release Secrets, .Release.IsUpgrade and CRDs, and how would you adapt a customer's existing chart that depends on each of those?

Design a GitOps repository layout for a customer with dev, staging and prod clusters, five teams, and a compliance rule that every prod change is reviewed by two people. Directories or branches? App-of-apps or ApplicationSet? Where do secrets live? How does a hotfix reach prod in ten minutes without breaking the rule?

Debug: an Application is permanently OutOfSync with selfHeal enabled, pods restart every three minutes, and the diff shows an annotation that keeps changing. Walk me through your investigation and the fix, including which fields you would ignore and the risk of ignoring them.

A deploy went Degraded at 3am. Compare git revert and argocd app rollback as recovery paths: what each does, which you run first and why, what state Git and the cluster are in afterwards, and what neither of them will undo.

You must run a schema migration before the new Deployment rolls, and the customer's DBA insists that a failed migration blocks the release. Show me the manifests: hook annotations, sync waves, delete policy, backoffLimit, and how health assessment gates the Deployment.

A customer's platform team says GitOps is too slow and wants CI to kubectl apply directly. Make the case for pull-based delivery in terms they care about (audit trail, credential exposure, drift, rollback), and tell me where you would concede.

The chart puts the helm.sh/chart version label inside Deployment spec.selector.matchLabels; a routine chart bump changes the selector, Argo reports 'field is immutable', the sync fails, and prod stays on the old version until someone applies Replace=true and takes an unplanned outage.

The app-of-apps root has prune: true; an engineer moves an Application file to a new directory in one PR, the root prunes the old Application first, the finalizer cascades and deletes the workload namespace including PVCs seconds before the new file is picked up.

A chart relies on lookup to reuse a previously generated admin password; repo-server has no cluster access so lookup renders empty on every sync, Argo writes a fresh random Secret, pods restart and sessions invalidate every three minutes, and selfHeal keeps the loop going until someone reads the Secret's history.

The HPA scales the Deployment to six replicas while the chart says replicas: 2 and selfHeal is on; Argo and the HPA fight, pods churn on every reconciliation, and p99 latency doubles during the customer's peak until /spec/replicas is added to ignoreDifferences.

Someone hot-fixes prod with argocd app rollback, which disables automated sync, and never reverts Git; three weeks later an unrelated commit through the app-of-apps re-enables sync and silently redeploys the broken revision at 2am.

An umbrella chart with eight subcharts takes 110 seconds to render; repo-server hits the 90-second ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT, every app sharing that repo-server flaps between Unknown and Synced, and on-call spends an hour chasing a phantom network problem.

CI promotes with `--set image.tag=1.10`, Helm coerces it to the float 1.1, the registry has no 1.1 tag, and because one pipeline template feeds all three environments, dev, staging and prod all ImagePullBackOff within the same minute.

A customer's security team says your workload cannot ship because it needs to write to disk and bind port 80. Walk me through exactly how you make it pass a `restricted` Pod Security Standard without asking for an exemption.

An attacker gets RCE in a pod running as non-root with the default ServiceAccount. Walk me through, hop by hop, everything they can reach in a default-configured EKS cluster, and tell me which single control cuts the most of it.

Design the RBAC model for a multi-tenant platform where each customer team can fully manage their own namespace but must never read another tenant's Secrets or run privileged pods. Which objects do you create, and where does namespace-level RBAC stop being sufficient?

Deployments in one namespace stopped creating pods after a policy change, but `kubectl get deploy` shows no error and there are no pod events. How do you debug this, and what are the three most likely causes?
A client asks whether Kubernetes Secrets are 'encrypted'. Answer them precisely, then describe what you would actually implement and how you would prove to their auditor that it works.

Compare enforcing 'no privileged containers' with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, Kyverno, and Gatekeeper. Which do you recommend for a 400-node regulated-industry cluster, and what is the failure mode of your choice?

You are told a workload must reach one external SaaS endpoint but the cluster has default-deny egress and a CNI with no FQDN support. What options do you present, and what is the operational cost of each?

A team labels namespaces with `enforce: restricted` in one PR; existing pods keep running so dashboards stay green, but every subsequent Deployment rollout silently fails at the ReplicaSet level and nobody notices until an unrelated deploy needs to scale during an incident.

A default-deny egress NetworkPolicy ships without a DNS allow rule, so every service resolves nothing, connection errors look like a database outage, and the team spends two hours on the wrong system before someone checks the CNI.

A validating webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail` and no kube-system exemption is deployed, its own pods get evicted during a node rotation, and the cluster can no longer admit any pod — including the webhook's replacement — requiring manual webhook-config deletion via a break-glass credential.

An application pod with no IAM role of its own quietly uses the node instance role via IMDS to read an S3 bucket; it works fine for a year, and the finding only surfaces in an audit after the same path is used to reach a bucket the workload was never meant to see.

Secrets are injected as env vars, the app's unhandled-exception handler ships the full environment to an error-tracking SaaS, and a production database password ends up in a third-party system with a different retention policy and access list.

A Helm chart from an internal platform team ships `automountServiceAccountToken: true` with a ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin 'temporarily for the migration', and it is still there eighteen months later on every install of that chart.
Falco is installed, generates 4,000 alerts a day from a noisy CI namespace, gets muted in Slack within a week, and is therefore silent on the night an actual `Terminal shell in container` fires.

A customer hands you an EKS cluster with one g6e.xlarge node and asks for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for Llama-3.1-8B for 50 internal users by Friday. Walk me through everything from node to first token: what has to be installed, every field in the manifest you would write, how you would expose it, and how you would know it is actually ready for 50 people.

Show me how you would compute the maximum number of concurrent 2,000-token conversations a 48 GB L40S can hold for an 8B GQA model at bf16, then tell me what changes if the customer insists on 32k context. Which two flags would you touch first and what does each cost?

A vLLM pod is stuck Pending with 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' on a node where nvidia-smi on the host shows the card. Give me your ordered diagnostic sequence, the commands, and the three most likely root causes with how you would tell them apart.

GPU utilization is 95% on the DCGM dashboard, but users complain the model is slow and p99 TTFT is 8 seconds. Explain why the utilization number is misleading, which vLLM metrics you would look at instead, and what the likely configuration fix is.

Design the autoscaling for this service. Why is CPU-based HPA wrong, what metric would you scale on, what threshold and cooldown, and how do you handle a 6-minute scale-up latency when a marketing team launches an internal announcement that triples traffic at 9 am?

The security team asks you to run three teams' models on one shared A100 with strong isolation, and the platform team suggests time-slicing. Compare time-slicing, MIG and separate nodes on isolation, utilization and operational risk, and tell me what you would recommend and how you would demonstrate the isolation property.

Streaming responses die at exactly one minute in production only. Debug it out loud: where in the path could a 60-second limit live, how do you prove which hop it is without customer downtime, and what is the fix at each candidate layer?

The customer's platform team upgrades the node kernel during a patch window; the DKMS driver no longer loads, nvidia-smi says 'NVML: Driver/library version mismatch', the device plugin reports 0 GPUs, and the vLLM pod sits Pending with 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' until someone reboots and rebuilds the module.

A rolling update of the vLLM Deployment with default maxSurge schedules a second pod on a cluster with one GPU; the new pod is Pending forever, the old one keeps serving the previous model, and the release 'succeeded' in ArgoCD because the Deployment never reported failure.

--max-model-len was left at the model's 131k default on a 24 GB card; vLLM reserved almost nothing for KV cache, num_preemptions_total climbed under 12 concurrent users, and p99 latency went from 2 s to 40 s while GPU utilization looked fine on the dashboard.

Long RAG answers were truncated mid-stream at exactly 60 seconds in production but not in staging; the difference was an AWS ALB with the default idle timeout in front of production, and vLLM logged nothing because the client, not the server, was disconnected.

The liveness probe used the same 30-second initial delay as a web service; on a cold node the 16 GB weight load took four minutes, kubelet killed the container at 30 seconds every time, and the pod CrashLooped for an hour before anyone read the events.

Time-slicing was enabled to 'share' one A10G between the dev and staging vLLM instances; a staging load test drove CUDA OOM, which also killed the dev replica mid-demo, and nobody could explain to the customer why two isolated namespaces went down together.

The pilot was sized at 50 users against a benchmark run with 128-token prompts and 128-token outputs; real prompts averaged 3k tokens of pasted documents, TTFT p95 was 9 seconds on day one, and the fix required a bigger GPU that had a two-week quota lead time.

A customer has no egress, an internal Harbor nobody has push rights to yet, and a corporate CA that intercepts TLS. Design the delivery end to end: what your build pipeline emits, how bits cross the boundary, how images and charts get relocated, what has to change on the nodes, and how you prove to their security team that nothing phoned home.

Explain tags versus digests in a relocation, and why skopeo copy --preserve-digests matters. What specifically breaks if a digest changes during relocation, and what happens to cosign signatures when you copy an image between registries?

Debug live: pods are in ImagePullBackOff after a relocation to the customer's registry. Walk me through your layers of investigation and the exact command at each layer, and tell me which error string distinguishes a trust problem from a credentials-scope problem from a path-rewrite problem.

A chart has fourteen subcharts and only six honour global.imageRegistry. Give me three mechanisms to force every image reference to the customer's registry, ranked by how much you would want to explain them to their platform team, and say how you would prevent a regression in CI.

Everything works on the host - curl, docker pull, helm - but the Python service inside the pod cannot reach the customer's internal API over HTTPS. Walk me through the diagnosis and the fix, and explain why the host tests were misleading.

How do you ship a security patch into an air gap where transfers happen every four weeks and need approval? Describe the delta bundle, the upgrade and rollback procedure, and what support and version-skew policy you would commit to in writing.

The customer's security officer asks you to prove that your install performed no outbound network access. What evidence do you produce, how do you gather it, and what would you do if the capture showed a single unexpected connection two minutes into the run?

The bundle is built on an Apple Silicon laptop without --all or --override-arch, so every image is linux/arm64; pods on the customer's amd64 nodes crash with 'exec format error' and there is no path to rebuild from inside the enclave.

helm template missed an image injected by a mutating webhook and one Helm hook Job, so 95 percent of the install succeeds and then a single Job sits in ImagePullBackOff reaching for docker.io at 02:00 the night before go-live.

Images were relocated by copying tags only, leaving the sha256-<digest>.sig signature tags behind in the source registry; the customer's policy controller denies every pod at admission and the install looks like an RBAC problem for three hours.

The private CA was added to the host trust store and every host-level curl works, but the application container is distroless with a stale certifi bundle, so only the app's outbound HTTPS calls fail and the team spends a day chasing a phantom network issue.

registries.yaml was edited by hand on the control-plane node during the visit and never added to the node bootstrap; two months later autoscaling adds a worker that cannot pull anything, and nobody on site knows why that node is special.

imagePullPolicy stayed Always with a :latest tag while images were preloaded from tarballs, so the first node reboot after the bundle was deleted from disk turns a working cluster into a cluster that cannot start a single pod.

NO_PROXY omitted .svc, .cluster.local and the pod CIDR, so in-cluster and kubelet traffic was routed to the corporate proxy which rejected it, producing intermittent DNS and API-server timeouts that were escalated as a Kubernetes bug.

Someone unblocked the install with --insecure-skip-tls-verify and strict-ssl=false 'temporarily'; the settings shipped into the runbook, the customer's audit found them six months later, and the deployment was frozen pending remediation.

Walk me through exactly what happens between `terraform plan` and `terraform apply`: what the lock protects against, what 'known after apply' means, why a plan can succeed and the apply fail, and what state looks like after a failed apply.

A customer has a hand-built VPC with six subnets, twelve security groups and an ALB and wants it under Terraform with zero downtime. Design the adoption: how you import, how you prove the plan is clean, what you do about resources whose config cannot be made to match, and what the first production PR contains.

Your PR plan shows `-/+ aws_db_instance.main (forces replacement)` because someone renamed the identifier. The customer cannot take downtime. Give me your options in order of preference and what each does to state.

Design Terraform CI/CD across dev, staging and prod in three AWS accounts. Where do credentials come from, how do you stop a fork PR from exfiltrating them, how do you stop two applies racing on the same state, and where exactly does a human approve?

A nightly drift job started returning exit code 2 every night on an aws_autoscaling_group and nobody changed anything. What is happening, what are three ways to fix it, and which would you choose for a customer whose platform team will own this in six months?

Workspaces versus directory-per-environment versus Terragrunt: pick one for a customer deployment you will hand over, defend it in terms of blast radius and credentials, and tell me what would make you change your mind.

An engineer ran `terraform state push` with a week-old file and now the plan wants to create everything. What do you do in the first fifteen minutes, and what structural change stops it from happening again?

A subnet list built with count gets a new AZ inserted at position 1; the plan replaces two subnets, the apply destroys the ones the customer's RDS subnet group depends on, RDS refuses the change, and state is left half-applied on a Friday evening.

Two engineers apply from laptops against the same S3 backend configured without locking; the second write overwrites the first's state, and the next plan proposes creating 40 resources that already exist, each failing with AlreadyExists.
A workflow uses pull_request_target so plan runs on forks with the apply role; a contributor's PR adds an `external` data source that curls the OIDC token and STS credentials to their server.

The RDS master password and an IAM user's secret key sit in plaintext in state, the state bucket grants s3:GetObject to an engineering-wide role, and the customer's SOC 2 auditor lists it as a finding against your delivery.

A module source pins `ref=main` instead of a tag; a colleague pushes an unrelated change, and the next prod PR's plan shows a NAT gateway replacement nobody asked for, approved by a reviewer who only read the PR description.
Nobody set ignore_changes on the EKS managed node group scaling_config.desired_size; every apply after the cluster autoscaler scales up resets the node count to 2 and evicts customer workloads.

An engineer with AWS_PROFILE pointing at the customer's production account applies the sandbox root because the code is identical and allowed_account_ids was never set; the plan output scrolled past and the prod NAT gateway is gone.

Draw a two-AZ VPC for a web tier, an app tier and Postgres that a bank's security team will accept. For every security group and NACL rule you write, tell me exactly what would happen if I deleted it.

A customer says the app behind your ALB returns 502 intermittently, about 3 percent of requests, only during deploys. Walk me through the investigation from ALB metrics to access logs to target-group settings, and name the two configuration values you expect to change.

Explain what happens at each hop when a browser requests https://app.customer.com served by an internet-facing ALB in front of instances in private subnets: DNS, TLS, the ALB node, the target, and the response path. Where does NAT happen and where does it not?

The customer wants zero internet access from the VPC. List the endpoints you need for an EC2 fleet pulling from ECR, logging to CloudWatch, reached over Session Manager and calling Bedrock. What changes if they also need to call an external SaaS API?

Flow logs show ACCEPT on ingress and REJECT on egress for the same 5-tuple. What is the cause, why does a security group never produce that pattern, and how would you confirm without touching production?

When would you put a Lambda function in a VPC and when would you refuse to? Cover cold starts, ENIs, NAT cost, concurrency, and the failure modes of async invocation against a customer system that is not idempotent.

Our Terraform created an ALB in two subnets, but one AZ shows UnHealthyHostCount equal to HealthyHostCount and the other is fine. Give me three plausible root causes in order of likelihood and the single command or console view that rules each one in or out.

A single NAT gateway in AZ-a serves private subnets in both AZs: AZ-a degrades, every instance in AZ-b loses egress to the model API and package repos, and the 'multi-AZ' pilot goes down with one zone while the customer's dashboard still shows healthy EC2.

The app security group allows tcp/8080 from the ALB subnet CIDRs instead of the ALB's SG ID; a later subnet re-carve or a second ALB in the same subnets silently widens access, and the customer's pen test flags the app port reachable from a jump host.

A custom NACL on the database subnet allows inbound 5432 but the return rule only covers 32768-60999; ALB health checks and NAT-sourced connections using ports below 32768 fail intermittently, half the targets flap unhealthy, and on-call chases a phantom application bug for a day.

The health check path is left at `/` returning 200 from an nginx placeholder while the real app crashed on boot; the target group is green, the ALB happily forwards, and users get 502 from the balancer while every dashboard is healthy.

A Lambda function is attached to the VPC but placed in a subnet whose route table has no NAT route: calls to the Anthropic API hang until the 30 s timeout, the async invocations retry twice with no destination configured, and the customer sees three duplicated webhook side effects hours later.

A data-ingest job reads 20 TB from S3 through the NAT gateway because nobody added the S3 gateway endpoint; the month-end bill has a 900 USD NAT data-processing line, and the customer's FinOps lead asks why your design doc did not mention it.

Someone resolved the ALB DNS name once and put the two IPs into the customer's on-prem firewall allowlist; the ALB scaled and rotated its nodes overnight and the integration went dark, with nothing in your logs because the packets never arrived.

A customer's RDS Postgres orders table was dropped by a bad migration at 14:07 UTC and they noticed at 15:30. Walk me through exactly what you do, in order, what you tell them about RPO before you start, how long it takes on a 500 GB Multi-AZ instance and why, and what the application team must do on their side.

Our Multi-AZ RDS instance failed over last night. AWS's event log shows 75 seconds of failover, but the application had errors for nine minutes. Give me the likely causes, how you would confirm each one, and what you would change so the next failover is invisible.

Design the storage layer for a document-processing pipeline: customers upload files from 1 KB to 2 GB, we extract text and embeddings, users query results, and everything for a customer must be provably deleted 90 days after they leave. Which of RDS, S3, DynamoDB and ElastiCache holds what, where do the keys live, and how do you prove deletion to an auditor?

A customer wants to migrate a 2 TB Postgres orders database to DynamoDB 'for scale'. What are the first five questions you ask, what answers would make you agree, and what answers would make you decline the work?

The S3 bill for a pilot went up four times month over month with no change in stored bytes. Give me your investigation order, the three most likely causes, and the CloudWatch or Cost Explorer evidence that would confirm each.

Compare a Multi-AZ instance, a Multi-AZ DB cluster and a read replica on replication mode, failover time, whether the standby serves reads, and cost. A customer with a read-heavy reporting workload and a 99.95% availability target asks which to buy; what do you recommend and what do you warn them about?

A DynamoDB on-demand table throttles at 3 a.m. during a nightly batch job even though on-demand 'scales automatically'. Explain the mechanism, then give three fixes ranked from least to most effort, and say which one you would ship this week.

The 'tested' backup has never been restored: the first real PITR comes up in the default parameter group and default security group, the app cannot connect, pg_stat_statements is missing, and a promised 15-minute RTO becomes two hours of a customer watching you read documentation.

skip_final_snapshot = true is left in the Terraform module from dev; months later someone renames the identifier or toggles encryption, the plan shows a replace nobody reads carefully, and the production database is destroyed with no snapshot.

A Debezium or DMS task is decommissioned but its logical replication slot is not dropped; WAL is retained, TransactionLogsDiskUsage climbs for weeks, storage autoscaling masks it until max_allocated_storage is hit, and the instance goes storage-full at 2 a.m.

After a Multi-AZ failover AWS reports 90 seconds of downtime but the application errors for nine minutes because the JVM cached the old DNS answer and the connection pool kept handing out dead sockets; the incident is blamed on RDS.

An SSE-KMS bucket with no Bucket Key takes a bulk backfill of small objects; every PUT calls KMS, the account hits the regional KMS request quota, the loader sees throttling it interprets as S3 flakiness, and the KMS line item is larger than the S3 storage line.

A lifecycle rule moves 40 million 8 KB log fragments to Glacier Flexible Retrieval to save money; transition requests, 40 KB per-object overhead and 90-day minimums make the month more expensive than Standard, and the objects the team then deletes are charged for the full minimum anyway.

A multi-tenant DynamoDB table uses tenant_id as the partition key; one tenant is 60% of traffic, the partition caps at 1,000 WCU regardless of on-demand mode, the SDK's retries hide the throttling as p99 latency, and the customer concludes DynamoDB 'does not scale'.

The customer's security team flagged an AWS access key in the environment of the worker we deployed on their EKS cluster. Explain to me, as if I were their CISO, why that is a finding, what you will replace it with, and what evidence you will send them to close the finding.

Walk through IAM evaluation for a request from an IRSA-assumed role in account A reading an object in account B's SSE-KMS bucket. Which documents have to agree, in what order are they evaluated, and where do you look first when it returns AccessDenied?

Design the identity model for a multi-tenant pilot where our control plane in our account reads each customer's S3 data in their account. What do their roles and trust policies look like, what stops customer X's ARN from being used to read customer Y's data, and who generates the ExternalId and why?

A pod on the customer's cluster logs 'Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity'. Give me the ordered checks you run with kubectl and the AWS CLI, and the three most likely root causes in order of frequency.
You inherit a nightly ETL role with AdministratorAccess. How do you shrink it to least privilege without breaking the job, how long does that take, and how do you know when you are done?

Whiteboard the policy for a worker that reads one SQS queue, reads objects under one S3 prefix and one Secrets Manager secret encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Then tell me what is still wrong with it and what you would need from the customer to fix it.

Design CI that deploys into a customer's account with zero stored secrets. Show me the trust policy, tell me which sub condition you choose and why, and describe what an attacker could do if you got it wrong.

A GitHub OIDC trust policy that conditions only on aud, or on sub with repo:org/*: any repository on GitHub (or any repo in the org) can assume the production deploy role, and the first sign is CloudTrail showing AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from a workflow nobody recognises.

The IRSA annotation is added to a ServiceAccount after its pods were created; the webhook only mutates at admission, so half the fleet keeps using the node role, which works because the node role is over-permissioned, and everything breaks six months later when the platform team finally tightens the node role.

EKS nodes run with an IMDS hop limit of 2 for Docker-bridge compatibility, so every pod can read the node role's credentials; one SSRF in one tenant's app becomes cluster-wide access to ECR, autoscaling and every bucket the node role was ever granted.

A worker policy names a Secrets Manager secret by the exact ARN copied from the console; Terraform recreates the secret with a new six-character suffix during a refactor and the worker starts failing with AccessDenied at 03:00 while the secret visibly exists.

A long batch job assumes the customer role through a CI role and requests DurationSeconds 14400; STS rejects it with the one-hour role-chaining limit, so someone 'fixes' it by baking a user key into the job, and the key is still there at the next audit.

The customer's MFA-required deny is written with Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent false; the key is absent on long-term-key requests so the deny never fires, and every IAM user with keys has been bypassing MFA since the policy was written.

A CI role holds iam:PassRole on Resource *; a contributor with push access passes the account's admin role to a throwaway Lambda, invokes it, and has full control of the account without a single access key ever leaving the building.

A customer gives you a VPC with two /24 private subnets and asks you to run a 60-pod application on EKS with room to double. Walk me through the IP budget with real numbers, what breaks first, the two ways you would fix it and what each fix costs in terms of node group changes and cluster downtime.

Explain exactly what happens from the moment a pod annotated for IRSA calls s3:GetObject to the moment it gets a 200: every component, file, environment variable and STS call. Then tell me what changes under EKS Pod Identity, and give me two concrete situations where you would still choose IRSA.

cert-manager's Challenge has been 'pending' for 40 minutes; the TXT record is visible in the Route 53 console. Debug it out loud: what do you look at first, what are the four root causes you would rule out in order, and which one is specific to running inside a VPC with private hosted zones?

Design the ingress and TLS layer for a customer with twelve internal services and three public ones. Compare one ALB per Ingress, a shared ALB via IngressGroup, and an NLB in front of ingress-nginx on cost, blast radius, where private keys live and what happens to a 90-second streaming response on each. What do you recommend and what would change your mind?

A new managed node group is CREATE_FAILED with 'Instances failed to join the kubernetes cluster' and no nodes appear in kubectl. Give me your ordered diagnostic sequence with the exact commands, the five most likely causes, and how you would get onto an instance in a customer account where SSH is forbidden.

Your terraform destroy of an EKS environment has been sitting on the VPC for fifteen minutes. Explain why, list the categories of resources that are almost certainly orphaned, describe the teardown script you would have written to prevent this, and tell me how you would prove to the customer's FinOps team that nothing is still billing.

A customer's cluster enters extended support in three weeks and runs a stateful application with a PodDisruptionBudget. Plan the upgrade end to end: what you check first, the order of control plane, add-ons and node groups, how you handle the PDB, how you know the deprecated API check is clean, and what the cost of doing nothing is per month.

A customer's /24 private subnets were sized for nodes, not pods; the VPC CNI's default WARM_ENI_TARGET pre-allocated a spare ENI's worth of IPs per node, the subnet hit zero free addresses at 40 percent CPU utilisation, and every new pod sat ContainerCreating with 'failed to assign an IP address to container' while the dashboard showed a healthy cluster.
