Someone added a custom launch template to set the root volume size, which silently reset the IMDS hop limit from 1 to 2; a pentest six months later showed any container could curl 169.254.169.254 and walk away with the node role's ECR and CNI permissions.

An IRSA trust policy was written with a StringLike on sub of system:serviceaccount:*:* to 'make it work', so every service account in the cluster could assume the S3 role; the fix required a rotation and an incident write-up because CloudTrail showed a dev namespace had actually used it.

terraform destroy ran for 20 minutes and failed on the VPC because the LB controller's ALB and security group and the CNI's ENIs were not in state; the engineer deleted the cluster manually, the ALB kept serving a dead target group and billing $16 a month for five months before FinOps found it.

The production Let's Encrypt issuer was used while iterating on the Ingress; after the fifth re-issue in a week the duplicate certificate limit tripped and the demo hostname had no certificate for the customer's Monday review because nobody had started with the staging directory.

Two clusters (blue and green) ran external-dns with --policy=sync and the same --txt-owner-id, so the A record for the API flipped between two load balancers every minute and users saw intermittent 503s that no single cluster's logs could explain.

A managed node group update to a new AMI stalled at one node for 15 minutes and failed with PodEvictionFailure because a single-replica Postgres had a PDB with minAvailable 1; the on-call ran it again with --force, which evicted the database mid-write and turned a routine patch into a data recovery.

A cluster quietly crossed into extended support and the control plane line jumped from $73 to $438 a month; the customer's finance team caught it before the platform team did, and the upgrade then had to be done under pressure across two minors with deprecated APIs still in use.

A customer runs a workload on EKS with IRSA, RDS Postgres, S3 and an ALB, and asks you to stand up the same thing on GCP for a newly acquired business unit next quarter. Walk me through the service-by-service mapping, name the three places the analogy is misleading enough to change the design, and tell me what you would warn them about before they commit a date.

Trace a request from one Cloud Run service to another that is deployed with `--no-allow-unauthenticated`: where does the caller get its token, what fields does Cloud Run check, what IAM binding must exist, and how do you distinguish and debug a 401 from a 403? Then describe the equivalent flow between two services on ECS behind IAM-authenticated endpoints.

Design a CI pipeline that deploys the same container to Cloud Run, ECS and Azure Container Apps with zero long-lived credentials. Name the primitive in each cloud, the exact trust condition you would set, and what an attacker who lands code in a fork pull request could and could not do in each.

Dokeo on Cloud Run shows p50 of 40 ms and p99 of 3.5 s and the customer says 'GCP is slow'. Using only Cloud Run metrics and Cloud Logging, how do you prove or disprove that in 20 minutes, what are the four most likely causes, and what is the fix and cost of each?

A customer security lead says 'no public ingress and no service account keys, ever'. Design ingress for Dokeo on Cloud Run for internal employees and for a partner webhook under those constraints, and explain how Domain Restricted Sharing and `run.allowedIngress` interact with your design. What would the same design look like on AWS?

Terraform apply creates a runtime service account and its bindings, and thirty seconds later `gcloud run deploy --service-account` fails with `Permission 'iam.serviceaccounts.actAs' denied`. Give me the two most likely causes, how you would tell them apart, and how you make the pipeline robust to both.

Explain how GCP's allow-policy inheritance, AWS's explicit-deny evaluation and Azure's scope-based role assignments each answer the question 'can this principal read that object?', and describe a permission that is trivial to express in one of the three and awkward or impossible in another.

The image is built on an Apple Silicon laptop without `--platform linux/amd64`; the first Cloud Run revision dies with `exec format error`, the error is buried in the revision log rather than the deploy output, and the team spends an hour rewriting the Dockerfile CMD before anyone checks the architecture.

Dokeo starts uvicorn with its default host `127.0.0.1` and port 8000; Cloud Run's startup probe never connects and the deploy fails with 'container failed to start and listen on the port defined by the PORT environment variable' while the app itself is perfectly healthy in the logs.

Nobody sets `--service-account`, so the service runs as the default compute SA with project Editor; the customer's security review flags it a week before go-live, and the rushed switch to a scoped SA breaks the deploy because no one had listed which secrets, buckets and Cloud SQL instances the app actually reads.

A demo needs a public URL; `--allow-unauthenticated` fails with 'users named in the policy do not belong to a permitted customer' due to Domain Restricted Sharing, and the FDE files for an org-policy exception that takes two weeks instead of fronting the service with a load balancer and IAP or shipping an authenticated client.

A FastAPI endpoint returns 202 and does its work in a `BackgroundTask`; with CPU throttled between requests the task never completes, the customer sees rows stuck in 'processing' only in production, and it takes days to connect the symptom to CPU allocation rather than to the code.

Traffic spikes, Cloud Run scales to its default 100 instances, each with a 10-connection pool, and Cloud SQL rejects with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved`; the fix is `--max-instances`, a smaller pool or a connection proxy, but the first instinct is to resize the database instance.

An engineer 'cleans up' IAM with `google_project_iam_policy` in Terraform; the apply removes the Cloud Build and serverless robot service-agent bindings the customer's platform team had added by hand, every deploy in the project fails for the rest of the day, and the bindings have to be reconstructed from the Cloud Asset Inventory history.

A secret is referenced as `:latest`, the DBA rotates the password in Secret Manager without redeploying, and for the next hour new instances authenticate with the new password while long-lived instances still hold connections on the old one, so failures appear only at scale-out and look like flakiness.

Design the path from `git push` to a pod running in a customer's EKS cluster such that their security team can verify the image was built from a reviewed commit, tested and scanned. Where does each gate live, what identity is carried between stages, and what is enforced at admission rather than in CI?

The pipeline is green but the customer says the fix is not live. Walk me through your debugging in order: which digest was pushed, what the GitOps repo contains, what Argo CD reports, and what `imageID` the pods actually run. Where are the places 'green' can lie?
Why deploy by digest rather than tag? Describe two concrete production failures that mutable tags cause, and how you make the registry itself refuse the mistake.

Your Trivy gate blocks on a HIGH CVE in glibc with no fix available in the base image. The customer wants the release today. What do you do, what do you write down, and how do you prevent the exception becoming permanent?

The customer's policy is no long-lived credentials anywhere. Explain exactly how a GitHub Actions job obtains permission to push to their ECR, what the OIDC `sub` claim looks like, and how you ensure only merges to main in the prod environment can assume the prod role.
All CI runs started failing this morning with a rate-limit error pulling the vulnerability database. What is happening, what is the fix in the next 30 minutes, and what is the durable fix?

A bad release went out through GitOps ten minutes ago. Give me the rollback sequence, the expected time to recovery, what makes it safe to do under pressure, and how you would turn it into a one-click job.

Every pipeline in the org turns red on Monday morning with TOOMANYREQUESTS pulling the Trivy vulnerability DB from ghcr.io, and the team responds by setting `exit-code: 0`, which quietly disables the CVE gate for months.

A `paths` filter or a renamed job means the required 'test' check either reports skipped (treated as passing, so an untested change merges) or never reports at all (so every PR sits pending and someone adds a bypass rule).

A Deployment references a mutable `latest` tag; Argo CD shows Synced and Healthy while two of three pods run last week's image because `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` kept the cached layer, and the customer sees inconsistent behaviour per request.

An ECR lifecycle rule with `tagStatus: any` or an aggressive count expires the digest the live Deployment points at, or deletes cosign's `sha256-*.sig` tags; nothing happens until a node is replaced at 3am, then pods fail ImagePullBackOff or are rejected by Kyverno.

A workflow uses `pull_request_target` and checks out the PR head to 'run the PR's tests with secrets'; a fork PR modifies `conftest.py` to print `$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` or the ECR token, and the customer's registry is writeable by a stranger.

`argocd app sync` returns success and the pipeline goes green, but the new pods crash-loop; Deployment health stays Progressing for the full 600s `progressDeadlineSeconds`, longer than anyone watched, and prod is on the old version while the release notes say otherwise.

The GitOps bump is committed with a departed engineer's PAT; the day their account is deactivated, deploys stop with a 403 in the least-read job of the pipeline, and the on-call spends two hours before finding it.

Here is a Cost Explorer view for a small multi-tenant SaaS: EC2-Other is the second largest line and has grown four times while EC2 instance cost is flat. What is in it, how do you find out, and what are the first two changes you would make?

Cost a small multi-tenant LLM product on EKS plus Multi-AZ RDS at 1, 20 and 500 customers. Which lines scale with tenants, which are steps, where does your model break down, and at what tenant count does a Compute Savings Plan start making sense?

A customer's CFO asks why the pilot costs 900 USD a month when they were told 'a few hundred'. Walk me through the investigation and what you would say in the meeting, including what you would refuse to promise.

Design per-tenant cost attribution for a pooled architecture where tenants share a database, a Kubernetes cluster and one LLM API key. What can you tag, what must you estimate, and how do you make the estimate defensible to a chargeback team?

You are asked to cut infrastructure cost 30 percent without touching reliability on a two-AZ EKS plus Multi-AZ RDS stack. Rank the levers you would consider, and tell me which ones you would refuse and why.
Explain prompt caching and batch pricing to a finance person, then tell me how you decide which traffic goes down each path and how you prove the saving after the fact.
A Savings Plan you recommended shows 60 percent utilisation three months in. What happened, how do you find out, and what do you do about it this quarter?

Cost allocation tags are activated in month two, so the pilot's first invoice cannot be split by tenant; the customer's chargeback team books the whole bill to the sponsoring department and the expansion conversation stalls on 'we do not know what this costs per team'.

Debug logging left on in one pod pushes CloudWatch Logs ingestion to 25 GB a day; logs quietly become the largest line on the invoice, larger than the EKS nodes, and nobody notices until invoice time because the budget was set on total spend rather than per service.

All traffic to S3 and the model API leaves through NAT; at 20 tenants NAT data processing exceeds the gateways and the compute combined, and a free S3 gateway endpoint would have removed a third of it on day one.

A three-year all-upfront RDS Reserved Instance is bought on a db.r6g.large; six months later the workload moves to a different family, the reservation is stranded, and 'unused commitment' appears in every quarterly review with your name on it.

Spot is used for webhook ingestion pods to save 70 percent; a capacity reclaim lands during a customer's bulk import, nodes disappear faster than the two-minute warning is handled, events are duplicated because the idempotency TTL was shorter than the retry window, and the saving is smaller than the one incident's service credit.

A preview environment per pull request is created with Terraform and never destroyed; forty stacks each with a NAT gateway, an ALB and a small RDS run for three months and the 'dev' account spends more than production.

The cost sheet is built in on-demand unblended cost while the customer's finance team reads net amortized in their own Cost Explorer; the two disagree by the Savings Plan and credits, and the FDE is accused of underquoting by 30 percent.

A customer's CISO says the DefenderMate alert dashboard must be 'five nines'. Walk me through the conversation: how you find the number they actually need, what 99.999 would cost on the current architecture, and what you propose instead.

Design the SLIs for an asynchronous pipeline that ingests webhooks, classifies them with a third-party LLM, and updates a dashboard. Where is each measured, what counts as a valid event, and what does an error budget mean when the biggest dependency is a provider you do not control?

Derive burn-rate alerting from first principles: why 14.4, why two windows, what the short window buys you, and what you lose if you only keep the long one. Then tell me how it breaks at ten requests an hour.
Our SLO dashboard shows 100% availability for the past week; the customer reports three outages. Give me every plausible explanation and the specific check that confirms or rules out each one.

The error budget is exhausted ten days into the window and the customer's product owner wants to ship a feature on Friday. What happens, who decides, what does the policy say, and how do you handle it if they overrule you?

A p99 latency alert fires every night at 02:00 and the team has learned to ignore it. Diagnose the alerting-design failure, fix it, and tell me what you would say in the retrospective about why it lasted so long.

You are the only engineer on a customer engagement with a two-person customer ops team. Design an on-call arrangement that is sustainable for a year and explain how you would measure and reduce toil over the first quarter.

The availability SLI is computed from the application's own request counters; during a 40-minute crashloop the pods emit nothing, the ratio has no data, the panel shows 100%, and meanwhile the ingress returned 503 to every request and the customer's SOC missed real alerts.

The latency SLO is 'p95 under 500 ms' but the histogram buckets are 0.1, 0.25, 1 and 2.5 seconds; `histogram_quantile` interpolates between 0.25 and 1 and reports 480 ms while real users see 900 ms, and nobody notices until a customer sends a screen recording.

Kubernetes readiness probes and a synthetic checker make up 35% of requests to the API; they are counted as valid and always succeed, so a 3% real-user error rate shows as 2% and the burn-rate page never reaches its threshold.

A single-window alert of 'error ratio above 0.1% for 10 minutes' fires 30 times a week on normal noise, the team routes it to a muted Slack channel, and a genuine six-hour slow burn that spends 40% of the budget is discovered from a customer email.

Every Grafana panel runs `increase(...[30d])` against raw counters; the dashboard takes 90 seconds to load and shows 'No data' during the very incident review where the customer's director asks how much budget is left.

The error budget policy exists as a document but was never signed by the customer's product owner; when the budget hits zero the release train continues, the number stops meaning anything, and the FDE has no leverage in the next reliability argument.

Weekend traffic drops to ten requests an hour; one failed request is a 10% error ratio, the 5-minute short window trips instantly, and the on-call FDE is paged at 03:00 for a single 500 that the caller retried successfully.

A customer says the trace for a failed request is missing in Tempo while successful ones are present. Walk through every place the decision to drop it could have been made, from SDK sampler to Collector to backend ingestion limits, and how you would confirm or rule out each in under ten minutes.

Design the telemetry for a webhook -> queue -> LLM classifier -> CRM write pipeline running across two services and a Redis queue. Which spans, which SpanKind on each, where exactly do you inject and extract context, which fields go on spans versus metric labels versus logs, and what do you refuse to record and why?

Here is a p99 latency panel showing 45 s while the largest finite bucket is 30 s and the customer insists no request took that long. Explain what histogram_quantile did, how you would fix the bucket layout for a 2-30 s LLM call, and how you would prove the real p99 today without waiting for new data.

A platform team reports Prometheus memory grew four-fold after your service shipped. Name the queries and endpoints you use to find the offending metric and label, then describe the code change and the Collector processor that make it impossible to recur.

Explain head versus tail sampling to a customer's CTO in two minutes, then to their SRE in detail: policies, decision_wait, the horizontal-scaling constraint, and how the spanmetrics connector must be positioned relative to the sampler.

Your SLO says 99.5 percent of HubSpot writes succeed within 5 s over 30 days. Write the SLI expression, the fast and slow burn-rate alert expressions with thresholds and 'for' durations, and argue why the pair beats a single error-ratio threshold on a pager.

The customer runs Datadog, not Grafana, and will not change. Which parts of your OpenTelemetry instrumentation carry over unchanged, what has to change, and how do you argue for OTel-native instrumentation without sounding like you are selling a migration?

Someone puts hubspot_contact_id or the raw request path with ids on a Prometheus label; a week later the customer's shared Prometheus holds two million series, head memory triples, the pod OOMs while replaying the WAL on every restart, and the customer's entire monitoring goes dark, not just yours.

The BatchSpanProcessor is created before gunicorn forks, or the worker exits without provider.shutdown(): spans sit in a dead export thread or an unflushed queue, the trace ends at the webhook's 200, and you spend a day debugging propagation headers when the problem is process lifecycle.

The webhook handler enqueues the job without injecting traceparent into the Redis Stream fields or Kafka headers, so every worker span is a new root; 'one trace from webhook to HubSpot write' is actually three unlinked traces and nobody notices until a customer asks why a write took forty minutes and there is no single trace to show them.

Tail sampling runs on two Collector replicas behind a round-robin Service without the loadbalancing exporter; halves of the same trace land on different instances, the ERROR policy fires on one half only, and Tempo shows truncated traces with missing parents that look exactly like an instrumentation bug.

/health, /ready and /metrics are not in OTEL_PYTHON_EXCLUDED_URLS; with 10 s probes per pod and 15 s scrapes, seventy percent of all spans are probes, the sampling budget is spent on noise, and the customer's Grafana Cloud bill doubles in the first month of the pilot.

A prompt or the raw webhook payload containing names and emails is set as a span attribute 'for debugging' and shipped to a SaaS tracing backend; the customer's DPO finds it during SOC 2 evidence collection and the integration is paused pending legal review.

Alerts are written on causes (CPU above 80 percent, restarts above 3) instead of symptoms; the HubSpot write path returns 429 for six hours with green CPU and zero restarts, 1,400 leads are never written, and the customer learns about it from their sales team on Monday.

The Collector is deployed without memory_limiter and with default resources; the first real traffic burst makes it the first pod OOMKilled, every SDK queue fills and drops, and the incident that caused the burst has no telemetry for exactly the minutes you need to explain it.

A customer says 'we need to know if the system can handle 5,000 concurrent users on Monday.' Turn that into a k6 test plan: which executor, what rate and duration, which thresholds, where the generator runs, and what you will and will not be able to claim from the result.

Your load test shows p99 climbing steeply at 400 rps while CPU on the API pods sits at 35 percent. Walk me through the next ten minutes: what you look at, in what order, and what each of the three most likely causes looks like in the evidence.

Explain coordinated omission to a customer engineer who insists their 50-thread JMeter run proved the system is fine. What would you change in the test, and what do you expect the new numbers to show?

Design the timeout and retry policy for a Temporal activity that writes to a third-party CRM with a p99 of 4 s and occasional 60 s stalls. Cover Start-To-Close, Heartbeat, the retry policy, idempotency, and exactly what happens when the worker pod is killed halfway through.

Kubernetes deletes a pod during a rolling deploy and users see connection resets for about three seconds even though the app handles SIGTERM. Explain the race that causes it and the two changes that eliminate it.

You have one afternoon in a customer's staging cluster to run chaos experiments before a go-live. Which three experiments do you run, what is the steady-state hypothesis for each, how do you control blast radius, and how do you write up the results so their change advisory board accepts them?

Under a spike, would you rather the API degrade uniformly (every request slower) or shed load (some 503s, the rest fast)? Defend your answer for an interactive LLM workflow product and describe how you would implement and prove it.
The load generator ran on the same VPS as the k3s node; CPU contention manufactured a bottleneck at 300 rps that did not exist, and a sprint went into tuning uvicorn for a phantom.

A closed-model test with 20 VUs reported a 180 ms p95 and 'passed'; on go-live morning real users arrived at an open rate, requests piled into the uvicorn backlog, and p95 hit 9 s while the test dashboards were being shown to the customer.

Every request was tagged by its full URL including UUIDs, so k6 and then Prometheus remote-write produced tens of thousands of series, the summary was unreadable, the write endpoint hit cardinality limits, and the one slow endpoint stayed invisible.

The Temporal activity writing to HubSpot had a 2-hour Start-To-Close and no Heartbeat timeout; a node reboot during patching killed the worker and 340 workflows sat 'Running' for two hours, the customer's ops team re-submitted them by hand, and because the activity had no idempotency key HubSpot ended up with duplicate records.

Chaos Mesh went onto a customer cluster without a target-namespace restriction, a fixed-percent PodChaos with a typo in its labelSelector matched every pod including ingress, and the experiment card had no abort condition and no one watching the dashboard.

Client retries with no jitter and no budget turned a 30 s Postgres failover into a 15-minute outage: API pods exhausted their pools retrying, readiness probes that hit the database failed, Kubernetes pulled every pod out of the Service, and the LLM gateway retried on top of it all.

A before/after report showed a 40 percent p95 improvement that was actually a warm cache and a replica count that changed between runs; the fix was reverted in production two weeks later when the regression reappeared, and the report's credibility with the customer went with it.

You are on-site with a customer and their production deployment of your platform starts returning 500s to a third of tenants. Their platform team is on the bridge, their VP joins ten minutes later, and your own engineering team is asleep in another timezone. Walk me through the first fifteen minutes: who is IC, what you say, what commands you run, what you post and where, and what you refuse to do.

Design the severity ladder and paging policy for a multi-tenant LLM classification service with an SLO of 99.9 percent successful webhook deliveries. Which alerts page, which create tickets, how do you avoid 40 notifications for one incident, and what does a single tenant's outage map to?

An incident was caused by a customer engineer running a schema migration in production without a review. Write the root-cause section of the postmortem out loud so that it is honest, blameless, and something their manager will sign. Then tell me the action items and who owns each.

During an incident someone proposes rolling forward with a hotfix rather than rolling back. Under what conditions do you accept that, under what conditions do you overrule it as IC, and how do you handle the fact that the person proposing it is the customer's principal engineer?

Your postmortem shows detection took 45 minutes because the customer noticed before any alert fired. Debug the alerting: what did the existing alerts measure, what should they have measured, how would you structure the new rules in Alertmanager or Grafana, and how would you prove the new alert would have fired for this incident?

The customer's finance team asks for your MTTR for the quarter. Explain why you would push back on a single averaged number, what you would report instead, how it ties to their contractual SLA and exclusions, and how you would present it in one page.

Describe a Temporal or queue-based system in which one bad message or workflow starves everything else. How do you detect it during the incident with the CLI, what is the immediate mitigation, and what retry-policy or error-classification change goes into the postmortem so it does not recur?

Three engineers on the bridge each 'just try something' in production at the same time; one rolls back the deployment while another applies a hotfix, ArgoCD self-heal reverts both, and the postmortem timeline cannot say which change fixed it or when the customer was actually impacted.

The first status-page update says 'a database issue' because someone saw connection errors; the real cause is a certificate that expired on the ingress, the customer's CTO has already forwarded 'database issue' to their board, and the postmortem review spends twenty minutes on the retraction instead of the fix.

The IC is also the strongest debugger, disappears into a terminal for fifteen minutes, nobody posts the 30-minute update, and the customer's engineering manager escalates to the vendor's CEO because the channel went silent.

A responder terminates every 'idle in transaction' backend in `pg_stat_activity` to clear a lock queue, including the logical-replication slot consumer, and the analytics replica falls two hours behind, producing a second incident during the first one.

The postmortem names the customer's junior engineer as having 'run the migration without approval', their manager refuses to sign off, the document is never published, and the same migration pattern causes a repeat outage three months later because no action item was ever created.

Twelve action items are written, none has a due date or ticket, all are 'add alert for X', and at the monthly review nine are still open; the customer concludes the vendor treats postmortems as paperwork.

A Kaupex activity with an unbounded retry policy fails forever against a decommissioned downstream API, the retries consume the entire task queue's worker capacity, and the team scales the worker pool from 4 to 40 pods before anyone runs `temporal workflow describe` and sees the single failing activity.

A customer wants 99.99% availability for an application that hard-depends on their SSO provider at 99.9% and on our LLM API at 99.9%. What do you tell them, what would you change in the design to get closer, and what number do you actually write into the SOW?

Design DR for a self-hosted Postgres plus a Kubernetes API tier with a 30-minute RTO and a 5-minute RPO across two regions, on a budget that rules out a hot standby. What replicates continuously, what stays cold, what must already exist in the DR region, and how do you prove the numbers to the customer?

Your restore drill came in at three hours against a one-hour objective. Walk me through how you break down where the time went, which phases are fixable with configuration versus architecture, and what you would ship this week.

A primary's pg_wal directory has grown to 400 GB and the disk is at 98%. Give me the candidate causes, how you confirm each in under a minute with pg_stat_archiver and pg_replication_slots, and the sequence of actions that recovers the disk without losing the ability to restore.

Should failover of a database-backed service between regions be automatic? Argue both positions, then tell me what you would actually build for a payments customer and how the switch would be implemented and protected.

A security questionnaire asks whether a compromised production admin credential could destroy your backups. Design the answer you want to give, name the controls behind each clause, and describe the test that proves it.

Compare a Multi-AZ standby, a cross-region read replica, continuous WAL archiving and a nightly snapshot: which failures does each recover from, what are their RTO and RPO, and in what scenario is the nightly snapshot the only thing that saves you?

The team says 'we have HA' because there is a Multi-AZ standby and two read replicas, then a migration runs DROP TABLE orders and every replica applies it within a second; with no WAL archive, the only recovery point is last night's pg_dump and the RPO is 20 hours.

archive_command has been failing for five weeks since the object-storage credentials rotated, pg_stat_archiver.failed_count is in the thousands and nobody alerted on it, pg_wal fills the disk and crashes the primary, and the 'backups' turn out to be unrestorable because the WAL chain has a gap.

The DR runbook restores an encrypted snapshot into the recovery account, which has no grant on the production KMS key; the restore fails with a KMS access error, the key admin is on holiday, and a 30-minute RTO becomes a day of support tickets.

A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 1 sits on a single-replica StatefulSet; the managed node-group upgrade stalls for hours, the on-call force-deletes the pod to unblock it, and the only instance of the service goes down during the change window.

Automatic DNS failover flips traffic to the DR region during a 40-second primary blip; both regions accept writes for six minutes before anyone notices, and failback needs a manual reconciliation of orders that the customer's finance team has to sign off on.

A 'multi-AZ' Kubernetes cluster runs Postgres as a StatefulSet with an EBS volume in one zone; when that zone is impaired the pod stays Pending forever because the volume cannot move, and the customer discovers their database was single-AZ all along.

The DR plan is a Confluence page last edited eighteen months ago; it references a deprecated CLI flag, a Terraform workspace that no longer exists and an engineer who left, so the real RTO is the time it takes to rediscover the system under pressure.

Design the preflight and support-bundle pair for shipping our product into a bank's air-gapped OpenShift cluster. What do you check before install, what do you collect after a failure, what do you deliberately refuse to collect, and how do you get the bundle out of the building?

A customer emails 'the classifier is down' and attaches a 4 GB support bundle. Walk me through your first fifteen minutes: what you open, in what order, and what you would say in the first customer reply.

Explain the preflight exit-code contract and how you would wire it into a Helm-based install so a FAIL blocks the release but a WARN does not. What is your policy for upgrades, and what is the escape hatch when the customer must upgrade during an outage?

How do you convince a CISO that a support bundle is safe to send? Describe the redaction mechanisms, how you verify them, what redaction fundamentally cannot protect against, and what you offer when the answer is still no.

Debug this: `analysis.json` says every check passed, but the customer's dashboard is empty and their users are complaining. Give me the three most likely reasons the bundle is lying to you and how you would distinguish them.
You cannot reproduce the issue, and change control means one more bundle in 48 hours. How do you spend that single request? Write me the message you send the customer's admin.

How do you decide what belongs in a support bundle in the first place, and how does that set change over the life of an account? What would you measure to know your support surface is actually improving?

The support-bundle spec uses `runPod` with `alpine:3`; in the customer's air-gapped cluster the image cannot be pulled, the collector writes an error file instead of data, and the one directory you needed is empty after a two-day change-control round trip.

The `logs` collector caps at `maxLines: 10000` and the classifier logs 400 lines a second, so the bundle contains the last four minutes and the panic that started the outage forty minutes earlier is gone forever, because the node rotated it too.

Redactors cover connection strings but not alert payloads, so the bundle carries customer hostnames, usernames and email addresses from LLM prompts into your ticketing system, and a support ticket becomes a notifiable data incident under the DPA.

The node-sizing check was written as a `warn` rather than a `fail` because someone wanted the pilot to install cleanly; the customer runs on 4 GiB nodes, the classifier starts OOMKilling under real alert volume three weeks later, and the preflight output has already scrolled out of anyone's terminal.

Preflights run only on install, never on upgrade; the customer moves their cluster to a newer Kubernetes minor on their own schedule, a removed API version stops the chart rendering, and the first signal is a failed ArgoCD sync at 01:00 in a region with no on-call.

The customer's admin runs the bundle with a ServiceAccount that cannot read Secrets or nodes; several collectors fail partially, the analyzers see no evidence of a problem, and `analysis.json` reports all-clear on a cluster that is actively broken.

Node clocks drift because NTP is blocked outbound and one component logs in local time with no offset; the reconstructed timeline puts the webhook after the database error, the wrong service is blamed, and two days of engineering go into a component that was healthy.

The 6 GB bundle bounces off the mail gateway, so the admin uploads it to a public file-sharing link with no expiry; it contains an unredacted Postgres URI, and the remediation is a customer-side credential rotation plus a security review of your entire support process.

You inherit a 4,000-line Python service where the SQLAlchemy models are the domain model and business rules live in the route handlers; the customer needs a batch CLI over the same logic next sprint and will not accept a feature freeze. Walk me through the restructure in the order you would actually commit it, how you keep every commit shippable, and what evidence you show the customer that nothing regressed.

Explain Repository and Unit of Work as you would implement them in Python, then tell me when they are overkill. Where do you draw the line differently for a two-week FDE pilot versus a system you are handing to the customer's platform team, and what is the cheapest version that still lets you swap the database?

Pick Protocol or ABC for the port to an LLM provider that a customer might implement themselves, and defend it. How does mypy verify that their adapter conforms, where exactly does that check happen, and what happens at runtime if their class is missing a method?

Debug this: after your deploy, workers intermittently raise `DetachedInstanceError`, and the customer's DBA shows you 200 Postgres connections in `idle in transaction`. Which layer is the bug most likely in, what is your hypothesis about the code shape that causes it, and what change fixes it structurally rather than by raising `max_connections`?

Two Temporal workers can compile the same task concurrently. Design the persistence so that a lost update is impossible: optimistic versus pessimistic locking, where the version check lives in the layered architecture, how the conflict surfaces to the caller, and the exact test you would write to prove it.

A customer runs the same service in two environments with different secret stores (AWS Secrets Manager in one, HashiCorp Vault in the other) and different model providers. Show me how settings and the composition root make that a one-file change per environment, what you validate at process start, and what you deliberately defer to first use.

Walk me through how you package a Python service so a customer engineer can install, run and extend it without you: what is in pyproject.toml, what the lockfile is a contract for, how a console script and an entry-point plugin work, and how the Dockerfile is structured so a dependency change does not rebuild the source layer.

Pydantic models are used as the domain model and the ORM model at once: an API field rename for one customer forces a migration and a domain change, `extra="forbid"` starts rejecting rows with legacy columns, and profiling shows a third of compile-loop CPU in validators that re-check data already validated at the boundary.

A SQLAlchemy session is opened at module import or held open across a 20-second LLM call: Postgres fills with `idle in transaction` connections, `pg_stat_activity` shows the pool exhausted, autovacuum cannot clean the tables those transactions pin, and the first symptom the customer sees is `DetachedInstanceError` and timeouts three days later.

`client = anthropic.Anthropic()` at module scope reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` at import time: tests cannot inject a fake, the second tenant onboarded reuses the first tenant's key, and when gunicorn preloads the app the forked workers share one HTTP connection pool and start failing with SSL errors under load.

A circular import that only manifests through the CLI entrypoint's import order ships to production because the test suite imported modules in a different order; the container crash-loops with `ImportError: cannot import name ... (most likely due to a circular import)` and nobody can reproduce it locally until they run `python -m kaupex`.

No lockfile is committed and the Dockerfile runs `pip install -r requirements.txt` with lower bounds only: the customer rebuilds the image six weeks later, pulls a new pydantic or SQLAlchemy minor, and the service fails at startup with changed validation semantics while the FDE who wrote it is on another engagement.

The repository accumulates forty ad hoc query methods, then a developer bypasses it with a raw `session.execute(select(...))` in the service layer 'just this once'; within a quarter every service test needs Postgres, the suite takes fifteen minutes, engineers stop running it locally, and regressions reach the customer.

Business rules live in the FastAPI route handler and are duplicated into a Temporal activity when the customer asks for batch mode; the two copies drift, the batch path skips a validation the API enforces, and a month of compiled tasks has to be re-run after the customer's audit finds the inconsistency.

Kaupex p99 latency triples every weekday at 09:00 while CPU sits at 15% and the database is idle. Walk me through diagnosis on a running pod with only `kubectl exec`, `py-spy` and the uvicorn logs: what are your top three hypotheses, and how does each one show up?

Design settings and secrets handling for a FastAPI service a customer will run in three places: a developer laptop, a staging namespace, and an air-gapped production cluster where secrets arrive as mounted files. What is the precedence order, how does a wrong value fail, and how do tests override it?

We are moving from 3 replicas with `--workers 4` to 12 replicas with one worker each on the customer's EKS cluster. What changes for connection pools, metrics scraping, probes, memory and graceful shutdown, and what would you set differently in each place?

A rolling deploy produces about eight seconds of 502s at the ingress each time a pod terminates, yet the application logs show every request completed with 200. Explain the race, the two fixes, and how you would prove which one closed it.

When would you reach for `BackgroundTasks`, a Temporal workflow, or a Redis stream for work that happens after the request returns? Give a concrete example of each and the failure the wrong choice produces in production.

Compare `--limit-concurrency`, the anyio thread limiter, the SQLAlchemy pool size and the load balancer's connection limit as load-shedding points. Under sustained overload, which one do you want to trip first, and why?

A customer's security team insists on `BaseHTTPMiddleware` to audit every request and response body. Explain what that does to streaming LLM responses and background tasks, and propose a pure-ASGI design that still satisfies the audit requirement.

An `async def` handler calls the sync OpenAI client for a 20 s completion; one slow prompt from one tenant freezes the worker's event loop, readiness probes time out at their 1 s default, kubelet restarts pods in rotation, and the customer reports that 'the API dies every morning at nine'.

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is left at 30 while `--timeout-graceful-shutdown` is unset and compile requests take 45 s; every rolling deploy SIGKILLs in-flight compilations, clients see connection resets, and their retries double the load on the freshly started pods.

uvicorn's default `--timeout-keep-alive 5` sits behind an ALB with a 60 s idle timeout; the ALB reuses a connection uvicorn closed a millisecond earlier and roughly 0.1% of requests return 502 with nothing in the application logs, which takes a week to attribute.

`pool_size=5, max_overflow=10` with `--workers 4` across six replicas plus Temporal workers exceeds RDS `max_connections` on a db.t3.medium; Postgres refuses with `FATAL: too many connections`, and because readiness checks the DB, every pod leaves service at the same moment.

A yield dependency commits after the response is sent under the default `scope="request"`; the commit fails on a unique-constraint violation, the client already received 201, and the 'created' task never exists, surfacing weeks later as a phantom-ID support ticket.

Shell-form `CMD uvicorn ...` in the Dockerfile means SIGTERM reaches `/bin/sh`, not uvicorn; every stop waits the full grace period then SIGKILLs, lifespan teardown never runs, and httpx connections and PgBouncer server slots leak until `server_idle_timeout` reaps them.

`BackgroundTasks` is used to send the customer's job-complete webhook; an OOM kill between the 200 and the task loses the callback, their system waits forever, and there is no queue to inspect because the work only ever existed in one process's memory.

A customer's security reviewer asks why your confidential backend uses PKCE when it already authenticates with a client secret. Explain the authorization-code injection attack, what `state` and `nonce` already cover, and what PKCE adds on top.

DefenderMate will be sold to 30 customers, each with their own IdP: Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace and one on-prem ADFS that only speaks SAML. Design login and tenant-claim handling. Compare trusting 30 issuers directly with brokering through your own IdP on `sub` stability, key rotation, JIT provisioning, offboarding, and blast radius when one customer's IdP is compromised.

After a Keycloak upgrade, about 3 percent of API calls return 401 for ten minutes every six hours and then recover on their own. Walk me through the diagnosis: what you look at in the token, in the API logs and in the IdP, and what the fix is.

Your API is stateless and validates JWTs locally. The customer's compliance team requires that a terminated employee loses access within 60 seconds. What do you change, what does each change cost in latency and operational complexity, and where do you refuse to go?

A user belongs to three tenants. Design the claim shape and the API contract for choosing the active tenant so that no client can escalate into a tenant it is not a member of. Where does the check live, what do you return on mismatch (403 or 404) and why, and how does this survive into background jobs?

A frontend developer is sending the ID token to your API 'because it has the user's email in it' and it works in dev. Explain what is wrong, what breaks first in production, and the fix on both the Keycloak side and the client side.

A pentest report says 'JWT accepted with alg=HS256 signed with the server's public key'. Explain the vulnerability class, how a verifier ends up vulnerable, and the exact code and configuration that make it impossible; then name the other two JWT header fields you also refuse to honour.

Keycloak behind the customer's ALB mints tokens with `iss` = `http://keycloak:8080/realms/prod` because `KC_HOSTNAME` and `KC_PROXY_HEADERS` were never set; every token fails the API's issuer check after the go-live DNS cutover, and the on-call 'fix' is to remove `issuer=` from `jwt.decode`, which stays in production for a year.

The API validates signature and `exp` but not `aud` because Keycloak's default token says `aud: account` and nobody added the Audience mapper; a token minted for the customer's internal wiki client in the same realm is accepted by DefenderMate's API and a contractor with wiki access lists alert data.

`tenant_id` is read from an `X-Tenant-Id` header 'because the frontend already sends it' and the token claim is never compared; the customer's pentest changes the header and reads another tenant's HubSpot write history, which is a breach notification and a renewal conversation, not a bug.

The IdP rotates its signing key on the first Sunday of the quarter; the API fetched JWKS once at startup with no refetch on unknown `kid`, so every pod returns 401 at 03:00 until someone restarts the deployment, and the incident is misdiagnosed as an IdP outage for 40 minutes.

A Temporal workflow stores the analyst's access token in its input so an activity can call the API 40 minutes later; it is expired, so the realm's Access Token Lifespan is bumped to 24 hours to make the demo work, and every leaked token is now a day-long credential.

The local user table is keyed on email; the customer's Okta admin changes an employee's address during a domain migration, JIT provisioning creates a second account, the old one keeps `tenant_admin`, and the audit trail for a disputed reclassification is split across two identities nobody can reconcile.

Full group paths and every client role are mapped into the access token and the BFF stores the whole token in the session cookie; for the customer's IT director, who is in 60 groups, the cookie exceeds 4096 bytes, the browser drops it, and only that one person is stuck in a login loop, on demo day.

Walk me through everything that happens between `node dist/main.js` and the first `tools/call` response of an MCP client: module resolution, the initialize handshake, transport framing, and where each class of failure would surface and how you would recognise it.

A customer's Node service handles 200 requests per second comfortably, then p99 jumps to three seconds whenever one specific report endpoint is hit, with nothing in the logs. How do you find the cause, what are the three most likely culprits, and what is the fix for each?

Design the type layer for a client that calls twelve MCP tools whose schemas are owned by another team. Where do types come from, where exactly do you validate at runtime, and what fails in CI on the day they change a schema without telling you?

Explain the difference between `Promise.race` against a timeout promise and `AbortSignal.timeout` passed into `fetch`. What leaks in the first approach, and how would you cancel a chain of three dependent async calls when the user closes the tab?

We have a mixed codebase with `require` in some files and `import` in others, and the build intermittently fails with `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`. What are the realistic options, and what would you recommend for a team that publishes a library consumed by both CommonJS and ESM customers?

You are handed a TypeScript service with `strict: false` and roughly four hundred `any`s, and the customer wants it hardened in two weeks without pausing feature work. What sequence of compiler flags and lint rules do you introduce, in what order, and how do you keep the team from reverting them?

How would you drain a Node HTTP server in Kubernetes behind an ALB so a rolling deploy produces zero 502s? Name every timeout that has to be ordered, the order, and how you would verify it before telling the customer it is safe.

The service passes every type check but crashes nightly with `ERR_UNHANDLED_REJECTION` because one `client.callTool()` inside an event handler was never awaited; `no-floating-promises` would have flagged it on the first commit.

An MCP server prints a `console.log` startup banner to stdout; the client's JSON-RPC parser hits `Starting DefenderMate...` as its first line, throws, and every tool call fails with an opaque parse error while the server process looks perfectly healthy.

The TypeScript client was generated from `/openapi.json` once in March; the backend made `tenant_id` required in June, the client kept sending `undefined`, and the resulting 422s were swallowed by a `catch (e) { console.error(e) }` for six weeks.

Behind an ALB with a 60 s idle timeout, `server.keepAliveTimeout` is left at Node's 5 s default, so the ALB reuses sockets Node has already closed and the customer sees intermittent 502s that never reproduce in a load test against the pod directly.

`JSON.parse` on a 40 MB tool result blocks the event loop for 800 ms, every concurrent SSE stream stalls, the liveness probe times out, and Kubernetes restarts the pod in the middle of the executive demo.

Results are validated with Zod's default strip mode, so the server's new `warnings` field is silently dropped and nobody notices for a month that the model is no longer being told when a scan returned degraded data.

CI runs `npm install` instead of `npm ci`, resolves a fresh transitive MCP SDK version with a protocol bump, and the handshake fails only in staging because every developer machine still has the old lockfile-resolved tree.

Here is an EXPLAIN ANALYZE: a Nested Loop whose outer Seq Scan was estimated at rows=1 and produced rows=48000, with an inner Index Scan showing loops=48000. Explain why the planner chose this, what you would check in pg_stats, and give three fixes ranked from least to most invasive with the risk of each.

A customer's multi-tenant SaaS has three tenants holding 70% of the rows and two thousand small ones; the same endpoint is 20 ms for small tenants and times out for the big three. Walk me through your diagnosis, covering plan caching and generic plans, statistics targets, partial indexes and partitioning, and tell me what you would actually ship this week and what you would defer.

Design the migration that adds a NOT NULL column with a default, a foreign key to accounts, and a unique index on (tenant_id, external_id) to a two-billion-row table on RDS with no maintenance window. For each step name the lock mode, whether it scans or rewrites, where it can fail, and how your migration runner recovers.

Explain MVCC as Postgres implements it: what an UPDATE physically does, what a HOT update is and what defeats it, how a forgotten idle-in-transaction connection or a replica with hot_standby_feedback causes bloat, and the four numbers you would put on a dashboard to catch it early.

Twenty workers pull jobs from a jobs table. Write the dequeue SQL that is correct under concurrency, explain the lock semantics that make it correct, and then describe what changes if each job triggers a non-idempotent external API call and the process can die between the call and the commit.

When would you choose SERIALIZABLE over explicit row locks, and when the reverse? Describe SSI briefly, the 40001 retry contract that the application must honour, the throughput cost, and give one concrete case for each choice from a system you have built.

A query on a customer database got 100x slower overnight with no deploy and no schema change. Give the first five catalog queries you would run, what each one would tell you, and the three most likely root causes in order of probability.

A 500M-row events table keeps the default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor of 0.2 while a nightly analytics job holds a transaction open for six hours; vacuum cannot clear anything behind that backend_xmin, the table reaches 3x bloat, every Index Only Scan reports thousands of Heap Fetches, p99 climbs weekly and the customer's response is to buy a larger instance.

The ORM emits WHERE lower(email) = lower($1) against a table with a plain B-tree on email; the plan is a 20M-row Seq Scan with Rows Removed by Filter, login p95 hits four seconds, and the fix nobody found for a month is a single expression index on lower(email).

A deploy runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ... without lock_timeout; it queues for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind a 20-minute report SELECT, every subsequent SELECT on orders queues behind the ALTER, the connection pool saturates and the entire application freezes until someone finds the head of the chain with pg_blocking_pids() and terminates it.

A migration script runs CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction on a 200M-row table, holding a SHARE lock that blocks all writes for 40 minutes; the follow-up attempt with CONCURRENTLY is cancelled by a timeout and leaves an INVALID index that is maintained on every write and used by nothing, silently taxing the table for the next year.

PgBouncer in transaction mode sits in front of a FastAPI service whose driver caches prepared statements; the app throws intermittent 'prepared statement "__asyncpg_stmt_12__" does not exist' errors only under load, the team blames the database, and the fix is statement_cache_size=0 or PgBouncer 1.21 with max_prepared_statements.

A job queue uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE LIMIT 1 without SKIP LOCKED, so twenty workers serialise on the first locked row and throughput equals one worker; when someone adds SKIP LOCKED but keeps a composite index ordered (created_at, tenant_id) the queue is fast for small tenants and scans the whole index range for the largest one because the equality column is not leading.

A prepared statement with a tenant_id parameter switches to the generic plan after five executions; the plan chosen for typical 2000-row tenants is a Nested Loop that runs 600000 times for the tenant holding 60% of the data, that one customer times out every hour, and no one connects it to plan_cache_mode because the query is fast every time they run it by hand with a literal.

A regulated customer wants to run our multi-tenant AI product but their security team says shared tables are unacceptable. Walk me through how you decide between arguing for pooled tables with RLS, moving them to a dedicated schema or database, and what evidence you bring to the meeting to change their mind or to concede gracefully.

Explain how a Postgres row-level security policy is actually evaluated inside a query, what USING versus WITH CHECK protect, how permissive and restrictive policies combine, and give me a concrete case where a correct-looking policy still leaks data.

We run the API behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode and set the tenant with `SET app.tenant_id` at the start of each request. Production shows occasional cross-tenant reads that never reproduce in staging. Debug it out loud, then tell me the fix and the test that proves the fix.

Design the encryption story for PII in a system where customers must be able to search by email, we must honour erasure requests within 30 days, and we keep 35 days of backups. Which layer encrypts what, where do the keys live, how does lookup work, and what exactly happens on an erasure request?

After enabling RLS, a dashboard query went from 40 ms to 6 seconds. The policy is `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid` and the query filters on a user-defined function. What is happening in the planner, and how do you fix it without weakening the policy?

Design an append-only audit trail for a multi-tenant system that a SOC 2 auditor will accept. How do you make it immutable when the table owner can always drop a trigger, what do you deliberately keep out of it, and how would you prove to the auditor that nothing was deleted last quarter?

Our RAG pipeline stores document chunks and embeddings in pgvector. A customer asks whether another tenant could ever see their documents in a model answer. Give me the complete answer: the retrieval query, the storage model, the tests, and the residual risk you would disclose.

A support tool needed read-all-tenants access, so an engineer added a second PERMISSIVE policy `USING (true) TO app_user` instead of a separate role; because permissive policies are ORed, every API request could read every tenant, and it was found by a customer who saw another company's name in an autocomplete dropdown.

RLS was enabled but never FORCED, and the API connected as the table owner because the Terraform module reused the migration credentials; RLS applied to nobody for eight months and the first indication was a penetration tester swapping a UUID in a URL.

Session-level `SET app.tenant_id` behind PgBouncer in transaction mode: under load, connections were reused mid-request and roughly one in 400 requests ran as the previous request's tenant, surfacing as 'random' data-corruption tickets nobody could reproduce in staging, which had no pooler.

The pgvector table for RAG had no `tenant_id` column because it was created from a notebook, so nearest-neighbour retrieval pulled another tenant's contract clauses into a prompt; the model summarised them fluently and the leak was only visible in the LLM trace store weeks later.

pgcrypto keys were interpolated as string literals by the ORM, so every encryption key sat in `pg_stat_statements`, the slow-query log and the APM tool's query capture, meaning the column encryption protected against nothing the volume encryption did not already cover.

The audit trigger logged `to_jsonb(NEW)` for the users table including plaintext PII columns, so the audit log became the largest unencrypted copy of customer data in the system and was excluded from the encryption review because 'it's just logs'.

A GDPR erasure request was fulfilled with `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ...` while the audit log, the embeddings table and 35 days of PITR backups still held the data; the DPO found out when the same person's name appeared in a support search a month later.

Design a rate limiter for a multi-tenant LLM gateway where tenants have both a requests-per-second burst limit and a tokens-per-day budget. Where does the state live, how do you keep the check atomic, what happens on Redis failover, and what do you return to the client?

A customer says their idempotency layer 'works' because they check Redis for the key before processing. Walk me through three ways it still produces duplicates and how you would fix each without a rewrite.

We see p99 latency spikes across all tenants every few minutes on an otherwise healthy Redis. Take me through your diagnosis: which commands you run, what you expect to see, and the three most likely root causes.

Compare Redis Streams with consumer groups to Kafka for a webhook ingestion pipeline handling 2,000 events per second with strict no-loss requirements. When would you accept Streams, and what specifically would you configure and monitor to make it safe?

Explain what happens to the data when a Redis node with `appendfsync everysec` and one async replica loses power. Now the same for RDB only. Which of your four workloads (cache, limiter, idempotency, stream) is acceptable under each, and why?

A Lua token-bucket script is running fine in one environment and returning `NOSCRIPT` intermittently in another. What is going on, what are two fixes, and which one would you ship to a customer on ElastiCache?

You inherit a customer's ElastiCache cluster running `volatile-lru` with `maxmemory` at 90 percent of RAM and a mix of cache and session data. What is wrong, what breaks first, and how do you migrate to a safe configuration with zero downtime?

A limiter written as `INCR` then `EXPIRE` times out between the two commands during a Redis blip; the counter key has no TTL, and one tenant is rate-limited to zero until someone runs `TTL` on the key three days later.

Cache and idempotency keys share one ElastiCache node with `allkeys-lru`; a marketing campaign fills the cache, dedup keys are evicted, Stripe retries a payment webhook, and the customer's ledger shows duplicate invoices that nobody connects to Redis.

A webhook stream is written with `XADD key *` and no `MAXLEN`; three weeks later the instance hits `maxmemory` with `noeviction`, every `SET` in the API returns `OOM command not allowed`, and the whole product goes down because a log was never trimmed.

A consumer group is deployed with random consumer names per pod restart and no XAUTOCLAIM loop; after a rolling deploy, thousands of entries sit in the pending list owned by consumers that no longer exist and are never processed.

An idempotency layer relies on Redis alone; Multi-AZ failover promotes a replica missing the last two seconds of writes, the client's retry re-executes, and two payouts are created because there was no unique index in Postgres behind the fast path.

A lock is released with a plain `DEL` after a slow LLM call ran past the 30 second lease; the DEL removes the next worker's lock, three workers process the same batch concurrently, and the bug reproduces only under load.

redis-py is constructed with default `socket_timeout=None` and three retries; when the instance stalls on a `BGSAVE` fork under memory pressure, every API worker blocks on Redis, the connection pool drains, and a 400 ms cache hiccup becomes a five minute total outage of the customer's API.

We stream LLM tokens over SSE and a customer reports 'the whole answer appears at once after ten seconds' only in their production environment. Walk me through how you would localise the buffering hop and what you would change at each candidate.

Design resumable streaming for a chat product running on 8 pods behind a load balancer. What do you store, where, with what retention, and what happens when a client reconnects with an event ID that has already been trimmed?
Why would you choose Redis Streams over Redis Pub/Sub for fan-out of a generation to multiple viewers, and when would Pub/Sub actually be the better choice?

A WebSocket-based agent console shows a spike of close code 1006 every day at 03:00. What are the three most likely causes, in what order would you check them, and what would you add so the incident is self-explanatory next time?

Explain backpressure in an SSE relay: name every buffer between the Anthropic API and the user's screen, and for a consumer that reads at 1 KB/s tell me exactly which one fills first and what your code does about it.

You need to load test a streaming endpoint before a go-live. Which metrics do you define, how do you generate realistic load for SSE given k6 buffers HTTP bodies, and how do you decide the concurrency number you will commit to in the customer's SLA?

EventSource cannot send an Authorization header. Give me two production-safe ways to authenticate an SSE connection for an enterprise customer with an SSO-issued JWT, and the security trade-off of each.

The customer's Nginx had `proxy_buffering on` (the default): tokens arrived in one 4 KB burst after several seconds, the product team concluded 'streaming does not work' and the fix was a single `X-Accel-Buffering: no` header.
ALB idle timeout at the default 60s closed every answer longer than a minute with a 1006 on the client; no heartbeat was being sent because the dev environment had no load balancer.

Generation kept running after the user closed the tab because the handler never checked `is_disconnected()`; the customer's Anthropic bill showed 30 percent of output tokens were never delivered to anyone.
Session state lived in a module-level dict; after scaling to 3 pods, one in three reconnects returned 'unknown session' and support blamed the browser.
A dashboard that broadcast one agent run to 40 viewers used an unbounded per-viewer list; one viewer on a hotel Wi-Fi made the pod OOM and took down the other 39.

A rolling deploy sent SIGTERM with a 30s grace period while streams ran for 90s; clients received an abrupt close with no `retry:` or resume, and the resulting duplicate requests doubled load on the new pods.
A stream token was passed as `?token=` with a 24-hour lifetime; it appeared in the customer's ALB access logs shipped to a third-party SIEM, triggering a security review that stalled the rollout.

A customer's architect insists on Kafka for a pilot that ingests about 5,000 documents a day from a SaaS webhook into our product. Walk me through how you decide, what you propose instead if you disagree, how you make that case without losing the room, and what facts would change your mind.

Define exactly-once in Kafka precisely: which components participate, which configs enable it, and where the boundary of the guarantee sits. Then our consumer writes to Postgres and calls a third-party REST API for every event; design effectively-once end to end and name what is still not guaranteed.

Debug this: lag on a single partition grows without bound while other partitions are healthy, consumer CPU is low, and the logs show repeated 'Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing'. Talk me through your hypotheses, what you check in what order, and the fix.

Design multi-tenant event ingestion for an AI product where tenants differ 100x in volume, per-document ordering matters, and one tenant's replay must never starve another. Topics per tenant or a shared topic keyed by tenant? Partition count, quotas, ACLs, and how the answer changes at 10 tenants versus 2,000.

A service writes an order row to Postgres and then publishes to Kafka. Sometimes there is a row and no event, sometimes an event and no row. Fix it, then compare the two relay implementations for the outbox (polling versus WAL-based CDC) on latency, load, failure modes and what happens when the relay is down for a day.

We need to add a field now and rename another field next quarter in an event schema consumed by four teams we do not control. Which compatibility mode do you set, what is the rollout order for producers and consumers, and what exactly breaks if you get the order wrong?

Configure a topic for durability at a customer who cannot lose a single event: replication factor, `min.insync.replicas`, `acks`, unclean leader election, rack placement. For each single- and double-broker failure, tell me precisely what the customer experiences and what, if anything, they lose.

A new consumer service shipped with the default `auto.offset.reset=latest`; because the group had no committed offset it skipped the entire backlog produced before its first deploy, and nobody noticed until a monthly reconciliation found 40,000 documents that were never embedded.

Each record triggered an LLM call with client-side retries, so a batch took longer than `max.poll.interval.ms`; the consumer was evicted, its partitions moved to a peer that reprocessed the same batch and was also evicted, producing a rebalance storm where lag climbed for hours while CPU sat near zero.

One malformed message from an upstream team made the deserialiser throw before `poll()` returned; the consumer crash-looped on the same offset for six hours and the fix (catch, publish to a DLQ with the offset in headers, commit) took ten minutes once someone looked at the offset in the logs.

Someone added partitions to a keyed topic to 'increase throughput'; murmur2 now mapped the same `document_id` to a different partition, the stateful downstream consumer saw updates out of order, and its last-write-wins logic reverted several documents to stale versions before anyone connected the two events.

A team turned on transactions and told the customer the pipeline was exactly-once, but the consumer also POSTed purchase orders to the customer's ERP; a rebalance re-delivered a batch and the ERP received duplicate orders, because Kafka transactions never covered the HTTP side effect.

A consumer group was offline for eight days during a migration, longer than `offsets.retention.minutes`; on restart the expired offsets fell back to `earliest`, replaying a week of events through a non-idempotent notification forwarder that sent every customer duplicate emails.

`advertised.listeners` was left pointing at `localhost:9092` inside Compose, so clients could connect for metadata but were redirected to an unreachable address; the producer hung and eventually failed with 'Local: Message timed out' and half a day was lost before anyone compared bind address to advertised address.

You need to insert a new approval step into a workflow with 30,000 executions in flight, some of which will run for another six weeks. Walk through the options (patching, Worker Versioning with pinning, a new workflow type on a new task queue), what each costs operationally, how you verify safety before deploying, and how you know when the old code path can be deleted.

Design the compensation strategy for a workflow that charges a card, reserves inventory in a partner system with a 60 s p99, and emails the customer. Which steps are compensated, which are idempotent by construction, what happens when a compensation itself fails permanently, and what does the history look like when the workflow is cancelled halfway through?

A customer reports 400 workflows have been Running for two days with no progress. Using only the CLI and Prometheus, how do you determine whether this is a non-determinism error, a starved task queue, no worker polling, or an activity retrying against a dead dependency, and what is the remediation for each?

Explain what a worker does when it receives a workflow task for an execution that is not in its sticky cache, why that makes queries against large histories expensive, and how slots, pollers, cache size and sticky timeout interact under a burst of 10,000 new workflows.

A signal handler and the main workflow coroutine both mutate the same list, and in production the list occasionally has duplicates. Explain the interleaving that causes it, how you fix it while staying deterministic, and how you write a test that reproduces the race reliably.

Why does Temporal retry a workflow task forever on an unexpected exception but fail the execution on `ApplicationError`? Give a case where the default is wrong for a customer, show how you change it, and describe the blast radius if you get it backwards.

A partner API allows 10 requests per second per account across your entire fleet and you run six worker pods. Where do you enforce the limit, what breaks if you do it inside the activity, and how do you prove the aggregate rate to the partner from your own metrics?

An engineer inserted a new `send_notification` activity ahead of an existing one without a patch; every in-flight execution hit a non-determinism error on its next workflow task, sat Running with `WorkflowTaskFailed` retrying all weekend, and the on-call terminated 2,000 workflows by hand because nobody knew that rolling back the worker image would have healed them.

A saga compensation deleted the CRM record by the id stored in Postgres, but the forward activity had crashed after HubSpot committed and before the id was stored; the compensation found nothing to delete, returned success, and the orphan records surfaced when the customer's sales team started calling leads twice.

The compile activity was `async def` and called a synchronous vendor SDK; one slow LLM response blocked the worker's event loop, heartbeats stopped, the server timed out twelve unrelated activities, and their retries on other workers doubled the load on the API that was already slow.

Query handlers were used as a polling API by a dashboard hitting 5,000 executions every two seconds; each evicted execution forced a full replay, `temporal_workflow_task_replay_latency` went to seconds, the sticky cache thrashed, and real workflow progress slowed to a crawl while the customer stared at a dashboard that said everything was fine.

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` stayed at the default 30 s while `graceful_shutdown_timeout` was five minutes; every rolling deploy SIGKILLed workers mid-activity, the activities were only retried after their ten-minute start-to-close timeout, and the customer logged each deploy as a ten-minute outage.

An entity workflow per tenant received one signal per event with no Continue-As-New; the busiest tenant crossed the 51,200-event ceiling after five months, the server terminated the execution, and the tenant's accumulated state existed only inside that history.

A patch was deprecated and deleted after checking for Running executions but not for closed executions still inside retention; during an incident a week later, `temporal workflow reset` replayed a history containing the marker against code with no `deprecate_patch` and the reset the customer needed failed.

A customer hands you three exports of roughly 50k customer records each with no shared key and asks for one clean list by Friday. Walk me through your plan hour by hour, and tell me exactly which numbers you would show them on Friday to justify that the result is correct.

Explain the Fellegi-Sunter model to a data steward who has no statistics background: what m and u mean, why log2(m/u) is a weight you can add up, and what the conditional independence assumption is costing you in their data.

Design the blocking strategy for a dataset where 40 percent of records have a null date of birth, surnames are heavily skewed (10 percent are one of five values) and addresses are free text. What rules do you write, how do you measure that they are good enough, and what do you do about the oversized blocks?

How do you choose a match threshold, and how does that choice differ between a billing system, a healthcare patient index and a marketing suppression list? What would you put in a contract or SOW as the acceptance criterion?

Debug: the monthly rerun produces one cluster containing 6,000 records that were 6,000 separate entities last month. Nothing in the code changed. What do you check, in what order, and how do you unwind the damage in the customer's downstream systems?

The customer's steward says record 12345 and record 98765 are clearly the same company but your system did not merge them. Walk me through the diagnosis: how do you tell whether it was blocking, a comparator, the model parameters, the threshold or the clustering step, and what evidence distinguishes each case?

You must link a hospital's patient records with an insurer's member records, and neither side may see the other's raw identifiers. What are your options, what does privacy-preserving record linkage actually protect against, and what would you tell both legal teams about the residual risk?

A blocking rule keys on postcode plus first initial; in the customer's data 38 percent of records have a null postcode, so those rows are never compared to anything and the match rate looks acceptable while an entire segment of the customer base is silently unresolved.

The placeholder phone number 000-000-0000 appears on 4,200 records; it survives normalisation, forms one enormous block, produces high-weight agreements, and transitive closure chains 4,200 unrelated customers into a single golden record that then receives one merged invoice.

The threshold was tuned on 500 pairs sampled from the grey band only, so the reported precision of 0.98 is a sample artefact; in production, where the score distribution is completely different, the real precision is 0.83 and the customer finds it before you do.

Entity IDs are generated as a hash of the sorted member record IDs; the monthly rerun adds 900 new records, 30 percent of entity IDs change, and every downstream dashboard, export and foreign key in the customer's BI layer breaks overnight.

Survivorship picks the most recently updated value for every field, but the support tool touches updated_at on every ticket view, so the 'most recent' legal name is whatever a support agent last typed rather than the billing system's authoritative value.

An upstream export starts prefixing phone numbers with a country code after a vendor upgrade; the phone comparison silently drops from agreeing to disagreeing, the match rate falls 20 percent, and because nothing errors the regression is only noticed weeks later in a revenue report.

The model treats city and postcode as independent fields, so a pair agreeing on both gets roughly double the evidence it deserves; a whole class of same-town different-person pairs crosses the threshold and merges two patients' medication histories.

Names, dates of birth and addresses are copied to a laptop or a cloud notebook to 'iterate faster' during the engagement; the linkage works, and the finding in the customer's next audit is that personal data left the approved boundary, which ends the project regardless of match quality.

It is day one on site. A Python service you have never seen returns 500s on about 2 percent of requests, starting 'sometime last week', and nobody who wrote it still works there. Walk me through your first 60 minutes minute by minute, and tell me what you say to their VP of Engineering at the end of it.

Explain `git bisect run` precisely: what each exit code means, why 125 exists, where the script must live and why, and how you bisect when the lockfile changes across the range or when the culprit turns out to be in an upstream package rather than this repo.

Design a landing protocol for a team of five FDEs so any of them becomes productive in an unfamiliar customer repo within 30 minutes. What is on the checklist, what is automated, what does it deliberately skip, and how would you measure whether it works?

A test reproduces the bug on your laptop and passes in the customer's CI. Give me the ordered list of things you check, and how you distinguish 'environment difference' from 'flaky test' from 'the bug is data-dependent and their fixtures are clean'.

You have a one-line fix and 40 minutes left in the session. How do you choose between shipping the fix, reverting the offending commit, and shipping a feature-flag guard? What changes your answer if the customer is inside a change freeze?
