How do you establish blast radius in a codebase you have known for two hours? Name the specific tools, and name what each of them misses.

The bug is in a third-party open-source library the customer depends on. Walk through the options - upstream PR, carried patch file, vendored fork, workaround in your own code - and explain the trade-off to an engineering manager who wants it fixed today.

A prospect sends a 300-question security questionnaire and wants it back in three days. How do you run that, and how do you decide what to answer yes, no, and compensating control?

A customer says they will only buy if we deploy entirely inside their VPC so no data leaves their account. What does that actually change legally, what does it change operationally for us, and what breaks in the product?

Their payments team currently posts card numbers to their own backend before forwarding to a gateway. How do you reduce their PCI scope, and what do you have to be careful not to promise while doing it?

Regulated data leaks into telemetry: full request bodies, prompts and completions land in a third-party log or LLM-tracing SaaS that is not on the subprocessor list and has a 30-day retention nobody disclosed.
Erasure is implemented in Postgres only, and the deleted subject reappears from an S3 export, the analytics warehouse, HubSpot, or a restored backup that nobody re-processed.

The control map claims 'encrypted at rest' pointing at RDS storage encryption, and the auditor's follow-up - who can read the plaintext - reveals that every engineer with prod read access can, so the control fails on effectiveness.

Evidence is gathered as screenshots in the week before the audit, and the request for a complete population of production changes in the period cannot be satisfied because the emergency-change path bypassed the pipeline and left no record.
Sales commits to HIPAA before anyone checks whether a BAA exists with the model provider and the log vendor, and PHI has already been flowing through both for weeks.
A seeded staging or demo environment is loaded from a production dump, sits outside the audited boundary with weaker access controls, and is real customer data nobody counted.

The blocker turns out to be a complementary user entity control in the cloud provider's own SOC 2 - customer-side MFA, key configuration, access review - that was assumed to be inherited and was never implemented.

You are on site with a customer and their analyst says she just saw a document in a search result that belongs to a different business unit. It is 4pm on a Thursday. Walk me through the next sixty minutes - what you declare, who you pull in, what you touch and what you deliberately do not touch, and what you say to her manager.

Design a tabletop exercise for a deployment of our product inside a regulated customer. Tell me the scenario, the injects and their timing, who is in the room, what you are measuring, and how you would know afterwards whether the exercise was worth their time.

Explain the tension between restoring service and preserving evidence in a suspected compromise. Give me two concrete decisions where those goals conflict in a Kubernetes and AWS deployment, and tell me how you would decide and who has the authority to make that call.

You have five minutes with the customer's board the morning after. Give me the briefing. Then I will ask you the questions they will ask, and you will not be allowed to say 'we are still investigating' more than once.

During the incident, the customer's CTO tells you to roll back to last week's release immediately. You believe the rollback will destroy the evidence you need and may not even remove the attacker's access. What do you do?

Your postmortem draft says the root cause was that an engineer disabled a check to unblock a demo. Rewrite that finding blamelessly and tell me what you would actually change - and how you would defend the rewrite to a customer executive who wants accountability.

How do you scope a suspected cross-tenant data exposure? Be specific about which logs, which fields and which queries you would need, and tell me what you would have had to instrument months earlier for that answer to take minutes instead of days.

Nobody declares for six hours because the first signal looks like a display bug, so the timeline in the postmortem starts at the moment someone finally believed a customer rather than at the first alert, and the 72-hour clock had already been running.

The FDE runs the bridge as commander, subject-matter expert and customer liaison at once, stops updating the customer while deep in a query, and the customer's VP escalates to your CEO because twenty minutes of silence read as a cover-up.

A well-meaning engineer restarts the suspicious pod to 'clear it', destroying the process memory and the only unrotated copy of the container filesystem, and the incident permanently loses the ability to answer whether data left the environment.

The compromised access key is revoked but already-issued STS session tokens keep working for another eleven hours because no Deny with a token-issue-time condition was attached, and the team believes containment is complete.

The scoping question - which tenants, which records, which time window - cannot be answered because audit logging captured the request but not the resource identifiers, so the customer is forced into an over-broad notification to every account.

A status page update written by an engineer uses the word 'breach' before legal has made a determination, and that sentence is quoted back in a regulator's follow-up and in a customer's contract termination notice.

The tabletop produces a tidy report with fourteen action items, none of them get a ticket or an owner, and the same missing break-glass access blocks the response during the real incident four months later.

A customer signed for 'an AI agent that triages our security alerts'. You get one 45-minute session with the SOC analyst before design starts. Give me your actual first six questions, in order, and tell me what each one is trying to disconfirm.

Your champion tells you the team spends 'hours a day' on manual reconciliation. Walk me through how you convert that into a number you would be willing to put in a board deck, including exactly what artefact you ask for and what you do with it.

How do you tell the difference between a customer who is genuinely enthusiastic and one who is being polite? Give me the concrete signals you look for in the session and the thing you ask for at the end that settles it.

You have finished discovery and concluded that the deliverable named in the signed SOW will not move the metric the buyer cares about. Your champion picked that deliverable and told their VP it would work. What do you do, in what order, and what exactly do you say to the champion?

Design the constraint interview for a healthcare customer who wants patient-intake summarisation. What do you ask, whom do you ask, and which single answer, if it comes back wrong, invalidates your default architecture?

In discovery you find that the customer's own platform team already built half of what you were hired to build, and it mostly works. How does that change your problem statement, your architecture and your relationship with that team?
Give me a time you built the wrong thing because discovery was thin. What was the specific question you failed to ask, how would you have asked it, and what is now in your script because of it?

You interview the champion and the VP, never the analyst who does the work, and ship a workflow whose second step the operations team is contractually forbidden from performing, which nobody discovers until UAT.

You demo Kaupex in the discovery call, get 'wow, that's exactly what we need', log it as validation, and only realise months later that no data export, no system access and no second meeting ever came out of that session.

The stated problem is a solution: they ask for a chatbot over their documentation, you build retrieval, and the real defect is that the documentation is three years stale - so the bot now answers confidently and wrongly at scale, which is worse than the search box it replaced.

Nobody measured the baseline, so at the quarterly review the customer's own analyst produces a number from a different definition that says the system made things slower, and you have no instrumented counter-argument.
Data residency comes up in month three: the customer's legal team will not permit egress to a hosted model API, the entire architecture assumed one, and the replan costs more than the original build.

The customer's platform team was treated as a delivery obstacle rather than interviewed, so they own the deploy, never schedule your change window, and the pilot sits in staging until the sponsor loses interest.
You say 'yes, we can do that' three times in a discovery room, the notes become the SOW, and you spend the engagement delivering scope that was never tied to the success metric or to anyone's budget.
You land on a new customer deployment on Monday morning. What do you write in week one, in what order, who reviews each document, and who has to sign which one?

Walk me through the site survey you would run before deploying an LLM application inside a regulated customer's VPC. Give me the ten questions whose answers would change your architecture, and say how each one changes it.
Mid-engagement the sponsor asks for a feature that adds about two weeks. It is a fixed-fee SOW. What do you do in the next hour, and which documents change?

Write me the ADR for choosing between pgvector in the customer's existing Postgres and a dedicated vector database. What goes in Context, what goes in Consequences, and what would make you supersede it later?
Your design doc's rollback plan says 'redeploy the previous image', but the release ran a destructive migration. How should that section have been written, and what else in the doc does that change?
How do you write a runbook that a customer's on-call engineer who has never met you can execute at 3am, and what do you deliberately leave out of it?
Six months after handover, how would you know whether the documentation you left behind is actually being used and is still true?

An unwritten assumption - the customer will provision the IAM role and VPN access in week one - slips six weeks, and because it never appeared in the SOW's assumptions or dependencies the team burns budget idle with no change order to point at.

The site survey misses a TLS-intercepting egress proxy and an internal-only mirror registry, so the first deploy dies on certificate validation and image pulls and week one goes to networking instead of the product.

The design doc is written after the code, so the customer's security architect vetoes the outbound model API call at the pre-go-live review and the entire retrieval path is redesigned in the final sprint.

No ADRs exist, so four months later a new CTO asks why Temporal rather than Celery, nobody can reconstruct the constraints that drove it, and the decision is relitigated in meetings that cost more than the record would have.

The runbook is a wiki page of screenshots from a UI that has since changed, with commands missing cluster and namespace context, so the on-call engineer restarts the wrong deployment at 3am and extends the incident by hours.
Success metrics were agreed on a slide but never instrumented, so at renewal there is no baseline and no measured delta and the engagement is judged on sentiment rather than evidence.
Scope creep is accepted verbally in a standup and never raised as a change request, so a fixed-fee engagement silently goes negative while the team is congratulated for being accommodating.

You have ten minutes with a CFO who has already decided this project is over budget, and you are the engineer who built it. What is on screen in minute one, what do you deliberately not show at all, and what is your ask at minute ten?

Walk me through a technical decision you had to defend to someone who could cancel the project. What was the actual trade-off, what did they push hardest on, and what did you change afterwards as a result?

Your live demo hangs at minute four - the model call has not returned in 20 seconds and the room is silent. Tell me exactly what you do in the next 30 seconds, and what you had to prepare in advance for that answer to be possible.
A customer's VP asks in the demo whether you can hold 100ms p95 and 99.99% availability. You genuinely do not know. What do you say in the room, and what actually happens downstream if you say yes?

Design the demo environment for a system you will show to twenty different prospects over a quarter. What is pinned, what is seeded, what is faked or replayed, how do you keep it honest, and what breaks first as the product changes underneath it?

Compute cost per 1,000 requests for an LLM feature in front of me. Now the customer tells you their real volume is 20x your assumption and their documents are three times longer - which parts of your number move, and which do not?
The champion loved the demo, and two weeks later the platform team blocks the rollout. What did you fail to do during that demo, and what is your recovery plan for the next meeting?

The demo runs against :latest images and a live provider endpoint, and a model deprecation or an unnoticed prompt-template change three days before the QBR turns a rehearsed flow into a wrong answer in front of the buyer.

The 'synthetic' seed data was quietly derived from a previous customer's export, a real company name appears on screen, and the meeting stops being a deal conversation and becomes a security incident.

Full-desktop screen sharing leaks a Slack notification, a calendar invite naming another prospect, or a terminal with a live credential in scrollback, and the customer's security lead notices before you do.
The CFO asks what it costs and the answer is 'it's pretty cheap', which converts a signable pilot into a three-week finance review and strands the champion with no numbers to defend internally.

A number said casually in the room - 'sub-200ms p95, 99.9% availability' - is copied verbatim into the SOW by the account team, and six weeks later it is a contractual obligation nobody sized or instrumented.
Everything is shown on a hand-picked happy path, the champion tries one genuinely messy record the next morning, it fails, and the internal narrative becomes 'it only works in their demo'.

Live debugging runs six minutes past the failure because the presenter cannot let go, consuming the entire defence segment so the trade-off and cost questions are never answered and the meeting ends unresolved.
Walk me through a write-up you published about your own work. What did you cut, and how did you decide what was safe to disclose about the customer?

You have 45 minutes to write the customer-facing incident summary for a 4-hour partial outage in the integration you deployed. What sections do you write, in what order, and what do you deliberately leave out of the first version?

A customer's on-call engineer has to run your failover procedure for the first time at 3am with no context. Write - out loud - the first five lines of that runbook, and tell me what makes them safe to follow.
Your post claims a 5x latency improvement. I'm the skeptical staff engineer in the room. Convince me the number is real.
How do you decide whether something belongs in a tutorial, a how-to, reference, or an explanation page - and give me an example of a doc you've seen that failed because it mixed two of them.
You wrote a design doc, three reviewers left conflicting comments, and one of them is the customer's architect who outranks the others. How do you converge the document without a meeting?

We want our FDEs publishing customer case studies. Design the process end to end: what gets written, who reviews it, what the legal and confidentiality gates are, and how you keep it from becoming marketing fluff.

The write-up leads with the journey ('when we first kicked off the project...') and buries impact and outcome under 800 words, so the exec who was forwarded it closes the tab before learning what happened.

A runbook says 'simply restart the service' with no expected output and no failure branch, so the customer's on-call at 3am runs it, sees an unfamiliar error, and escalates to you anyway - the doc bought nothing.
A screenshot in a published post contains a hostname, an internal email address or a partially visible token, and the account's security team finds it before you do.
Commands in the post were written from memory or from a shell with unexported env vars already set, so they fail for every reader on a clean machine and the top comment is someone pasting the error.

An incident report names an individual or a team as the cause, the customer's manager reads it, and the next incident gets reported to you late or not at all because people learned that honesty is punished.

Performance claims quote an average instead of a percentile and omit the baseline, so a sceptical engineer in the customer's review reproduces a different result and the whole document loses credibility.

Diagrams live in a Figma or Lucidchart file outside the repo, drift from the deployed architecture within two sprints, and are then used by a new joiner to reason about a system that no longer exists.

Recruiter screen, minute six: 'So that we do not waste each other's time - what are your compensation expectations for this role?' Answer it out loud, and then I am going to ask you the same thing twice more.
You have our offer and one from a competitor. Tell me what it would take for you to sign with us today - and be specific, because I have to take it to a committee and defend it.

Walk me through how you would compare two offers where one is a public company paying RSUs and the other is a Series C paying options. What do you need to know about the Series C before you can even put the two on the same page, and how would you present that comparison to your partner at home?
We cannot move base - it is the top of the band for this level. But I can add equity. Talk me through what you would want to know before you decide whether that is a good trade for you.

A customer's VP tells you two weeks before go-live that the deployment is unacceptable without a feature that is not in the SOW, and threatens to escalate to your VP. You cannot deliver it and hold the date. How do you run that conversation, and what do you actually say first?

You accepted our offer three weeks ago. During onboarding you discover you were slotted one level below what the hiring manager described in the loop, and the equity in the grant notice is 20% below what the letter implied because of the conversion date. What do you do, in what order, and with whom?

Tell me about a negotiation you lost - with an employer, a vendor or a customer. What did you concede too early, what would you set as your walk-away if you ran it again, and how would you know in the moment that you were about to fold?
You give a number in the first recruiter screen, the whole process gets calibrated to it, and you never learn that the band topped out 35% higher because nobody had a reason to tell you.

You hint at a competing offer you do not have, the recruiter asks a specific follow-up about the level and structure, and the resulting stumble costs you both the credibility and the offer in a field small enough that people compare notes.

You win a 6% base bump and accept the level as offered, so you sit two years under a lower ceiling with smaller refreshes, and the promotion you were verbally promised needs a committee packet nobody prepared.

You compare a Series B option grant against public RSUs by multiplying shares by the last preferred price, ignoring strike, the liquidation preference and future dilution, and discover at an acqui-hire three years later that common holders received nothing.

The hiring manager promises a specific region, a travel ceiling and a six-month equity review on a call, none of it enters the offer letter, and eleven months in you are on a different account, travelling four days a week, reporting to someone who never heard the promise.

You take a sign-on bonus with a full twelve-month clawback, the deployment turns out to be staff-augmentation work with no engineering ownership, and leaving in month eight now costs you cash you have already spent.

You negotiate entirely over email, your carefully framed package arrives at the compensation committee as a single bald number with no justification, and the answer comes back as a flat no you have no conversational room to reopen.

A payments customer wants an agent that runs the dispute queue end to end. Which steps would you let it perform, which would you refuse, what regulatory clocks constrain the design, and what exactly must the system log so their examiner can reconstruct a decision two years later?

You have read access to a hospital's EHR and are building an intake assistant. Walk me from scheduling to a paid claim, name the interface you would use at each hop, and tell me the first three places the workflow actually breaks for the staff rather than for the software.

A prospect emails you a CSV of sample data the night before a demo. Talk me through your next ten minutes - once for a fintech customer, once for a hospital - and tell me precisely what differs between the two.

Design an invoice-exception agent for a procurement organisation that is audited under SOX. What identity does it run as, what records can it change, and how would you demonstrate to an auditor that no approval in the system was made by the agent?
Explain to me, as the customer's VP of Global Trade, why your system will not classify our goods or file our customs entries - and then tell me what it will do that is still worth paying for.

In healthcare, what is the difference between data that is de-identified and data you are permitted to send to a model vendor? Give me a concrete case where a team gets that distinction wrong and does not notice.

Pick a domain you have never worked in. How do you get to a credible discovery call in three days, and how would you tell the difference between genuine understanding and repeating jargon back at the customer?

Someone drops a 'quick sample' extract into Slack the night before a demo and it contains live PANs or unscrubbed clinical narratives, so the demo itself becomes a reportable disclosure and a PCI scope expansion before a single line of integration code exists.

The agent is given write access to the vendor master or the payment run so the workflow demos end to end, and the customer's SOX auditor records it as a segregation-of-duties failure that forces the integration out at renewal.

Payment success is modelled as the card authorisation or the ACH submission, so the product reports money that later returns under R10 up to sixty days afterwards, and the operations team stops trusting every number the system produces.

Free-text notes are sent to a model endpoint with no BAA because a data scientist removed the name column and called it de-identified, ignoring the seventeen other Safe Harbor identifiers embedded in the narrative text.

A prior-authorisation assistant optimised on approval rate quietly nudges toward diagnosis codes that get approved, which is billing fraud rather than a hallucination bug, and the eval set never catches it because it only scored approvals.

The generated 856 is syntactically valid but its shipment-order-pack hierarchy or SSCC labels are inconsistent, retailers reject it days later via 824 and levy vendor compliance chargebacks that exceed the value of the automation.

An export-controlled drawing is pasted into a shared workspace or shown on a troubleshooting screen share with a non-US engineer, which is a deemed export the customer's trade compliance officer is obliged to self-disclose.

We have 40 customer-managed installs. Twelve are current, twenty are one minor behind, six are three minors behind and two are air-gapped and have not upgraded in a year. Design the support and skew policy you would publish, and tell me what you would do about the two air-gapped installs specifically.

Walk me through renaming a column that the application reads on every request, in a product shipped to customers who upgrade at different times and who may roll back. Give me the phases, which release each phase ships in, and the exact point after which rollback destroys data.

A customer runs your pre-upgrade preflight and it fails on a rule you added last month. They tell you it is a false positive and ask you to give them a flag to skip it. What do you do, and how do you decide whether they are right?

Design the gate that stops an unsupported version jump. Where does it run, what does it read to know the current version, what does it do when the customer's cluster has no network egress, and how do you make it impossible to bypass accidentally while still bypassable deliberately with an audit trail?

Debug: an upgrade reports success, all pods are Ready, and two hours later the customer reports that a feature configured in their values file has stopped taking effect. Where do you look, in what order, and what are the three most likely causes given what you know about Helm and CRDs?

You need to remove a deprecated API field. Tell me how you decide it is safe, what evidence you need from the fleet, how long the notice period is and why, and what you do about the one customer who is still calling it two weeks before removal.

A P1 security fix must reach every supported install this week, including two that are three minors behind and one that is air-gapped. Describe your release plan end to end: which branches get the fix, what you build, what you test, in what order the cohorts go, and what you tell each customer.

A customer three minors behind runs the upgrade straight to current; the intermediate release's backfill never executed because the jump skipped it, the new column stays NULL for their historic rows, and it surfaces six weeks later as blank fields in their month-end report rather than as an error.

The pre-upgrade hook Job carries `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: hook-failed`, so when the gate correctly blocks a bad upgrade the pod and its logs are deleted; the on-site engineer re-runs the upgrade three times looking for the reason and eventually disables the hook.

An upgrade is rolled back with `helm rollback` after a failed release, but the migration had already dropped the old column in its contract phase, so the previous application version crash-loops on `SELECT` and the only recovery is a point-in-time restore that loses two hours of the customer's writes.

Someone adds `--force` to `helm upgrade` to get past a stuck immutable field; Helm deletes and recreates the StatefulSet's resources, the PVCs are reprovisioned empty, and a database that was never in the backup rotation because 'it is just a cache' turns out to hold the customer's queue state.

`ALTER TABLE ... SET NOT NULL` runs during the customer's business hours behind a long-running analytics transaction; the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request queues and every subsequent read blocks behind it, so a metadata change reads to the customer as a twenty-minute total outage caused by your release.

The chart's CRDs live in `crds/` and Helm never upgrades them, so after three releases the new controller is silently ignoring fields the customer configured; nobody notices until a support case shows a policy that is present in the YAML and absent in behaviour.

An engineer hand-patches an urgent fix directly onto the customer's install during an incident and never opens the backport PR; the next scheduled upgrade cleanly reverts the fix and reproduces the original incident, this time with no goodwill left.

Argo CD auto-sync is enabled uniformly across the fleet with no rings, so a chart change with a bad default reaches all forty installs within a sync interval and the rollback has to be executed forty times, in forty change windows, by hand.

Show me the weekly update you would send in week three of an engagement where the customer still has not granted the data access you asked for on day one. Read me the first two lines, and tell me what you deliberately left out.

You learn on Tuesday that a milestone three weeks out will slip by two weeks. Who do you tell, in what order, in what medium, and by when? Draft the first 60 words of the note and tell me how you arrived at the new date.

Design the communications plan for a twelve-week deployment into a regulated customer with an exec sponsor, a platform team that did not ask for you, and a security reviewer who has already vetoed two vendors: channels, cadence, artifacts, response-time commitments, escalation ladder, and what you do in week one.

You have asked the same person for the same firewall change four times over three weeks. Write the escalation. Who is on it, what does it say, what do you do the day before you send it, and how do you keep working with that person afterwards?

Define what your amber means precisely enough that someone else could apply it to your project without asking you. Then tell me about a time you reported amber when your own leadership wanted green, and what happened.
Here is a real status update [handed a bad one]. Tell me everything wrong with it, rank the problems by cost to the engagement, and rewrite the first 40 words.

It is 02:00 during a Sev1 and the customer's CTO joins the bridge asking for a root cause and an ETA. What do you say, what do you refuse to say and why, and what exactly is in the written update you send 30 minutes later?

Five weekly updates say green because the team is working hard, then the go-live date moves in week six; the sponsor hears it first from their own platform lead, and the renewal conversation becomes about whether you can be trusted rather than about a two-week slip.

The ask is buried in paragraph four as 'we'll need someone to approve the IAM role'; nobody owns it, three weeks pass, and when the slip is challenged the trail cannot be reconstructed because it lived in a Slack channel with 90-day retention.

The update goes out Friday 18:00 customer-local before a public holiday, as a Google Doc link their SSO cannot open and an inline screenshot that strips on forward; the 'you never told us' conversation then happens in the steering committee.

An escalation email goes to the sponsor's boss with no warning, over a ticket the counterpart was already unblocking; that person is embarrassed in front of their VP and stops volunteering information for the remaining ten weeks.

During a Sev1 the FDE speculates in the exec-visible channel that 'it looks like their firewall change caused this'; root cause turns out to be the vendor's own migration, and the retraction damages the account more than the 47-minute outage did.

The weekly update quotes a p95 latency from a Grafana panel whose filter excludes one tenant, so the number disagrees with the customer's own dashboard by 40%; after that single mismatch every figure in every future update is treated as marketing.

A decision taken verbally on a call - 'we'll use your existing Postgres rather than RDS' - is never written up or filed as an ADR; a new platform lead reverses it in month three, three weeks of integration work is rebuilt, and there is nothing to point at.

An incident note is sent with a screenshot containing a tenant id and an alert payload holding customer PII, and the sponsor forwards it to a partner organisation; a communications artifact becomes a reportable data incident of its own.
Why forward-deployed rather than a product engineering role at the same company? Be specific about what you get from it and what you give up.
This role is roughly 40% travel, mostly to customer sites in other timezones, sometimes at short notice. Walk me through what that actually looks like in your life, and tell me where your limit is.
What do you think is the hardest part of getting our product into a customer's production environment? You have not worked here - I want your hypothesis and what it is based on.

You are three weeks into a deployment and it is clear the thing in the SOW will not solve the customer's actual problem. Your champion has already told their VP it will. What do you do, and in what order do you talk to whom?
What are you looking for in compensation, and how did you arrive at that number?
You have another offer. Tell me honestly how you are comparing them - what would make you pick us, and what is the thing about us that worries you?
Six months in, what would make you conclude this was the wrong job? Give me the concrete signal you would be watching for.

You say 'I'm totally flexible on travel' in the loop, get staffed on a rotation you cannot sustain, and the account team loses a quarter re-staffing the engagement - the reputational damage lands on you, not on the recruiter who wrote it down.

You give the first number in the screening call without having calibrated the level, anchor 25% under band, and the offer comes in exactly where you anchored, permanently resetting every future refresh and promotion off that base.

The 'why this company' answer is assembled from the homepage and the About page, the interviewer is the person who wrote neither, and the answer reads as interchangeable across their three closest competitors.

You quote a metric in the narrative round that you cannot reconstruct in the resume-defence round two weeks later, and the loop's feedback becomes 'inflates impact' - the single hardest tag to recover from in a debrief.

Sponsorship or a border constraint surfaces after the offer rather than in the recruiter screen, the role turns out to be budgeted without it, and the offer is withdrawn for a reason that had nothing to do with your engineering.

You accept a private-company offer on a headline total-comp figure without the share count, preferred price or exercise window, and discover at exit that the equity was worth a fraction of the number you traded base salary for.

You claim comfort with air-gapped or clearance-gated customer sites you have never worked in, get assigned to exactly that account because it is the one that needed the answer, and cannot do the work.

You say you cut lead qualification from 48 hours to under 4. Define both numbers precisely for me: what event starts the clock, what event stops it, is that a median or a mean, and over how many accounts?

Walk me through the enrichment agent. Now go one level down: how many concurrent workers, what bounded them, what happened when a page hung, and how did you verify the run actually completed for every domain rather than just the ones that succeeded?
Your scoring model outputs a composite 0-100. How were the weights chosen, and how would you know today whether the score has any relationship to accounts that actually closed?

During the window where reply rate improved, you also changed the target list and the copy. Design me the experiment you would run now to separate those effects, given you only get one production sending fleet.

Tell me about a time this system produced confidently wrong output that nobody noticed for a while. How was it eventually detected, and what did you add so it would be caught in an hour instead of a week?
Pick the bullet on your resume you are least proud of technically and tell me why - then tell me what you would build instead today and what that would cost you.

A customer's data engineer reviews your integration and says the webhook consumer can double-write contacts on retry. Is he right? Walk me through your idempotency story and what you would change if he is.

A rate is quoted with a silently favourable denominator - positive replies over delivered rather than over sent - and when the interviewer recomputes it over sent, the number drops by a third and every other figure on the page becomes suspect.

The before-number was never measured; it was estimated after the fact to make the after-number look good, and the candidate cannot say who timed the 'two weeks' or where the '6+ hours per batch' came from.

An improvement is claimed from a window in which the list source, the copy and the sending infrastructure all changed together, so the causal story collapses on the first 'how do you know it was the pipeline?'

The candidate describes an LLM scoring system entirely at the level of 'the model evaluates fit' and cannot state a weight, a schema, a parse-failure path or a single validation against closed-won outcomes - which reads as having operated a tool rather than built a system.

A throughput claim covers only the successful subset: the automated pass finished in 30 minutes for the 60 domains that did not time out, and the failures were silently dropped rather than retried or reported, so the real end-to-end coverage was never measured.

Ownership is stated in the first person for work a four-person team did, the interviewer asks one implementation detail that only the actual builder would know, and the ambiguity retroactively taints the honest bullets too.

Confidential material leaks in the enthusiasm to prove a claim - a screenshot with customer names, a prospect list, or a live API key visible in a terminal recording - which ends the loop regardless of how good the answer was.
Walk me through the take-home you were least happy with. What did you cut, what did the cut cost, and what would you have done differently with the same five hours?

You have five hours and a customer corpus of 200,000 heterogeneous documents. Describe exactly what you build, what you deliberately do not build, and how you would prove to the customer that retrieval is good enough to deploy.

Your agent has a tool that issues refunds. Design the boundary around it: schema, authorisation, idempotency, approval, audit, and the tests that prove a malicious document in the context window cannot trigger it.

An eval you built as a CI gate starts failing intermittently on unchanged code. Debug it out loud - what do you check first, and how do you decide between fixing the harness, the judge, or the threshold?

A customer reruns your nightly ingest for the same day after a partial failure and their revenue metric doubles. What is the most likely cause, how do you confirm it, and what do you change so it cannot happen again?
How would you set the pass threshold on an LLM-as-judge gate when you have 50 human labels and no baseline? Tell me what agreement number would make you refuse to ship the gate at all.
We give candidates a take-home and half the submissions look identical. If you were designing our rubric, what would you score that actually separates a senior FDE from a strong generalist?
Four and a half hours go into ingestion, parsing and a beautiful abstraction layer, and the submission never produces an answer to the actual question the prompt asked.

The repo runs perfectly on your laptop and fails on the reviewer's machine because an env var was already exported in your shell, a CLI was installed globally months ago, or the seed data was gitignored.
The RAG demo answers confidently on a question with no supporting document, and the reviewer's first test - an off-corpus question - produces a fluent hallucination with fabricated citations.
The agent's write tools have no approval gate or idempotency key, so a retried step double-sends a notification or double-updates a record, and the audit log has no way to prove which call did it.
The eval harness reports a single aggregate number with no variance, so a re-run swings by more than the regression it is supposed to gate and the customer stops trusting the check within two weeks.
The pipeline silently drops malformed rows instead of dead-lettering them, so the mart is built from a subset nobody counted and the dashboard understates volume for a quarter before anyone notices.
The walkthrough runs seventeen minutes, narrates code line by line instead of intent, and buries the demo at minute nine - so the reviewer stops at minute three having seen nothing work.
A hospital network's COO tells you: 'we want to use AI to reduce patient no-shows.' You have thirty minutes. Go.

You are four weeks into a ten-week deployment and the customer's security team just confirmed that no hosted model API is reachable from their network. Re-plan out loud: what changes, what gets cut, and what do you tell the sponsor tomorrow morning?
Size the data-ingestion workstream for a customer you have never worked with before. Give me a number, tell me how you got it, and defend the pessimistic end.
You have two engineers and eight weeks. Show me the phase plan, then tell me which phases a second engineer actually shortens and which ones they do not.
How do you decide the very first thing you build in an engagement? Give me an example where the obvious first thing turned out to be wrong.
What would make you recommend that a customer stop this project? Be specific: which metric, measured on which dataset, in which week.
The customer's data science team already has a model they say is 92% accurate and they want you to 'just productionise it'. Decompose that.
You start drawing architecture in the first two minutes, the interviewer writes 'proposed before understanding', and the remaining 28 minutes of good work do not overturn it.
The plan carries no baseline, so 'reduce denials by 20%' is unfalsifiable and the pilot ends in a meeting where the customer and you quote different numbers from different queries.
Access and security review are a footnote rather than a workstream, so the model sits finished on your laptop for six weeks waiting on a VPC peering approval nobody was chasing.
The decomposition is layer-by-layer - all ingestion, then all modelling, then all UI - so the first end-to-end result lands in week six and reveals the join key is not unique.
Every workstream is a single-point estimate with no range or confidence, so the first slipped date reads as incompetence instead of the uncertainty you had already priced in.

You accept the customer's stated solution ('we need a dashboard', 'we need a fine-tuned model') as the problem, deliver it exactly to spec, and it goes unused because the real blocker was a disputed definition or an absent decision owner.
The plan has no cut list, so when the timeline is halved mid-engagement the customer chooses what to drop and drops the evaluation, leaving you unable to prove the thing worked.

Design a grounded question-answering system over two million documents for forty enterprise tenants, one of which will not allow any data to leave their network. Give me the shared architecture, then tell me exactly which components change for that tenant and what capability they lose.

You are told the assistant is 'not accurate enough'. Before touching the prompt, how do you determine whether the problem is retrieval, the generation step, the chunking, or the question distribution - and what measurement distinguishes each?

Walk me through your latency budget for a streamed answer with a p95 target of six seconds. Where does the time actually go, which component would you cut first, and how does the answer change if the customer requires reranking and a guardrail check on the output?

Your agent takes write actions in the customer's billing system. Design the boundary: authorisation model, idempotency, approval gates, step budget, audit trail, and the test that proves a malicious document in the knowledge base cannot trigger a refund.
The customer wants unit cost cut by half without a quality drop they can notice. Give me the levers in order, quantify each one, and tell me which of them you would refuse to pull and why.

I want to push back: you chose a self-hosted open-weight model on four GPUs instead of a hosted API. Defend it with arithmetic, tell me the volume at which the decision flips, and describe the migration for a live customer if it flips.

How would you gate a deployment on an LLM-as-judge score when you have 150 human labels and no baseline? Tell me the agreement number below which you would refuse to ship the gate, and what you would do instead in the meantime.

The design assumes a hosted provider throughout; the customer's security review then forbids prompts leaving their network, and the whole retrieval, serving and tracing stack has to be re-chosen on site because the in-VPC swap was never rehearsed.

Multi-tenant retrieval filters by tenant_id after the top-k vector search, so small tenants get near-empty result sets and their users are told the answer is not in the corpus while the documents sit in the index.

A document deleted for a GDPR request is removed from the source of truth but never tombstoned in the vector index, so the assistant keeps citing it for weeks and the customer discovers it before your monitoring does.

The fallback ladder silently drops to a smaller model during a provider incident with no counter and no eval score attached, so quality degrades for two days and the customer's first signal is an angry end user rather than a dashboard.
The agent's write tools run under a service account with broad permissions and no idempotency key, so a retried step double-refunds a customer and the audit log cannot prove which invocation did it.

Cost was estimated on average prompt length; production prompts carry conversation history and ten retrieved chunks, input tokens triple, prompt caching never hits because the prefix changes per request, and the bill lands at four times the number given to the customer's finance team.

The LLM-as-judge gate was never calibrated against human labels, so it passes a release that humans consider clearly worse, the team stops trusting the gate within a month, and it is disabled in CI without being replaced.

Here is a 900k-row export and a question about monthly revenue. Talk me through your first three minutes before you write any aggregation - what do you check and what would make you stop and ask me something?
You join orders to a customer attributes table and the row count goes from 84,000 to 310,000. Walk me through how you diagnose it and what the correct query looks like if attributes change over time.
Write, out loud, the query for each customer's second-largest order. Now do it in a dialect without QUALIFY, and tell me what changes if two orders tie exactly.
You used an assistant to generate this loader. Show me a line you rejected and tell me why - and tell me what class of bug you have learned to look for first in generated code.
Your extraction pipeline reports 98% success but the customer says records are missing. The code has no errors in the logs. How do you find out what happened?

Halfway through a build the customer says the metric must be per local business day, not UTC, and they need twelve months backfilled idempotently. What do you change, what do you drop, and what do you tell them by end of day?
You are on a screen share with a customer's data engineer and your first answer turns out to be wrong. What do you actually say, and what do you do next?

You merge two customer tables without checking cardinality, the many-side fans out, and every revenue number you present to the customer is inflated by a factor nobody notices until finance reconciles the quarter.
A numeric column arrives as object because of thousands separators, the sum silently concatenates strings or coerces to NaN, and the dashboard ships with a metric that is off by orders of magnitude.
A LEFT JOIN with the right table's column filtered in WHERE quietly becomes an INNER JOIN, so customers with no matching rows vanish from the report and the customer's own count never matches yours.
Timestamps are compared across a mix of tz-aware and naive datetimes, so daily aggregates are shifted by hours and month boundaries land in the wrong bucket for every customer outside UTC.
You accept assistant-generated code with a bare except that swallows parse errors, and the pipeline reports success while silently discarding every malformed record for weeks.

You go quiet for four minutes debugging, the interviewer loses the thread, and the write-up says 'strong coder, unclear how they would work with a customer in the room' - which is a no for an FDE role.
You spend twenty of your twenty-five minutes perfecting ingestion and never produce a number, so there is nothing to grade on the axis that actually matters.

You are two weeks into a deployment. The customer's lead architect - who built the rules engine you are replacing - says in front of his VP that your approach will not scale and that they have seen this fail before. What do you say next, word for word, and what do you do after the meeting?

A customer asks in the room whether you can have this live before their board demo in three weeks. You genuinely do not know. Give me your actual answer, and tell me what you would need to say instead if it turns out the answer is no.

Their compliance lead says no customer data may leave their VPC and no third-party model may be used. Walk me through how you keep the project alive - what you ask, what options you put on the table, and what you would refuse to promise.
Run discovery on me: I am a support operations director drowning in tickets and I have already decided I want a chatbot. You have ten minutes to find out whether that is the right thing to build.
Here is the documentation for an internal service you have never seen. In twenty minutes, get a working call through and tell me what the system's failure modes are - narrate as you go.

Tell me about a time you told a customer or a stakeholder something that turned out not to be true. How did you find out, how did you handle it, and what did you change about how you commit to things?
Your champion just left the company and the new VP wants to cancel in 30 days. You get one 30-minute meeting. What is your agenda, and what is the single artifact you bring?

A date is committed in the room that silently depends on the customer's security review or identity team, and when it slips by three weeks the customer records it as the vendor missing a deadline rather than their own queue.

The pilot is scoped off the workflow the champion described, and in week three the data turns out to arrive as a nightly fixed-width SFTP drop rather than the API everyone referred to, invalidating the ingest design.

The engineer wins the argument with the customer's architect on technical merit, publicly, and the architect - who owns the change-approval process - becomes a permanent silent blocker on every subsequent request.

'It needs to be accurate' is accepted without defining an error budget, a threshold or a human-review route, so a 92%-precision system that saves real money is judged a failure against an unstated 100% bar.

A capability is asserted from memory during a demo - a parameter, a connector, a limit that does not exist - and the customer's engineer finds the doc page contradicting it within the hour, which costs more trust than saying 'I do not know' would have.
Scope added mid-meeting is absorbed silently rather than parked, and the four-week pilot quietly becomes ten weeks of work still owed on the original date.
The meeting ends warm with no owner, no date and no written recap, and by the next call the customer remembers a broader promise than was made, with no artifact that can settle it.
Tell me about a time you deployed something at a customer site that broke in production. What broke, how did you find out, and what did you say to the customer in the first hour?
Describe a time a customer stakeholder was firmly against your technical recommendation. Walk me through how it resolved - and if they won, what did you do to make their approach succeed?
Give me an example of a project where nobody could tell you what success looked like. How did you decide what to build, and what did you write down?
Tell me about the most expensive mistake you have made - in money, in time, or in a customer relationship. What is different about how you work now because of it?
Describe a system you handed off and left. How do you know it survived? What did the team hit that you had not documented?
Tell me about a time you had to say no to a customer, or tell them the thing they asked for was the wrong thing. What did you say, and what happened next?
Give me a time you had to get people who didn't report to you - possibly at the customer, not your company - to change how they worked. What actually moved them?
The Result is 'the customer was happy' with no number, so the story is unfalsifiable and the interviewer moves on without writing down a single piece of evidence.
You inflate a metric slightly - 40% instead of the 15% you can actually source - and it collapses under one credibility probe, which retroactively discredits the other nine stories.
Every story is 'we' with no separable personal contribution, and the panel cannot tell whether you led the work or sat next to it.
The failure story is a cost-free failure (a flaky test, a missed typo), which reads as either dishonesty or as never having owned anything that could break.
Three of your ten stories come from the same project, so 'give me a different example' takes you to material you have not rehearsed and you improvise a weaker version of a story you already told.
You burn 90 of 180 seconds setting up the situation, get cut off in the middle of the Action, and never reach the result that was the entire point.
You recite the company's values language back at the interviewer, which reads as coached and makes them discount the stories that would otherwise have landed.

Walk me through the DefenderMate architecture at the container level, then tell me exactly where tenant isolation is enforced. If I compromise one tenant's API token, what can I reach, and what stops an unscoped query from ever leaving your data layer?

Kaupex has a compile step, a human approval that might take three days, and a publish step. The box reboots after publish has partially succeeded. Walk me through what state exists, what a retry does, and how you know the retry is safe.

Pick the worst outage you had in any of these three systems. Give me the timeline: what triggered it, how you found out, how long detection took, what you did in the first ten minutes, and what you changed so that class of failure cannot recur.

Your case study says classification p95 is under a minute. How is that measured, from which point to which point, over what window, and what happens to that number when the model provider starts returning 429s for twenty minutes?

A customer wants Dokeo running in their own cluster, and their security team forbids the managed pieces you rely on. Take me through the chart and the image: what changes, what you lose, and how you keep one codebase across their environment and yours.

You listed 'move classification to a durable queue' as something you would change. Why did you not do it originally, what specifically would force the change, and what does the migration look like while the system stays up?

If I gave you two weeks on any one of these three systems with the goal of handing it to a customer's own engineers to operate, what would you build, what would you write, and how would you know at the end that the handover actually worked?

A credential is scrubbed from the working tree but not from history, or scrubbed from history but never rotated, and the key is still live in a customer's Slack integration or LLM provider account weeks after the repo goes public.
The public repo abstracts a client system so thinly that the architecture diagram plus the client's own public marketing identifies them, breaching an NDA that nobody re-read before publishing.

The page claims a latency or throughput number that came from a laptop benchmark in a good mood; an interviewer asks how it was measured and at what percentile, the answer collapses, and every other claim on the page becomes suspect.

`docker compose up` works only on the author's machine because an image is unpinned, a healthcheck is missing so the app races Postgres, or a required environment variable is undocumented — the reviewer hits an unhandled stack trace in the first two minutes and never returns.

The architecture diagram shows the intended design rather than the deployed one, omitting the cron job and the shared database, so the first follow-up question exposes that the author is describing a system they did not actually operate.
A screenshot taken from a live environment ships with real tenant names, an internal hostname and a session token visible in a URL bar, and it is served from a CDN long after the image is swapped.

The case studies are published once and never touched; the architecture changes, the links rot, the numbers refer to an instance size that no longer exists, and a reader in month six is evaluating a version of the system that stopped being true.
Walk me through the deployment in your write-up. What would you refuse to run that way for a customer with a SOC 2 audit next quarter, and what would you put in its place?
Your agent has shell access and a CRM it can write to. Draw the blast radius. If I get an injected instruction into a record the agent reads, what do I actually get, and what stops me?

The scheduled job silently stopped delivering three days ago and nobody noticed. Walk me through detection and diagnosis using only what is on that box, then tell me what you would add so the third day never happens again.

A customer wants exactly this, inside their VPC, with no egress to a hosted model provider and their own SSO in front of it. What in your design survives, what has to be replaced, and what is the first thing you tell them they cannot have?
Your post claims a specific cost and latency per job. I am skeptical. Tell me how you measured it, what the sample was, and what you did not control for.

Your titles have been engineering titles, but your profile and this post position you as a forward deployed engineer. Make the case for the jump - what have you shipped that is FDE work rather than backend work?

You are the first FDE we hire and we want the team publishing deployment write-ups. Design the process: what gets written, who reviews it, what the confidentiality and security gates are, and how you stop it becoming marketing.
A HubSpot private-app token sat in an early commit of the config repo, the working tree scan passes, the repo goes public, and the key is scraped and used before you notice.

The write-up covers only the happy path, the first serious comment asks what happens when the model decides to run a destructive shell command, and with no answer in the post the whole thing reads as a demo.
The commands link to main instead of a tag, an upstream release renames a config key two weeks later, and every new reader fails at step three while the top comment is a stack trace.

The profile rewrite happens with 'Share profile updates with your network' still enabled, so the entire network - including the current employer - gets notified line by line that you are repositioning.
The headline stays 'Full-Stack Developer | React | Node | Python', so every recruiter search for 'forward deployed' or 'solutions architect' misses the profile no matter how good the write-up is.
A terminal screenshot leaves the host IP, gateway hostname and shell prompt visible, and scanners find the exposed port before the post is 24 hours old.

The post goes out cold with no direct sends, collects a few hundred impressions from people who cannot hire you, and the conclusion drawn is that writing does not work rather than that distribution never happened.
Walk me through your search. Which other companies are you talking to, how did you pick them, and what does that list tell me about what you actually want?

You are the first FDE on a new product. Two hundred customers have asked for a deployment and you have capacity for six this quarter. How do you build the shortlist, what do you measure, and what exactly do you say to the other one hundred and ninety-four?
You have been dropped into an account where you know nobody. Map the stakeholders in your first week: who do you need to find, how do you find them, and what is the one question you ask each of them?
Design the tracker for twelve concurrent customer deployments run by three engineers. What are the fields, what are the states and legal transitions, and what single metric would you put on the wall?

How do you decide to stop working an account that is not converting? Give me the actual criteria, not the principle - and tell me about a time you kept pushing past the point where you should have stopped.
Your champion offers to introduce you to their CTO next week. What exactly do you send the champion beforehand, and why that and not more?

You are comparing two engagements - one with a bigger logo and a worse-defined problem, one smaller with a crisp problem and an engaged owner. How do you compare them quantitatively, and what would change your answer?

The sheet is built in one enthusiastic weekend and never re-verified, so by week four a third of the reqs are closed, you apply into dead requisitions, and you read the resulting silence as rejection instead of as a stale list.

You ask a weak-tie contact for a referral before they have seen any of your work, they submit a lukewarm one-line referral, and the req is now burned - a tepid referral is strictly worse than a cold application and it costs you the contact too.

You filter on the word 'Remote', skip the 'must be authorised to work in the United States' line buried in the requirements, spend five weeks in a loop, and the offer dies at the immigration check with the hiring manager annoyed at both of you.

You anchor your expectation on a US band for a role that will be paid on an India GCC band, and either price yourself out of a screen you would have passed or accept feeling cheated - because you never recorded which band the number came from.
You submit all forty applications in week one, rejections and offers land months apart, and you negotiate the only offer you have with zero concurrency and therefore zero leverage.

You automate against the professional network from your primary account, get restricted or banned, and lose the connection graph that twenty of your forty rows depended on - to save an hour of clicking.

'Applied' becomes a terminal state: a dozen rows sit with no owner and no next_step_due, the pipeline silently drains over six weeks, and you conclude the market is bad when what actually happened is that nobody was assigned the follow-up.

You are running three customer deployments at once and all three escalate in the same week. Walk me through how you decide what gets your Tuesday, and what you actually say to the two customers who do not get it.

Design the tracking system a four-person deployment team would use to run forty concurrent accounts through a seven-stage onboarding funnel. What is the schema, what is the weekly ritual, and what alert fires when an account is stuck?

A customer onboarding funnel used to convert 30% of pilots to production and now converts 8%. You have stage-entry timestamps for 200 accounts and nothing else. How do you find out what changed, and what would you need to be sure?
Tell me about a time you forced a decision out of a stakeholder who kept slipping the date. What was the exact sentence you used, and what would you have done if they had said no?

A customer asks for a price before you have scoped the work, and pushes twice. What do you say the first time, what do you say the second time, and what does giving them a number too early cost you later?
Where else are you in process, and when do you need to decide? Give me your literal answer - then tell me why you phrased it that way.
You have a signed offer with a Friday deadline and your first-choice company is two rounds behind. Walk me through what you do in order, and what you say to each side.

You apply to your three dream companies in week one, get rejected on a rusty systems round, and burn requisitions carrying a 6-12 month cooldown - so the only companies you actually wanted are closed exactly when you finally get sharp.
You answer the recruiter's compensation question with a number in the first ten minutes, and every subsequent conversation negotiates down from an anchor you set 25% below the published band.
Wave one lands four onsites in the same week; by Thursday you are on four hours of sleep and you fail the one loop that mattered for reasons that have nothing to do with your ability.

The tracker goes stale in week three, two companies quietly stop replying, and you find out the requisitions closed only when you eventually check - the classic silent failure of an uninstrumented pipeline.
Your offers arrive six weeks apart, so you have no parallelism at all and accept a five-day exploding offer with zero leverage while the two loops you actually wanted are still at round two.

You imply a competing offer that does not exist, the recruiter checks with a counterpart in a small market where everyone knows everyone, and you lose both processes plus the referral network that fed them.

You spend your warm introductions in month six on loops you are not yet ready for, convert none of them, and cannot re-spend that social capital for a year because the same contacts now have a data point on you.

Explain why appending to a Python list is O(1) but inserting at index 0 is O(n), what structure you use when you need both ends, and what amortized complexity means. When does the amortization argument stop being a fair thing to tell a customer?

Given an array of up to 10^5 integers and a target, decide whether two of them sum to it. Give me the brute force and its cost, then the optimisation, and tell me precisely what you traded to get it and when that trade would be the wrong one.

Write a topological sort. Now: the input is a customer's pipeline config and it contains a cycle. How does your code detect it, and what exactly does the error message say so their engineer can fix it without calling you?
Debug: this solution passes the provided samples and times out on the hidden tests. Walk me through how you find the accidental quadratic with no profiler, and what you would change first.
Your BFS over a 2000 x 2000 grid runs out of memory. Where is the memory going, what are three ways to cut it, and which one would you pick if this were running on a customer's 2 GB container?

When is a heap the right answer instead of just sorting, and vice versa? Give me the concrete n and k where you would switch, and tell me how you would get a max-heap and a stable tiebreak out of Python's heapq.
You are 25 minutes into a 45-minute screen. You have a working O(n^2) and you can see an O(n log n) but you are not sure you can land it. What do you do, and what exactly do you say to me?

You write list.pop(0) inside a loop because it read fine on the 200-row sample; the customer's 2 million-row nightly export turns a four-minute job into six hours and misses the delivery SLA that your team wrote into the statement of work.

You go quiet for four minutes debugging an index error, the interviewer loses the thread entirely, and the write-up reads 'competent coder, unclear how they would work in front of a customer' - which is a no for an FDE role regardless of whether the code compiled.
You reach straight for the clever O(n) solution, tangle the hash-map bookkeeping, and hand in nothing at minute 45 when the brute force you skipped would have passed and left ten minutes to optimise.

You claim O(n) for a loop that contains `if x in some_list`, the interviewer asks you to walk the complexity again, and you cannot see it - the scorecard records that you do not reason about cost, which is the exact signal the round exists to test.
A recursive DFS you shipped over a customer's dependency graph works on the 300-node test fixture and dies with RecursionError on their 50,000-node production graph, at 02:00, in a job with no retry.

You mark BFS nodes visited at dequeue rather than enqueue; the queue fills with duplicates, memory blows up on a 2000x2000 grid, and the same bug in a customer's crawler quietly multiplies API calls until they hit a rate limit.

You group customer records with a hash map keyed on a raw string that was never normalised for case and trailing whitespace, so 'Acme Corp ' and 'acme corp' become two accounts and the dedupe report you presented is wrong in the meeting.

You memorised specific solutions rather than patterns, so a one-clause variation - duplicates now allowed, k may exceed n, the array is rotated - leaves you with nothing to say and no way to rederive it.
Derive the SVD of this 2x2 matrix at the whiteboard, then tell me what happens to U, Sigma and V if I multiply one column of A by 1000, and what that implies for PCA on unstandardised features.

A customer's linear regression reports R^2 = 0.94, but the coefficient on their most important feature flips sign when a week of new data arrives. Diagnose it in linear-algebra terms, name the first two numbers you would compute, and give two different fixes with their trade-offs.

Explain why solving least squares through the normal equations is numerically worse than QR or SVD. Quantify it: what happens to the condition number, and roughly how many correct digits remain in float64 when kappa(X) = 1e8?
Write the ridge solution in the SVD basis and use that expression to explain to a non-mathematical stakeholder what regularisation is actually doing to their model.

Design: a customer has a 3-million-document TF-IDF matrix over a 200k-term vocabulary and wants topic clusters on a 32 GB box. Walk me through the factorisation you would use, the memory arithmetic, how many components you would keep, and how you would defend that number.

Debug: after a fine-tune, a retrieval system's recall@10 collapses and every query returns near-identical results. What do you compute on the embedding matrix, in what order, and what does each result rule in or out?

What is the difference between an eigendecomposition and an SVD, when does the eigendecomposition fail to exist, and for which matrices do the two coincide? Then tell me what np.linalg.eigh assumes and why calling eig on a covariance matrix is a bug rather than a style choice.

A one-hot encoder without drop='first' plus an intercept makes the design matrix exactly rank-deficient; LinearRegression calls lstsq and silently returns one arbitrary minimum-norm solution, so the coefficients shown to the customer as feature importance are one of infinitely many and shift with row order or library version.

PCA is fitted on the whole dataset before the train/test split, so the components encode test-set variance; cross-validation comes back several points high, the deck quotes that number, and the model degrades exactly when it reaches the customer's production data.

PCA is run on unstandardised columns where one feature is in dollars and another is a probability; component 1 is essentially that one column, the 'explains 92 percent of variance' line is meaningless, and truncating to two components discards every real signal.

np.linalg.eig is used on a covariance matrix instead of eigh; round-off yields complex eigenvalues with 1e-18 imaginary parts, someone takes .real, the eigenvectors come back unsorted, and the 'top two components' actually plotted are components five and one.

np.linalg.svd is called with the default full_matrices=True on a 2e6 x 300 matrix; the job requests a 2e6 x 2e6 U, the pod is OOM-killed, and the incident is investigated for a day as a Kubernetes memory-limit problem rather than a one-word API fix.

A vector index is built without L2 normalisation and scored by inner product; a handful of high-norm vectors win almost every query, offline recall looks acceptable because those items happen to be popular in the eval sample, and users see the same five results for unrelated searches.

Two runs of PCA produce sign-flipped components and the dashboard's axes invert; a day is spent hunting a data-pipeline bug that is only the SVD's sign ambiguity, which nobody pinned with a deterministic convention such as forcing the largest-magnitude loading positive.

A model is 'compressed' by truncating weight matrices to rank 16 from a spectrum that was never plotted on a log axis; sigma_17 onward still carry 30 percent of the Frobenius mass, accuracy drops eight points, and the regression is blamed on quantisation instead of the truncation.

Derive the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits when the model ends in a softmax. Show the softmax Jacobian explicitly, show what cancels, and explain why PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss takes logits rather than probabilities.

Write down Adam's update and derive the bias-correction terms from first principles. What exactly is the magnitude of Adam's first step for a single coordinate, and what does that imply about warmup and about Adam's tolerance for badly scaled losses?

Define the condition number of a smooth strongly convex problem and state gradient descent's convergence rate in terms of it. Why does momentum help, what rate does Nesterov achieve, and what would you change about the data instead of the optimiser to get the same win?

Debug: a customer's training run produces NaN loss at step 40. Give me your ordered checklist, what you would log, and how you would distinguish a learning rate that is too large from a numerically unstable loss from an fp16 problem.

A customer says 'your model does not learn'. Design the experiment sequence that determines whether the problem is a bug in the gradients, an optimisation problem, or a data problem - and tell me which single experiment you run first and why it is the most informative.

When would you reach for L-BFGS instead of Adam, and what specifically breaks about L-BFGS under stochastic minibatch gradients? What problem sizes and smoothness assumptions make it the right default?

Explain what makes a loss convex, give me the certificate for logistic regression's negative log-likelihood, and then explain why non-convexity in a neural network is not the practical obstacle people assume it is.

The gradient check is run on a float32 model with h = 1e-8, so roundoff dominates and every partial disagrees by ~1e-2; the engineer concludes 'finite differences are just noisy', ships a sign error in one backward path, and the model trains to a worse-but-plausible loss that nobody questions.

The gradient check is done at a point where a relu or an abs is exactly at its kink, the central difference straddles two different linear pieces and reports a huge mismatch, and a correct backward implementation gets 'fixed' into a wrong one.

optimizer.zero_grad() is missing inside the training loop, so PyTorch's accumulate-by-default behaviour makes the effective step grow with every iteration; the loss looks fine for 200 steps then diverges, and a day is spent hunting for a bad batch in the customer's data.

L2 regularisation is added into the loss while training with Adam and called 'weight decay'; the adaptive denominator scales it per coordinate so the highest-gradient weights receive the least decay, the model overfits anyway, and the diagnosis lands on 'we need more data' instead of switching to AdamW.

Features arrive on wildly different scales (revenue in dollars beside a 0-1 flag), kappa is around 1e12, plain SGD zigzags and plateaus, and the team reports back that 'a linear model does not work on this data' - a conclusion about optimisation dressed up as a conclusion about the domain.

scheduler.step() is called once per epoch while using OneCycleLR (or a per-batch warmup), so the learning rate completes its whole schedule in the first few hundred steps, training silently stalls at a mediocre plateau, and the run is reported as converged.

The training file is sorted by label or by date and the DataLoader is built with shuffle=False, so each minibatch gradient is a biased estimate of the full gradient; loss still decreases, validation on an equally sorted split still looks fine, and the model is systematically worse on the customer's live traffic.

Optimiser comparison plots use a linear y-axis on raw loss over 50 epochs, so three methods look indistinguishable at 'about zero' while one is two orders of magnitude closer to the optimum; the slowest method is adopted because its curve happened to look smoothest.

Derive Bayes' theorem from the definition of conditional probability, then use it: a test with 99 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity on a disease with 1 percent prevalence comes back positive. Give me the posterior, and then tell me in odds form how many independent positive tests it takes to get past 95 percent.

You are handed a column of per-account monthly API-call counts. Walk me through choosing a distribution: what do you compute first, what would make you reject Poisson, what would you fit instead, and what specifically goes wrong downstream if you choose wrong?

State the central limit theorem precisely, including its assumptions. Then give me three concrete situations in real product data where it does not apply, and how you would build an interval in each case.

Design: a customer wants to know whether variant B's 3.4 percent conversion beats variant A's 3.1 percent with 900 users per arm. Do it as a Bayesian - pick the prior and defend it, write down the posterior, say which quantity you report to the business, and tell me what you would do if the prior-sensitivity check changed the answer.
Explain conditional independence using a collider example, then tell me how you would decide whether a given feature belongs in a model that has to keep working on next quarter's data.

Debug: a fraud classifier has AUC 0.88 in validation, but the ops team says its 0.9-probability alerts are right about a third of the time. Nothing in the training loop errored. Where do you look, in what order, and what is your leading hypothesis?

You need samples from a distribution with no closed-form inverse CDF. Walk me through inverse-transform versus rejection sampling: what each requires, how you would choose the proposal, what the acceptance rate is, and why neither is what you would use in fifty dimensions.

Per-account API calls were modelled as Poisson because the mean matched, but the variance-to-mean ratio was 11; every standard error in the capacity forecast came out roughly three times too narrow and an ordinary busy week was reported to the customer as a five-sigma anomaly.

A latency dashboard reported mean +/- 2sd on a log-normal distribution, giving a lower bound of -40 ms and a 'p95' that 12 percent of requests exceeded; nobody caught it until the customer's SRE replotted the histogram on a log axis.

The isotonic calibrator was fitted on the same rows used to train the model, so the reliability diagram was a perfect diagonal in the notebook and badly S-shaped in production - a leakage bug that presents as a calibration success.

An A/B readout applied a normal-approximation interval to a 0.15 percent conversion rate with 800 users per arm; np was 1.2, the interval ran below zero, and the 'significant' 40 percent lift was a single extra conversion.

Eight parallel bootstrap workers were each seeded with seed + worker_id, the streams overlapped, replicates were correlated, and the resulting confidence interval came out about 30 percent too narrow with no visible symptom anywhere in the output.
