A churn model conditioned on 'opened a support ticket', a collider between product dissatisfaction and account size; the coefficient flipped sign relative to the population, the model validated beautifully on the historical split, and it inverted on the next cohort.

A Monte Carlo check of a posterior used 2,000 draws and matched the analytic answer to two decimals by luck; when the prior changed the two diverged, and because no MC standard error was ever reported, three days went into debugging an analytic derivation that was correct.

Per-row log costs were averaged and exponentiated to produce a 'mean cost per call' 18 percent below the invoice - Jensen's inequality, escalated to the customer as a billing discrepancy before anyone checked the arithmetic.

Derive Welch's t-statistic and its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, then tell me exactly when you would use it instead of the pooled Student version and what happens to the false-positive rate if you get that choice wrong.

Write out the sum-of-squares decomposition for one-way ANOVA and show that F = MSB/MSW. For k=2, what is the relationship between this F and the two-sample t? What does a significant F entitle you to say, and what does it not?

A customer's data scientist says 'the 95% CI is [1.2, 4.8], so there's a 95% chance the true lift is in that range'. Is that correct? Give the correct interpretation, and describe how you would empirically verify that an interval you wrote actually has 95% coverage.

Design: we have budget to human-label 2,000 evaluation examples once, and we want to know whether a new retriever beats the incumbent. Specify the design, the estimand, the test, the interval, how many examples you actually need, and how you would present a null result to the customer.

Debug: an offline eval reports the new model is 4 points better with p=0.004, but the online A/B shows no difference. Walk me through the candidate explanations in the order you would check them, and say which of them a confidence interval would and would not have caught.
When does the bootstrap fail? Give me at least three concrete cases, and for each one tell me what you would do instead.

You have 6 model variants and want to know which beat the baseline. Lay out the testing strategy: omnibus or not, which post-hoc procedure, FWER or FDR, and how you would explain the multiplicity correction to a product manager who thinks you are hiding a win.

The pilot readout says '0 failures in 40 calls, so reliability is 100%'; the Wald interval collapsed to zero width at phat=0 and the Wilson bound (or the rule of three, ~7.5%) would have shown the honest upper limit before it reached the customer's slide.

Two models are compared with a paired t-test over 10 cross-validation folds; the folds share training data so the variance is understated, the p-value is manufactured, and the 'significantly better' model loses in production.

A significant ANOVA F is driven entirely by one cohort with n=3 and huge variance created by a mislabelled category in the source table - a data-quality bug read as a scientific finding because nobody printed n_j, mean_j and s_j before testing.

A flat A/B result is sliced by 30 customer segments until one comes back at p=0.03; nobody adjusted for the family, and the resulting 'the product works for mid-market healthcare' claim does not replicate in the next quarter.

The team runs Shapiro-Wilk on 50,000 latency measurements, gets p<1e-20, abandons the t-test for a rank test that answers a different question (stochastic dominance, not means), and then reports the result as a difference in means anyway.

The bootstrap resamples rows when the data is clustered by user - one heavy user contributes 400 rows - so the interval is several times too narrow and the model's apparent lift survives a resampling check it should have failed.

The evaluation harness computes p = 1 - f.cdf(F, dfn, dfd) instead of f.sf(F, dfn, dfd); for large F the subtraction cancels to exactly 0.0 in float64, the test suite's 1e-6 comparison against scipy passes on the easy datasets and hides the bug until an extreme statistic appears.

A pooled Student t-test is used on cohorts of size 900 and 60 where the small cohort has three times the variance; the equal-variance assumption inflates the Type I error, and the resulting 'significant' improvement is an artefact of the imbalance rather than of the model.

Derive the per-arm sample size for a two-sample test of proportions from the rejection rule and the power requirement. Baseline conversion is 4%, the product team wants to detect a 5% relative lift at 80% power and α = 0.05 two-sided, and you get 40,000 eligible users per day. How long does the test run, and what are three legitimate ways to shorten it without changing α or power?

Explain to a customer's VP of Product, who has been checking the dashboard every morning, exactly why that invalidates the p-value. Then explain what a confidence sequence guarantees that a fixed-horizon confidence interval does not, and what it costs them at the planned sample size.

Debug: an A/A test on your platform returns significant results about 15% of the time on the click-through-rate metric but exactly 5% of the time on revenue per user. What are the two most likely causes, how do you distinguish them from the assignment and exposure logs, and what is the fix for each?

Design: a customer wants to know whether their new AI-assisted support triage reduces time-to-resolution. Agents work in teams, they talk to each other, and only 6 of their 30 teams handle the relevant ticket volume. Give me the design - randomisation unit, estimand, how you get a standard error you would defend, and what you would tell them you cannot measure.

Write down the CUPED estimator, prove it is unbiased, and derive the variance reduction factor. What exactly goes wrong if the covariate is measured during the experiment instead of before it, and what test would catch that mistake before the readout ships?

A customer has no experiment - they rolled the feature out to their EU region in March and want the impact. Draw the DAG you would sketch with them, state the identifying assumption for difference-in-differences in one sentence, name the plot that would falsify it, and say what you would do differently if six regions adopted it at six different times.

You are handed a readout showing a 22% lift on the primary metric with p = 0.001, computed on the users who were exposed to treatment versus everyone in control, with a 60/40 assignment split. List everything you would check before letting that number leave the building, in the order you would check it.

The team watched the dashboard daily and shipped the first day p dipped below 0.05; the fixed-horizon test had no sequential bound, the true false-positive rate for that procedure was above 25%, and the effect vanished on full rollout while the customer had already told their board about it.

CTR was computed as total clicks over total impressions with an impression-level standard error while randomisation was by user; the SE came out roughly four times too small, an A/A test would have flagged it, and a 0.4% 'significant' lift was pure noise.

A 50.4/49.6 split with a p-value of 1e-6 on the SRM chi-square was waved through as 'basically balanced'; the imbalance came from treatment users crashing before their telemetry flushed, so the surviving treatment users were systematically healthier and every metric looked better.

The guardrail was a two-sided test on p95 latency that came back p = 0.3, reported as 'no regression'; it was powered to detect only a 40 ms change, the true regression was 18 ms across every request, and support tickets started three weeks after launch.

In a two-sided marketplace, treatment buyers absorbed inventory that control buyers would otherwise have bought; the measured 12% conversion lift was mostly redistribution, and the global rollout produced a fraction of it because the control group had been the source of the gain.

Analysts compared users who actually opened the new panel against the entire control group; conditioning on a post-treatment engagement variable reintroduced selection bias, turning a roughly flat effect into a reported 35% lift that no rollout ever reproduced.

CUPED was applied with a covariate computed over the experiment window rather than the pre-period; the adjustment absorbed part of the treatment effect itself, shrinking the estimate toward zero, and the A/A validation that would have exposed it was never rerun after the covariate changed.

Forty segments were sliced post-hoc with no correction, one came back at p = 0.03, and 'the feature works for enterprise users on Android' became a roadmap commitment built on an expected-by-chance result in a segment of 900 users.

Derive cross-entropy loss from maximum likelihood. Then, using CE(P,Q) = H(P) + KL(P||Q), tell me which term your optimiser can reduce and which it cannot, and what that means for a model whose validation loss has been stuck at 0.42 nats for twenty epochs.

KL is not symmetric. Sketch the result of fitting a single Gaussian to a bimodal target by minimising KL(P||Q) and then by minimising KL(Q||P), and tell me which direction a VAE's ELBO uses and which one ordinary supervised training uses.

Debug: your language model's loss goes 3.1, 3.0, 2.9, then nan at step 4000. Walk me through what you check and in what order, and say which candidate causes would show up in the logits, which in the data loader, and which only in the loss implementation itself.

Design: a customer has a fraud label with a 0.2 percent base rate and wants a number they can multiply by transaction value to set a review threshold. What loss do you train, what do you do about the imbalance, and how do you guarantee that what you hand them is a probability rather than a score?

Explain why perplexity is not comparable between two models with different tokenisers and what you would report instead. Then tell me what a perplexity of 11.6 on a 27-symbol character model actually says about that model.

A stakeholder says 'the model is 99 percent confident'. What do you check before letting that sentence leave the room, what plot do you produce, and what is the cheapest correct fix if the number is wrong?

Someone rebalanced the classes by reweighting and reports better recall. Explain what the reweighting did to the implied prior, write down the logit correction that returns the outputs to the true base rate, and tell me when you would reach for focal loss instead.
A team reports 'loss 2.1' with no unit; the model was training in nats while the published baseline was in bits/char, so a real gap of nothing at all was chased for a month across a factor of 1.4427.

The training script does softmax, then log, then NLL instead of log_softmax plus NLL; one logit reaches 90 on a hard example, the softmax underflows to exactly 0 on the true class, the loss becomes inf and the gradients nan - and because the nan appears mid-epoch it gets filed as a corrupt data batch.

Class weights were added for imbalance and never undone; the model is calibrated for a 50/50 world, the customer's ops team sets a 0.5 threshold on the raw output, and a review queue sized for 20 cases a day receives 900.

Mutual-information feature screening put a near-unique transaction identifier at the top of the list because the plug-in estimator's finite-sample bias rewards high cardinality; the column survived into training, cross-validation looked superb, and the model was worthless in production.

label_smoothing=0.1 was set on the training criterion but not on the evaluation criterion, so validation loss came out below training loss, the team concluded the model was underfitting and burned three more days of GPU on a larger one.

A drift monitor computed KL(current || reference) over binned features; one reference bin was empty, KL returned inf, the dashboard clamped it to its axis maximum, and a genuine distribution shift a fortnight later was invisible because it produced the identical clamped value.

A distillation script passed raw student logits into torch.nn.KLDivLoss with reduction='mean'; the loss was divided by N*C so the distillation term shrank by a factor of the vocabulary size, contributed nothing to the gradient, and the student quietly trained on hard labels only while the config claimed otherwise.

Model selection was done on AUC because 'the customer only cares about ranking', but the customer's actual decision multiplies the predicted probability by transaction value; the winning model was badly overconfident, and every expected-cost figure they acted on was wrong by roughly a factor of three until log loss and a reliability plot were finally checked.

Derive the log-sum-exp trick and show it is an exact identity, not an approximation. Then tell me what happens when an entire row of logits is -inf, why that occurs in a padded transformer batch, and what you would change in the masking to fix it.

Your training loss goes 3.1, 3.0, 2.9 and then nan at step 4000. Walk me through your triage in order, and say which candidate causes would show up in the forward activations, which only in the backward pass, and which in the data loader - and how you would tell them apart with evidence rather than intuition.

Why can var = mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2 return a negative number in float64? Write the Welford update on the whiteboard, tell me what M2 is, and extend it to a merge formula so I can compute the variance of a 400 GB dataset in parallel chunks.

A customer's linear model gives different coefficients from ours on the same data. Their code solves the normal equations, ours calls np.linalg.lstsq. Explain what the condition number of X has to do with it, how many digits each approach retains, and what you would tell them to change in their feature preparation.

Here is a Python loop that computes pairwise distances over 50000 rows of 100 features. Rewrite it as a broadcast NumPy expression, tell me the peak memory before you run it, then tell me why the fast gemm-based version is numerically dangerous in float32 and what you would do instead.

The same script on my laptop and on the customer's 64-core server agrees to only seven decimal places. Give me every mechanism that could explain that, say which ones are acceptable to ship, and describe how you would pin the ones that are not.
When is vectorising a loop the wrong move? Give me two concrete situations, and tell me how you would benchmark to make that case to a teammate who believes all loops are bugs.

A standardiser computes variance as mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2 on a Unix-timestamp column near 1.7e9; catastrophic cancellation makes the result slightly negative, np.sqrt returns nan, the whole feature becomes nan, the imputer replaces it with the column mean of 0, and the model trains happily on a constant column while the feature-importance chart still lists it.

An ID column is cast to float32 somewhere in a Spark-to-pandas hop; above 2^24 consecutive integers are no longer representable, distinct customer IDs collide onto the same value, the train/test split leaks, and offline AUC beats production by fifteen points.

A residual is computed as y - yhat where y has shape (n,) and yhat has shape (n, 1); broadcasting yields an (n, n) matrix, the loss becomes the mean of n^2 terms, it still decreases smoothly during training, and nobody notices until the deployed model's predictions are off by a constant factor.

Feature counts are accumulated with `counts[idx] += 1` where idx contains repeats; the read-modify-write applies once per unique index, so every count above one is wrong, the pipeline runs clean, and the downstream frequency-encoded feature is quietly garbage until np.add.at is used instead.

A metric helper clips probabilities to [1e-15, 1-1e-15] before taking a log, so a model that outputs hard 0 and 1 predictions scores a finite, respectable log loss instead of infinity; the clip flatters the very overconfidence the metric was supposed to expose.

An attention mask fills padded positions with -inf; a row that is entirely padding makes max(z) = -inf, so z - max is nan inside softmax, the loss becomes nan at a random step deep into training, and the incident is filed for two days as a corrupt data shard.

A nearest-neighbour or RAG retrieval computes squared distances in float32 via the ||x||^2 - 2xy + ||y||^2 expansion on high-magnitude embeddings; cancellation leaves the small true distances as rounding noise, the returned neighbours are wrong but plausible, and the retrieval quality drop is blamed on the embedding model.

A gradient check passes because np.allclose's default atol=1e-8 declares an analytic gradient of 1e-9 equal to a numeric gradient of 3e-9; a whole branch of the backward pass is effectively dead, training converges to a worse optimum, and it is never revisited because there is a green test.

Derive the normal equations, then tell me what happens when X'X is singular, what numpy's lstsq returns in that case, and why you would never implement the estimator as inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y even when it is invertible.

Explain ridge versus lasso three ways: the constrained-optimisation picture, what the SVD says each one does to a principal direction, and the prior each corresponds to. Then tell me which you would choose for a customer with 4000 rows, 900 heavily correlated features and a mandate to name the drivers - and what you would say about the stability of that list.

Write down the bias-variance decomposition for squared loss and tell me exactly what the expectation is taken over. Which of the three terms can you estimate from a single customer dataset, which cannot, and how would you get a number for the one that can?

Derive the gradient and the Hessian of the logistic negative log-likelihood. Why is there no closed-form solution, why is the problem convex, and what does the Hessian tell you about what happens when one feature perfectly separates the classes?

Debug: cross-validated R-squared is 0.98 but the holdout file the customer sent back scores 0.42. Walk me through your checks in order, and say which candidate causes would show up in the learning curve, which in a feature-versus-target audit, and which only in the pipeline code.

I show you a learning curve where training error is 0.02, validation error is 0.31, and the gap has not closed by the largest training size. What do you do, and what would have to be different in that plot for 'get more data' to be the wrong recommendation?

A stakeholder points at a coefficient of 1.8 on 'number of support tickets' in a churn model and asks whether reducing tickets will reduce churn. Answer them, and tell me what you would need to change about the study to be allowed to say yes.

StandardScaler was fit on the full dataset before cross_val_score, so every validation fold's mean and variance leaked into training; the CV RMSE looked excellent, the customer's fresh extract scored 30 percent worse, and it was investigated as data drift for a week.

Ridge was fitted on unscaled features where lot area is in square feet and a flag is 0/1; the penalty barely touched the large-unit column and crushed the flag, so the coefficient ranking presented as 'the drivers of price' was really a ranking of measurement units.

A lasso selected twelve of nine hundred features and the deck called them 'the twelve drivers of churn'; the features were pairwise correlated above 0.9, a different random seed selected a different twelve, and the customer had already staffed a team against the first list.

Someone set C=0.01 in LogisticRegression believing C was a penalty weight rather than its inverse; the model collapsed to nearly the base rate, and because AUC was still 0.62 nobody noticed until an ops threshold was set on the probabilities.

One-hot encoding kept every level alongside an intercept in an unpenalised OLS; X'X was singular, lstsq quietly returned the minimum-norm solution out of infinitely many, and the coefficients that were compared across two quarterly refits were not even the same estimand.

A perfectly separating feature - a status flag set only after the outcome - drove logistic coefficients to infinity, but scikit-learn's default L2 returned a tidy finite number with a 0.999 AUC, so a leaked column was presented as a model rather than caught as a bug.

Residuals fanned out with fitted value and nobody plotted them; the plain OLS standard errors were far too narrow, three 'statistically significant' drivers were reported to the customer, and none survived when HC3 robust errors were finally used.

Alpha was tuned by GridSearchCV and the best cross-validated score from that same search was quoted as the model's performance; the selection bias was worth several points, and the honest nested-CV number arrived only after the contract had been signed against the optimistic one.

Derive the gradient-boosting leaf value for log loss from a second-order expansion. Start from L = -[y log p + (1-y) log(1-p)], get g and the Hessian, write w_j* = -G/(H + lambda), and then tell me what min_child_weight is thresholding and why that value means something completely different on a regression problem.

Write the split-gain formula XGBoost uses and explain from it, not from documentation, what gamma and lambda each do to the resulting tree. What happens to gain when a candidate child contains only rows the model already predicts confidently?

Debug: training RMSE is 0.02 and validation RMSE is 1.4 and rising after round 300, on 6000 rows with 400 features. Give me the order in which you turn knobs and the reason for each, and tell me which of those changes you expect to help least.

When would you pick LightGBM over XGBoost and when would that choice actively hurt you? Explain leaf-wise versus level-wise growth in terms of capacity and variance, and give me the parameter that is your guardrail in each library.

Design: a customer has three years of daily demand per SKU, 40 features, heavy zero-inflation, and wants a number their ordering system can act on plus an interval. What objective, what validation split, what do you do about categorical SKU identifiers, and what do you hand them to show the model is trustworthy?

A colleague shows you a random forest with 0.99 cross-validated AUC and a feature-importance chart. What are the first four things you check, and for each one say what the symptom would look like and what it would do to the reported number?

Explain why bagging needs deep unpruned trees while boosting needs shallow ones. Use the Var(mean) = rho*sigma^2 + ((1-rho)/B)*sigma^2 decomposition in your answer, and say what random forests change to attack which term.

Mean target encoding was computed over the entire training set before the CV split, so each row's feature encodes its own label; cross-validated AUC came in at 0.97, the model shipped, and production AUC was 0.61 with no code change to blame.

num_leaves was left at LightGBM's default 31 on an 8000-row dataset with min_data_in_leaf untouched; leaf-wise growth drove one branch deep enough to isolate individual rows, training loss went to nearly zero, and the model memorised the training set while every default-looking parameter appeared reasonable in the config.

The evals list passed to xgb.train ended with the training set rather than the validation set, so EarlyStopping watched training loss, never triggered, and the run trained to the 5000-round cap - the log looked clean and nobody noticed until inference latency tripled.

feature_importances_ from a random forest was presented to the customer's leadership as 'the drivers of churn'; the top feature was a near-unique account identifier whose MDI score came from cardinality bias, and a quarter of retention budget was reallocated on the strength of an artefact of the fitting procedure.

A booster was validated with a plain KFold on data holding dozens of rows per customer and months of history; the same customer appeared in train and validation folds, every metric was inflated, and the model that won selection was the one best at recognising customers rather than predicting behaviour.

Predictions were generated with the full ensemble instead of iteration_range=(0, best_iteration + 1) after an early-stopped fit, so the overfit tail of trees was included at inference; scores drifted from the validated numbers by a few points and the discrepancy was investigated for a week as a feature-pipeline mismatch.

A demand model was trained with reg:squarederror on right-skewed daily counts and predicted negative demand for low-volume SKUs, which the downstream ordering system clipped to zero; the clipping hid the misspecification, and the real problem - the wrong noise model, needing count:poisson or a Tweedie objective - went undiagnosed for a full planning cycle.

A booster trained on two years of prices was asked to forecast a period above the historical maximum; because a tree's prediction is the boundary leaf's constant, every forecast flatlined at the highest observed value, and the flat line was read as a stable market rather than an extrapolation failure.

Derive the soft-margin SVM dual from the primal. Where exactly do the box constraints 0 <= alpha_i <= C come from, and what does complementary slackness tell you about a point with alpha_i = C versus one with 0 < alpha_i < C?

Explain what C and gamma each do, geometrically and statistically. I hand you a model with 90 percent of rows as support vectors, 100 percent training accuracy and 55 percent test accuracy - which knob do you move, in which direction, and what do you expect n_SV to do?
Why does k-NN break down in high dimensions? Give me both the volume argument and the distance-concentration argument, then explain why a linear SVM on 30,000 TF-IDF features is perfectly fine.

Multinomial Naive Bayes assumes words are conditionally independent given the class, which is plainly false for text. Why does it still classify well, and where precisely does the false assumption show up in the model's output?

Design: a customer has 12 million support tickets, 60,000 TF-IDF features, 8 classes at a 200-to-1 imbalance, needs a label in under 30 ms at p99, and retrains monthly on one 32 GB box. Pick a model, defend it against the other two, and tell me what you would measure to discover you were wrong.
Debug: an RBF SVM cross-validates at 0.97 and scores 0.71 on the customer's holdout from the following month. Give me your ordered hypotheses and the specific check for each, cheapest first.

Someone shows you a ComplementNB text classifier at 94 percent accuracy on a 20-to-1 imbalanced dataset and wants to route tickets on its predict_proba. What do you ask for before you believe the number, and what would you have plotted?

Features were never scaled before an RBF SVM, so the exponent -gamma||x - x'||^2 is dominated by the one column measured in dollars; every binary flag is invisible to the kernel and two weeks are burned sweeping a gamma grid that cannot repair it.

StandardScaler or TfidfVectorizer was fitted on the full dataset before train_test_split; k-NN and SVM validation scores come in three to five points high, none of it reproduces on the customer's holdout, and the gap is misdiagnosed as distribution drift rather than leakage.

C was tuned on a 5,000-row prototype and carried over to the customer's 500,000-row table; because scikit-learn's C weights a summed rather than averaged hinge loss, the effective regularisation is roughly 100 times weaker and the model memorises while the code diff shows no change at all.

n_SV came back at 92 percent of the training set and nobody looked; gamma was large enough that each support vector covered only itself, so the deployed artefact was an expensive 1-NN with perfect training accuracy, a 40 MB model file and chance-level generalisation.

k-NN was benchmarked on a 5,000-row sample where it beat everything, then deployed against 8 million rows; the index no longer fits the pod's memory limit, p99 latency is 900 ms against a 50 ms SLA, and no hyperparameter fixes it because the cost is structural.

A hand-rolled MultinomialNB shipped without smoothing, or with alpha = 0; one word appearing only in the test set gives a log-probability of negative infinity for one class, and every document containing it is assigned to the other class regardless of the other four hundred words.

A 99-to-1 imbalanced dataset was reported at 98.7 percent accuracy with k = 25; every neighbourhood was majority-class so the model never predicted the positive class even once, and the metric flattered a classifier with exactly zero recall on the only class the customer cares about.

predict_proba from SVC(probability=True) was used for ranking while predict supplied the label; Platt scaling was fitted by internal CV on a small set, the two disagreed on about 1 percent of rows, and the customer's audit surfaced records labelled approved with an approval score of 0.42.

Derive the threshold that minimises expected cost for a calibrated binary classifier given C_fp and C_fn, and tell me what has to be true about the model for that derivation to hold. Then tell me what you do instead when the constraint is not a cost but a team that can review 50 alerts a day.

A customer's model reports 0.94 AUC in cross-validation and 0.62 in production two weeks after launch. Walk me through your diagnostic order - what you check first, second and third - and for each candidate cause tell me the specific artefact that would confirm it.
Explain what cross-validation actually estimates. Given 5-fold scores of [0.81, 0.84, 0.79, 0.86, 0.80], what would you quote to a customer, and why is std/sqrt(5) not the standard error you want?

You are handed a table with a customer_id, an event timestamp, and a label defined as 'churned within 60 days'. Design the evaluation from scratch: the splitter, the purge and embargo, the metric, the threshold procedure, and the three sanity checks you run before you show anyone a number.

Two models have identical ROC-AUC of 0.88. One has log loss 0.31 and the other 0.47. Explain how that is possible, tell me which one you would ship and under what conditions, and describe exactly what you would do to the worse one and what would and would not change afterwards.

Design a leakage screen you could run automatically over any customer feature table before training. What does it compute, what is the threshold for flagging, what are its false positives, and what does it fundamentally not catch?

Someone reports an expected calibration error of 0.01 and concludes the probabilities are trustworthy. What questions do you ask about how that number was computed, and what would you ask to see instead?

A churn model trained on a warehouse snapshot included `days_since_last_login`, which the ETL recomputes nightly against the current date; churned accounts stopped logging in, so the feature encoded the label, cross-validated AUC was 0.97, and live AUC was 0.61 in the first week.

Medical images were split randomly instead of by patient, so scans of the same 400 patients appeared on both sides; the model learned patient identity, reported 0.95 AUC in the pilot, and dropped to near chance on the customer's next hospital.

SMOTE was applied to the whole dataset before cross-validation, so synthetic minority points interpolated from validation rows sat in every training fold; recall looked transformed, the customer sized a review team from it, and the real recall was roughly half.

Feature selection picked the top 200 of 40,000 columns by correlation with the target on the full dataset, then a clean 10-fold CV ran on the survivors; the model reported 0.88 AUC on data whose labels were randomly permuted, and nobody ran that sanity check for four months.

A demand forecaster was evaluated with shuffled K-fold on a time-indexed table, so every fold trained on the future to predict the past; MAPE looked excellent, and the first real four-week-ahead backtest was three times worse.

Class weights were used for a rare-event model and never undone; the scores were calibrated for a balanced world, the ops team applied the default 0.5 threshold, and a queue built for 20 cases a day received 900 on the first Monday.

The reported metric was 99.4 percent accuracy on a 0.6 percent fraud base rate - a model that predicted 'not fraud' unconditionally scored 99.4 percent, and the deck went to the customer's executive sponsor before anyone plotted a confusion matrix.

ECE was reported at 0.008 with 10 uniform-width bins on predictions that all fell below 0.05; nine bins were empty, the single populated bin averaged an overconfident and an underconfident region together, and the reliability diagram drawn later with quantile bins showed a systematic 3x overstatement of risk.

Derive the smoothed target encoding formula from a Beta-Binomial posterior. What does the smoothing parameter mean in units of data, how would you choose it for a column where 80 percent of categories have fewer than five rows, and why must the encoding be computed out-of-fold?

A customer has a 0.2 percent positive rate and their model reports 0.99 ROC-AUC. Write down the relationship between precision, TPR, FPR and prevalence, and use it to explain to their VP why that number tells you almost nothing about whether the model is deployable.

Explain what SMOTE does geometrically and state the assumptions it makes. Given a table with 40 numeric and 12 categorical columns, 3 percent positives, and an XGBoost model, would you use it? Justify with the control arms you would run and the metric you would compare on.

Design the validation scheme for a fraud model where each customer has many transactions, fraud is 0.5 percent, the data spans two years, and the model will score transactions in real time. Name the splitter, the metric, the threshold-selection procedure, and every feature-engineering step that has to move inside the fold.

Debug: a colleague's pipeline scores 0.93 PR-AUC in cross-validation and 0.21 on the holdout month. You have their notebook. What are the four things you check, in order, and what would each look like in the code?

class_weight='balanced' versus SMOTE versus threshold tuning: derive what each one does to the loss, the decision boundary and the predicted probability, and say which you would reach for when the model's output is consumed as a probability rather than a ranking.

Permutation importance says a feature has zero importance, but dropping it and refitting makes the model measurably worse. Explain how both results can be true, and what you would do to get an importance ranking you would show a customer.

The target encoder is fit on the full dataset before the split, so a 10k-cardinality merchant ID becomes an almost perfect in-sample predictor; CV reports 0.95 PR-AUC, production reports roughly the base rate, and the column looks like the model's most important feature in SHAP the whole time.

SMOTE is applied to X, y before StratifiedKFold, putting interpolants of the same positive in both train and validation; the score jumps twenty points, nobody can reproduce it on the holdout month, and the team spends a week blaming distribution shift.

ROC-AUC is chosen as the headline metric because it reads 0.98; at the operating threshold the customer can actually staff, precision is 4 percent, their analysts drown in false positives, and the model is switched off in week three.

A per-card historical fraud rate is computed over the entire dataset rather than an expanding window, so every training row knows about future frauds on that card; the feature dominates importance rankings and contributes nothing after deployment.

class_weight='balanced' is used for a model whose output feeds an expected-loss calculation; discrimination is fine but the probabilities are inflated by the implicit prior shift, so the customer's reserve numbers are systematically too high and no one traces it back to the weighting.

Features are selected once with SelectKBest on the whole dataset and cross-validation is run afterwards on the surviving columns; the selection already saw the validation labels, so every subsequent score is optimistically biased and hyperparameter search happily overfits into the gap.

Multiple transactions per card are split with plain StratifiedKFold rather than StratifiedGroupKFold, so the model memorises cards instead of behaviour and scores far better in CV than on any card it has never seen.

SMOTE is run on one-hot encoded columns, producing synthetic rows with 0.37 in a binary indicator and impossible category combinations; the model learns off-manifold structure, and the customer's domain expert loses confidence in the whole engagement the moment they inspect a generated row.

Derive the probability that random search finds a configuration in the top p fraction of the space within n trials, and use it to justify a trial budget to a customer. Then tell me what assumption of that derivation your actual search space usually violates.

Explain how TPE picks its next point. Write down what l(x) and g(x) are, how gamma enters, and why maximising expected improvement reduces to maximising the density ratio. When would you use a Gaussian-process surrogate with expected improvement instead, and what does the closed form of EI look like?

Design: a customer gives you a 200k-row tabular dataset, a LightGBM baseline, one 8-core box and four hours. Specify the search space, the CV scheme, the objective, the budget, the pruning strategy, and exactly how you will report the result so it holds up when they retrain next quarter.

Your Optuna study reports 0.93 AUC on the best trial and the held-out test set returns 0.87. Walk me through your diagnosis in order. Which candidate causes are leakage, which are selection on noise, and what experiment separates the two?

Successive halving eliminates on a fraction of the training rows. Explain the bias that introduces, give me a concrete case where the eventual best configuration is eliminated in the first rung, and describe how you would change the resource or the schedule to avoid it.

You have optimisation-history, param-importance and slice plots from a 300-trial study. For each plot, tell me one specific pattern that would make you stop the search, one that would make you widen a range, and one that would make you delete a parameter from the space.

A customer needs AUC above 0.85 and p99 inference latency under 40 milliseconds. How do you set the search up so you are not silently choosing their trade-off for them, and what artifact do you hand back?

The scaler and target encoder are fitted on the full training frame before the Optuna loop starts, so every one of 400 trials scores against leaked statistics; CV reports 0.91 AUC, the customer's holdout returns 0.84, and the search is blamed for overfitting when the harness was wrong before the first trial.

LightGBM early stopping is evaluated on the same fold that produces the trial's score, so the validation set is used twice and every configuration looks a little better than it is - uniformly enough that the ranking survives and nobody notices until the gap appears in production.

The MedianPruner is left at n_warmup_steps=0, so low-learning-rate configurations that are slow for the first 100 trees and best at 900 are killed at trial step 20; the search converges confidently on a high-learning-rate model that is measurably worse at full fidelity.

TPE with 500 trials is compared against random search with 500 trials, but TPE pruned 60 percent of its trials at low fidelity; the comparison is reported as trials-for-trials, TPE looks dramatically better, and the same experiment measured in wall-clock shows no difference.

learning_rate is sampled uniformly on [1e-4, 1e-1] instead of log-uniformly, so 90 percent of draws land above 1e-2, the optimum near 3e-3 is never sampled, and the slice plot showing every good trial pressed against the left edge of the range is never looked at.

HalvingRandomSearchCV eliminates on n_samples with min_resources='smallest', so the first rung ranks configurations on 3 percent of the data where heavily regularised low-capacity models dominate; the high-capacity winner is eliminated in rung one and can never come back.

Two workers run study.optimize against the same SQLite storage with a fixed sampler seed; the run is presented as reproducible, but the sampler conditions on whichever trials committed first, so the rerun for the customer produces a different winner and the whole result loses credibility.

The tuned model beats defaults by 0.004 AUC while the fold-to-fold standard error is 0.02; the improvement is written into a deliverable as a real gain, the customer retrains on next month's data, the ordering flips, and the tuning process is what gets distrusted.
Derive the two k-means update steps from the objective. Why must the distance be squared Euclidean, what does Lloyd's algorithm guarantee about convergence, and what does it explicitly not guarantee?

I hand you a 200k x 80 table of account behaviour, mixed numeric and categorical, and ask for segments I can act on. Walk me through the preprocessing, the distance, the algorithm, how you choose the number of segments, and what artefact you would show me to convince me the segments are real rather than an artefact of the objective.

Explain what DBSCAN's eps and min_samples do and how you would set them without grid-searching for a pretty answer. What is a border point, why is its assignment order-dependent, and how do you score a new point tomorrow against a fitted DBSCAN model?

Derive PCA from both the covariance eigenproblem and the SVD and state what Eckart-Young gives you. Why do real implementations use the SVD rather than forming X^T X, and what exactly does it mean that two implementations' components match 'up to sign'?

A colleague shows a UMAP plot with two large well-separated islands and one small one, and concludes there are three customer types and that the small one is very different from the others. Which parts of that conclusion are supported by the method, which are not, and what would you compute before it goes in front of the customer?

Compare Ward linkage with k-means. Under what conditions do they produce similar partitions, why is Ward restricted to Euclidean distance, and when would you pay the O(n^2) memory cost to get the hierarchy instead?

Debug: your pipeline produced six stable segments in the pilot, and after the customer's next data drop it produces two giant segments plus 30 percent noise. What are the four things you check, in what order, and what would each look like in the data?

Columns were not standardised before k-means, so annual_revenue in dollars dominated the squared-Euclidean objective; the 'behavioural segmentation' delivered to marketing was a revenue quantile split with extra steps, and nobody noticed until a segment was defined by a currency conversion.

The scaler and PCA were fit on the whole table before the downstream classifier's train/test split, so the clustering-derived features carried information from the test rows and the supervised metric was inflated by several points that evaporated in production.

k was chosen from an elbow that did not exist on a smooth inertia curve; the selected k=4 had a mean silhouette of 0.19 with two clusters containing substantial negative-silhouette membership, and the segmentation did not reproduce on the next quarter's data.

DBSCAN was run over 60 one-hot columns with the default eps=0.5; distance concentration meant the result was either one giant cluster or 90 percent noise, and eps was tuned until the cluster count looked plausible instead of until the k-distance knee justified it.

A t-SNE plot with two clean, well-separated blobs went into a customer deck as evidence of two customer types; the same data showed six blobs at perplexity 5 and one at perplexity 50, and a permuted-data null produced visually similar structure.

Cluster IDs were regenerated on every nightly retrain with no stable-ID mapping, so the dashboard's 'Segment 3' quietly became a different population and every trend line in the customer's QBR deck compared two unrelated groups.

A border point's DBSCAN assignment was used to justify an account's segment; because border points go to whichever cluster reaches them first, re-running with shuffled row order moved several hundred accounts between segments and the customer found it before the team did.

PCA was applied before clustering to 'remove noise', with components chosen at 95 percent cumulative variance on unstandardised data; the discarded low-variance directions were exactly the ones separating the two groups the customer cared about, and no downstream algorithm could recover them.

Derive the Shapley value from its axioms, then show how KernelSHAP recovers it as a weighted linear regression. What is the Shapley kernel, why does it diverge at |z| = 0 and |z| = M, and how does a correct implementation handle those two coalitions?

Your permutation importance ranking on the test set contradicts the customer's domain expert, who insists feature X drives their business. Walk me through the diagnosis: what do you check, in what order, and what does each outcome tell you?
Explain the difference between a PDP, an M-plot and an ALE plot for a feature correlated at 0.8 with another. Which do you show the customer, and what exactly do you say about the other two?

Debug: your from-scratch KernelSHAP values sum to 0.31 for a row where the model's margin minus the base value is 0.44. Give me four candidate causes ranked by likelihood, and the single check that distinguishes each one.

Design: a fraud model scores 40 million transactions a day and compliance wants a per-decision explanation retained for seven years. What do you compute, when do you compute it, what exactly do you store, and what do you tell them the stored numbers do and do not mean?
After seeing your partial dependence plot, a stakeholder asks whether increasing X will increase Y. What is your answer, and under precisely what assumptions would the PDP support a causal statement?
Give me two distinct mechanisms by which a SHAP value of zero does not mean the model ignored that feature, and say how you would detect each one.

Permutation importance is computed on the training set for a deep, barely regularised ensemble; every feature looks important because the model memorised, the customer trusts the ranking, drops the one feature you called weak, and held-out AUC falls.

monthly_spend and annual_spend/12 are both in the frame; each permuted alone costs the model almost nothing, both score near zero, the team removes both to simplify the pipeline, and recall drops six points overnight.

xgboost.plot_importance is pasted into a deck with the default importance_type='weight', so the chart is really a split-count ranking dominated by a high-cardinality near-identifier, and the customer's team spends a sprint investigating a column that carries no signal.

A PDP over a feature correlated at 0.9 with another is presented as 'raising price from 10 to 200 does nothing to churn'; the flat curve came from scoring rows that cannot exist (price 200 with plan='free'), and the ALE plot on the same data shows a steep effect.

TreeSHAP is run with the default path-dependent perturbation and the output is described to a compliance reviewer as each field's contribution to the decision; two correlated fields split credit for a decision the model actually made on only one of them.

A waterfall reading '+1.4 for income' is quoted as a probability change when the explainer returned raw log-odds, so the real effect is about five percentage points, and the correction arrives after the deck is already with the customer's risk committee.

LIME explanations for a disputed case are regenerated a week later with a different seed and num_samples; the top three features change, the customer sees two versions of the same explanation, and nobody had ever printed the local R^2 of 0.18 that would have shown the surrogate never fit in the first place.

The KernelSHAP background was shap.sample(X_train, 100) with no seed and was never saved; six months later, during a dispute, the stored attributions cannot be reproduced and there is no way to show the explanation attached to that decision was ever correct.

Derive the prediction-interval variance for an ARIMA h-step forecast from the MA(infinity) representation, then tell me three reasons the empirical coverage of that interval will be below nominal on real data and what you would do about each.

I hand you three years of daily sales for 1800 store-product pairs and ask for a 16-day forecast. Walk me from raw CSV to a defended model: what you plot first, how you decide the transform and the differencing orders, what you can and cannot use AICc for, and how you decide between 1800 SARIMAs and one LightGBM.

ADF gives p = 0.28 and KPSS gives p = 0.01 on the same series. What does each test's null hypothesis say, what do you conclude, and what do you do next? Now tell me what it means if ADF gives p = 0.02 and KPSS also gives p = 0.01.

Design an honest backtest for a model whose features include a 28-day rolling mean and a target encoding of store_id, refitting quarterly in production. Specify the window type, the gap, the fold spacing, the refit cadence, how hyperparameters are selected, and one automated test that would fail if any of it leaked.
A colleague's Prophet model reports 8% MAPE in backtest and 22% in production. The code has no obvious shuffle. Where do you look, in what order, and which three checks would you run first?

Explain MASE: write the formula, say why the denominator is in-sample rather than out-of-sample, and explain what MASE = 0.85 means. Then tell me when you would refuse to use it and what you would use instead.

Your per-store forecasts and your national forecast disagree by 3%. Explain to the customer's CFO why that happens, then describe bottom-up, top-down and MinT reconciliation and which one you would ship and why.

You fit SARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1)_7 and Ljung-Box on the residuals gives p = 0.003 with a clear ACF spike at lag 30. Interpret it, and tell me what you change about the model versus what you change about the features.

The backtest used sklearn KFold or a random train_test_split, so future weeks trained the model that predicts past weeks; MASE came out at 0.4, the deck said 'beats baseline by 60%', and the first live month came in at 1.2.

Rolling features were built as df.groupby('store').sales.rolling(7).mean() without a .shift(1), so every training row contained its own target inside the window; the model looked near-perfect in backtest and collapsed to seasonal-naive quality in production because that feature is unavailable at forecast time.

The Box-Cox lambda and the StandardScaler were fitted on the full series before folding, so every fold's training data carried summary statistics of its own test window; the leak is small, invisible in any plot, and consistently makes the reported error 5-15% too low.

Forecasts were produced on a log scale and exponentiated back without the bias adjustment, so every number shipped was a median; the customer summed 54 store forecasts into a national plan that ran a few percent under actuals every single month and nobody could find the bug.

res.get_prediction(dynamic=False) was used to generate the 'backtest' chart, so every plotted point was a one-step-ahead prediction conditioned on the true previous value; the fit hugged the data beautifully and the model had never once forecast 16 days ahead.

The series was differenced twice 'to be safe' - d=1 plus D=1 on a series that only needed the seasonal difference - which pushed a root of the MA polynomial onto the unit circle; statsmodels enforced invertibility silently, the innovation variance roughly doubled, and the prediction intervals shipped twice as wide as they needed to be.

MAPE was the reported metric on retail data containing zero-sales days; the zero rows were dropped to avoid the division by zero, which quietly removed exactly the hardest observations, and the surviving asymmetry made the systematically under-forecasting model look like the winner.

Prophet was fitted with the default changepoint_prior_scale on a series whose last six weeks were a COVID-style dip; it placed changepoints in that window, extrapolated the dip as the new trend, and produced a confidently declining 12-month forecast with intervals that never covered the recovery.

The Kaggle test window's oil price and onpromotion columns were joined as exogenous regressors and the model was praised for its accuracy; in the customer's deployment neither column exists for future dates, so the whole feature set had to be rebuilt and the accuracy claim retracted.

Derive the regularised matrix-factorisation objective with user and item biases and give me the SGD update for p_u and q_i. Now fix Q and derive the closed-form update for p_u. Which would you run on two billion interactions on the customer's Spark cluster, and why?

Held-out RMSE improved from 0.912 to 0.897 but recall@10 fell from 0.28 to 0.24. Explain the mechanism that produces both at once, tell me which number you take to the customer, and say what you would change about the training objective.

Design a recommender for a marketplace with 4M buyers, 900k listings, no ratings, only clicks and purchases, and 60 percent of listings younger than seven days. Specify model, loss, negative sampling, split, metrics, cold-start path and serving architecture, then tell me where it fails first.
How does an isolation forest score a point? Write the score formula, explain what c(psi) is and where it comes from, and say why the score normalises expected path length rather than using raw depth.

Your isolation forest has PR-AUC 0.31 on labelled historical fraud, but in the pilot the top-100 queue is 95 percent legitimate high-value transactions. List your hypotheses in the order you would test them and say what evidence would settle each.
When would you tell a customer not to use an isolation forest? Give me three concrete data situations and the alternative you would reach for in each.

With 492 positives in 284,807 rows, model A has precision@100 of 0.34 and model B has 0.38. Is B better? Explain how you decide, and what exactly you would put in front of the customer to justify the choice.

A random 80/20 split is taken over a timestamped interaction log, so a user's later sessions sit in train and predict their earlier ones; offline recall@10 reads 0.31, the pilot delivers 0.06, and the model is blamed instead of the protocol.

Truncated SVD is run on the ratings matrix with unobserved entries left as stored zeros; the factors learn to predict near zero, held-out RMSE still looks respectable because the held-out set is zero-heavy too, and the top-K lists are effectively random.

The top-K candidate set is not filtered against the user's training history, so recall@10 is inflated by re-recommending items the user already consumed; the metric halves the day the filter is added, which is the week after the quarterly review.

Model selection is done on RMSE alone: k = 64 beats k = 16 on RMSE by fitting mid-scale ratings on popular items, but recall@10 drops, and the shipped model is worse than the one it replaced while the dashboard says it improved.

The cold-start path is never exercised because every demo user has history; on stage a brand-new tenant's user hits the id lookup, raises a KeyError or returns an empty list, and the meeting is about reliability for the rest of the hour.

The isolation forest is fitted on raw columns including transaction_id and a monotonically increasing timestamp, so the trees isolate on those; the top 100 anomalies are simply the newest, highest-id rows, and the analyst queue is abandoned within a week.

contamination is left at its default and predict() is wired straight to the alert queue, generating around 1,400 alerts a day for a team that can review 100, of which roughly 96 percent are noise at a 0.172 percent true rate.

The detector is selected on ROC-AUC of 0.95 and described as excellent, while precision@100 is 0.04; the pilot is judged on analyst hours wasted, not on ranking theory, and the project is cancelled with a technically fine model.

Derive the backward pass for a two-layer MLP with softmax cross-entropy. Show me why dL/dz at the output collapses to yhat - y, and then write the shapes for a batched implementation and tell me where the 1/B goes.

Derive the Xavier initialisation variance condition from scratch, then tell me what changes for ReLU and why the constant becomes 2/n_in. Which assumptions in that derivation are false after the first gradient step, and does it matter?

A colleague's from-scratch net trains but converges to a worse loss than the PyTorch equivalent with identical hyperparameters. Design the debugging sequence - what do you check first, second and third, and what does a gradient check that passes at 1e-7 rule out and not rule out?

Explain exactly what dropout does at training time and at evaluation time, why the 1/(1-p) scaling exists and which side it is applied on, and what happens numerically if someone forgets model.eval() in a network that also has batch norm.
Training loss goes to NaN at step 4,300 having been healthy before. Give me the four most likely causes in order, and the specific instrumentation that distinguishes them.

A customer's 20-layer network learns nothing - the loss is flat at ln(C) from epoch 0. Walk me through diagnosing it from activation and gradient histograms alone, and tell me which of activation choice, init scale, learning rate and normalisation you would change first and why.

Design an ablation over three activations, three initialisers and three regularisers that you would put in front of a customer's ML team. How many runs, what is held fixed, what do you report, and how do you keep someone from reading seed noise as a result?

The 1/B from a mean-reduced loss is applied both in the loss backward and again in the layer backward; gradients are B times too small, the model trains but plateaus early, and three days go into 'the features are too weak' before anyone runs a gradient check.

A softmax is applied inside the model and CrossEntropyLoss is applied on top of it; nothing crashes, the gradients are wrong but still descend, and the model reaches 82 percent instead of 89 percent - a silent modelling error that no test catches without a reference implementation.

The gradient check passes at 1e-7 on a net with dropout accidentally disabled by the fixed seed path, and the dropout backward mask scaling bug ships anyway - the check must be run in the exact configuration being trained, not a convenient one.

A 10-layer ReLU net initialised with 0.01*randn has forward activations that decay to zero by layer 6; the loss sits flat at ln(10) = 2.30 for every epoch and gets diagnosed as 'the dataset is too hard' rather than as a variance-propagation failure fixed by one line of Kaiming init.

Validation is computed without model.eval(), so batch-norm uses batch statistics of the validation minibatches and dropout stays on; the validation number is both noisy and optimistically biased, and the model that wins the ablation is the one that got the luckiest eval batches.

Standardisation statistics (mean and std of Fashion-MNIST pixels) are computed over the whole dataset before the train/val split, leaking validation information into training; the reported gap is smaller than the true one and the customer's held-out result is worse than the deck promised.

Weight decay is added as lambda*w inside the gradient while using Adam, so the effective decay is divided by sqrt(v_hat) per parameter; the regularisation strength varies wildly across layers, the lambda sweep looks flat and non-monotonic, and the conclusion 'L2 does not help here' is recorded as a finding.

Each ablation cell is run once with a different random seed; the 27-cell table has a spread of +/- 1.2 points that is entirely seed noise, and the README recommends a configuration that is not reproducibly better than three of its neighbours.

Derive the condition on the learning rate for gradient descent to converge on a quadratic with Hessian H. What is the optimal step size, what is the convergence rate in terms of the condition number, and how does momentum change that rate? Then tell me what you would actually look at in a training log to decide whether a run is violating that bound.

Write Adam's update from memory, including the bias corrections, and derive why the corrections are needed. Where does eps sit in PyTorch's implementation, and what changes if you move it inside the square root? Why is Adam's typical learning rate two orders of magnitude smaller than SGD's?

Explain the difference between L2 regularisation added to the gradient and decoupled weight decay under an adaptive optimiser. Which parameters would you exclude from weight decay in a transformer, and why is excluding LayerNorm gains not just a micro-optimisation?

Describe exactly what BatchNorm computes in training mode and in eval mode, including how the running statistics are updated. A model scores 94 percent in training-mode evaluation and 61 percent after calling model.eval(). Give me three candidate causes in order and the experiment that distinguishes them.

Debug: a training run is healthy for 4,000 steps and then goes to NaN, and it does so at a different step each time you rerun it. It uses fp16 autocast with a GradScaler, gradient clipping and a warmup+cosine schedule. Walk me through your triage, in order, and say what each observation would rule out.

Design: a customer has a 20 GB GPU and an 8-hour nightly window, and their current fp32 run takes 14 hours. Walk me through what you change, in what order, and what you measure to prove the model is unchanged - include the optimiser-state and activation memory arithmetic and where mixed precision does and does not help.

You raise the batch size from 256 to 2048 on eight GPUs. What happens to the gradient noise, what do you do to the learning rate and why, what does gradual warmup fix, and what would make you say the linear scaling rule has stopped applying?

Weight decay is passed to torch.optim.Adam instead of AdamW, so the penalty is divided by sqrt(v_hat) per parameter; the lambda sweep comes out flat and non-monotonic and the team records 'regularisation does not help on this dataset' as a finding.

scheduler.step() is called once per epoch while T_max was specified in optimiser steps, so a 30-epoch cosine schedule completes inside the first epoch and trains the remaining 29 at eta_min; the curve looks like a healthy early drop followed by a permanent plateau and gets blamed on model capacity.

clip_grad_norm_ is called before scaler.unscale_(), so the norm being clipped is the fp16 loss-scaled norm; clipping becomes a no-op at scale 65536 and catastrophically aggressive after the scaler halves a few times, producing an instability that appears and disappears with the loss scale.

Validation is run without model.eval(), so BatchNorm uses each validation minibatch's own statistics and dropout stays on; the reported accuracy is both noisy and optimistically biased, and the config that wins the ablation is the one that drew the luckiest eval batches.

A model is trained with .half() applied to the weights instead of autocast with fp32 master weights; updates smaller than the fp16 spacing of the parameter are lost entirely on every step, so the loss decreases for a while and then stalls with a perfectly flat curve and a grad norm that is still nonzero.

Batch size is raised from 128 to 1024 for throughput while the learning rate and the epoch budget stay fixed; the run takes one eighth of the optimiser steps, ends two points below baseline, and the large-batch result is written up as a generalisation gap rather than as an under-trained run.

A job is resumed from a checkpoint that saved only model.state_dict(); Adam's moment buffers restart at zero and the bias correction restarts at t=1, so the loss spikes at exactly the resume step and the incident is investigated as corrupted training data.

cudnn.benchmark is on and no seeds are fixed, so two runs of the identical config differ by 0.4 points; a genuinely neutral change is shipped as an improvement and a genuine 0.3-point regression is dismissed as noise, in the same week.

Derive the backward for y = x @ W + b where x is (B, T, D) and b is (D,). Give dL/dx, dL/dW and dL/db including exactly which axes are summed, then tell me how you would implement it as a `torch.autograd.Function` and prove it with `gradcheck` - including why the test must run in float64.

Explain reverse-mode versus forward-mode autodiff in terms of Jacobian-vector and vector-Jacobian products. Which one does `.backward()` perform, what is the compute and memory cost of a backward pass relative to a forward pass, and when would you reach for `torch.func.jacfwd` instead?

Debug: training loss is decreasing but each step takes 400 ms and `nvidia-smi` shows 20 percent utilisation. Walk me through the profiling run you would set up and how you would distinguish dataloader-bound from launch-bound from host-sync-bound - name the specific evidence you would look for in each case.
Your run produces NaN loss at step 3000 under fp16 autocast. Give me your ordered checklist of causes and the check for each, and explain what the GradScaler is doing at the moment the NaN appears.

Distinguish `torch.no_grad()`, `torch.inference_mode()`, `.detach()` and `requires_grad_(False)`. Give one situation where each is the correct tool and one where using it instead of the right one silently produces a wrong result rather than an error.

Write out the Adam and AdamW update rules. Where exactly does weight decay enter in each, why does that difference matter, and how would you configure `param_groups` for a transformer with biases, LayerNorm gains and embeddings?

Design: a customer hands you 4 TB of JPEGs on an NFS mount and one A100. Design the input pipeline - map-style Dataset or IterableDataset, worker count, collate, caching, sharding, augmentation seeding - and tell me how you would prove to their team that the GPU, not the loader, is the limit.

The validation loop compares a (N, 1) prediction to a (N,) target, so MSE broadcasts to an N-by-N matrix of pairwise errors; the loss is smooth, small and decreasing, and the model has simply learned to predict the mean of the target.

Somebody passes `softmax(logits)` into `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`; the double softmax squashes the gradient, the loss flattens just under ln(C), accuracy sits barely above chance, and the team spends two weeks blaming label quality instead of one line of code.

`total_loss += loss` inside the epoch retains every iteration's graph, so memory grows linearly and the run dies with a CUDA OOM near the end of epoch one; it gets misdiagnosed as 'the batch size is too large' and the batch is halved, which merely delays the crash.

The eval loop never calls `model.eval()`, so dropout stays active and BatchNorm uses the eval batch's own statistics; validation accuracy is noisy and pessimistic, model selection picks the wrong checkpoint, and the effect reverses if the customer later evaluates with batch size 1.

Latency is benchmarked with `time.time()` around the forward pass without `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, so the number measured is kernel launch time; the deck says 8 ms per inference and production measures 35 ms in front of the customer.

An `IterableDataset` streaming from sharded files is used with `num_workers=4` and no `get_worker_info()` sharding, so every worker emits the same records; each epoch trains on four copies of a quarter of the data, and the only symptom is a train/validation gap nobody can explain.

Augmentation uses `np.random` inside `__getitem__` with `num_workers>0` and no `worker_init_fn`; all workers inherit the same NumPy seed, the same augmentation sequence repeats every epoch, effective augmentation diversity collapses, and the model overfits in a way that looks like a regularisation problem.

A custom `Function`'s backward forgets to sum the incoming gradient back over a broadcast bias dimension; `gradcheck` on a square test input passes by coincidence, tolerances get loosened when it later fails on a real shape, and the bias gradient is wrong by a factor of the batch size on every batch.

Derive the receptive field at the last conv stage of ResNet-18 for a 224x224 input, showing the jump and RF recursions. The customer's objects are 15 pixels across in a 4K frame - what do you change in the architecture or the input pipeline, and what does each option cost in latency and memory?

Write the gradients of the loss with respect to the weights and the input for a 3x3, stride-1, padding-1 conv layer. Why is dX a full convolution with the 180-degree rotated kernel, what changes when the stride is 2, and how would you verify your implementation so that passing the check actually means something?

A 56-layer plain CNN has higher training error than a 20-layer one. That is not overfitting - what is it? Write the gradient expression for a residual block that shows what the identity shortcut fixes, and say what breaks that argument when the shortcut is a 1x1 projection.

You are fine-tuning an ImageNet ResNet-50 on 800 customer images. Walk me through linear probe vs full fine-tune, exactly what you do with the BatchNorm layers in each case, what learning rates you use per parameter group, and how you would know within one epoch that it is working.

Debug: detection mAP is 0.61 overall, but AP for one class is 0.08, AP_small is 0.04 while AP_large is 0.72, and AR@100 is 0.79. What do you look at, in what order, and what are your top two hypotheses with the experiment that distinguishes them?

EfficientNet-B4 has fewer FLOPs and parameters than ResNet-152 but runs slower on the customer's T4. Explain compound scaling, explain precisely why the FLOP count misleads here, and describe how you would choose a backbone against a 30 ms per-frame budget on their hardware.

Design: a customer wants conveyor-belt defect detection at 20 fps with 300 labelled images and roughly a 2 percent defect rate. Specify the model, the labelling and split strategy, the augmentation policy and what it assumes, the metric you report, the threshold you ship at, and what you would refuse to promise in the SOW.

The customer's 4,000 images came from 60 video clips; a random split puts adjacent frames in both train and test, validation accuracy reads 0.98, and the model collapses to 0.62 on next month's footage - the split had to be grouped by clip.

The frozen-backbone arm of the ablation calls requires_grad_(False) but leaves the model in train() mode, so BatchNorm running_mean and running_var keep adapting to the new domain; the frozen and fine-tuned rows come out nearly identical and the table's headline conclusion is wrong.

The same transform object is passed to the train and the validation Dataset, so RandomResizedCrop and ColorJitter run at evaluation time; validation accuracy is noisy and several points low, and two days go into tuning a learning rate to fix what is purely a measurement bug.

Training normalises with ImageNet mean/std after ToTensor while the production service feeds uint8 BGR straight from cv2.imread with a different resize interpolation; accuracy drops from 0.91 to 0.40 and is escalated as a data-quality problem for a week.

A defect classifier on 3 percent positives is reported at 97 percent accuracy - exactly the always-negative baseline - and the customer signs off on a model that has never flagged a defect, because PR-AUC and per-class recall were never on the slide.

mAP is computed at score threshold 0.05 with maxDets 100 and reads 0.61, but the shipped service runs at 0.5 and misses half the objects; the evaluation and the deployment are measuring different operating points and nobody says so out loud.

Default anchor scales of 32-512 px are kept on a dataset whose objects are 10-20 px, so no anchor ever reaches the positive IoU threshold, the box head receives almost no positive samples, recall ceilings near 0.3, and three weeks are spent tuning loss weights that cannot fix it.

The NumPy conv2d gradient check passes in float32 with eps=1e-2, hiding a transposed axis in the dW accumulation and a missing np.add.at in col2im; the layer still trains, just to a mediocre plateau that looks convincingly like a data problem.

Derive backpropagation through time for a vanilla RNN with tanh. Show me the term that vanishes, state the condition on W_hh in terms of its singular values, and then tell me exactly which part of the LSTM and which part of the GRU cancels that term.

Write the LSTM equations. Now compute dc_t/dc_{t-1} and explain why that expression, and not the number of parameters, is why LSTMs learn long-range dependencies. Where does the gradient still vanish in an LSTM?

A customer's seq2seq translation model scores well on their test set but collapses on anything over about twenty tokens. Walk me through your diagnosis, and write the equations for the fix. What would you plot to prove the diagnosis before you change any code?

Explain teacher forcing and exposure bias. Design a validation protocol for a sequence-to-sequence model that cannot be gamed by teacher forcing, and tell me what you would report to the customer alongside the headline number.
Why is dot-product attention divided by sqrt(d_k)? Derive it. Then tell me what happens to the softmax Jacobian if you omit it at d_k = 512, and what the observable training symptom would be.

Design: the customer needs to classify streaming sensor sequences on an edge device with 200 ms of budget and no GPU. Argue for or against a GRU versus a small Transformer, using complexity, memory and the streaming constraint, and say what you would measure before committing.

Debug: a from-scratch LSTM passes a float64 gradcheck at 1e-7 but trains to a worse loss than nn.LSTM with identical hyperparameters and copied initial weights. What does the passing gradcheck rule out, what does it not rule out, and what are the first three things you check?

The loss is averaged over every position in the padded tensor instead of over mask.sum(); batches that happen to contain long sequences look better, validation loss changes when you change batch size, and the model that wins the sweep is the one whose batches were most padded.

The encoder uses the RNN's h_n without pack_padded_sequence, so the 'sentence summary' handed to the decoder is the state after k pad tokens; the model still trains, but its quality depends on how the DataLoader happened to bucket lengths and never reproduces on the customer's differently sorted data.

Validation is run teacher-forced because the same forward() is reused for train and eval; the notebook reports 98 percent, the demo in front of the customer free-runs and produces repetition loops, and the gap is diagnosed as a deployment bug rather than exposure bias.

bidirectional=True is left on a decoder or a next-token language model; validation perplexity collapses to near 1 because every position sees its own future, the result is presented as a breakthrough, and the model cannot be run causally at inference at all.

Attention alpha is masked by multiplying by zero AFTER the softmax rather than adding -inf before it, so the distribution no longer sums to one, mass silently drains as batch padding grows, and the heat map looks plausible while the context vector is systematically shrunk.

The from-scratch LSTM returns h_t but keeps feeding c_{t-1} through the loop; the gradient check still passes because forward and backward agree with each other, and the model trains to a mediocre plateau that is blamed on the dataset being too small.

Gradient clipping is applied per-parameter-tensor rather than on the global norm; the descent direction is rotated at every spike, training becomes erratic in a way that looks like a bad learning rate, and the LR sweep comes back flat and uninformative.

Beam search is added with beam=10 and no length normalisation; outputs get systematically shorter, exact match drops below the greedy baseline, and the conclusion recorded is that beam search does not help on this task.

Derive scaled dot-product attention at the whiteboard and justify the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor. What exactly happens to the forward pass and to the gradients if you drop it, and at what value of d_k does it start to matter?

Walk me through every tensor shape in a decoder block for B=4, T=1024, d_model=768, n_head=12. Where is the O(T^2) term, what is the peak activation memory, and how does FlashAttention change that number without changing the maths?
I have a decoder-only model whose validation loss is 0.08 and whose generated text is gibberish. Give me your ordered hypothesis list and the specific assertion you would write to test each one.

Explain pre-LN versus post-LN in terms of the gradient on the residual path. Why does post-LN need learning-rate warmup, and what would you expect to see in the loss curve and grad-norm log if someone removed warmup from a post-LN model?

A customer says the model 'gets dumber' past 8k tokens even though the API accepts 32k. Explain what is actually happening in terms of positional encoding, and describe two mitigations and the trade-off each one makes.

Design a controlled experiment that proves positional encoding matters, on a 10M-parameter character-level model with a 4-hour compute budget. What do you hold fixed, how many seeds, what do you measure, and what result would falsify the claim?

Explain the KV cache: what is stored, how big is it for a 32-layer, 32-head, d_head=128 model at 8k context in bf16, why generation without it is quadratic, and what MQA or GQA changes about that arithmetic.

The causal mask is built once for block_size but sliced wrong (or omitted at inference), so training sees the future; val loss drops to 0.2, the ablation table looks spectacular, and the model generates incoherent text - the metric flatters a model that has learned nothing about prediction.

Head splitting reshapes to (B, T, d_head, n_head) instead of (B, T, n_head, d_head), so each 'head' reads an interleaved stride of the feature vector; the model still trains and the loss curve looks normal, just a few percent worse, and the bug survives to production because nothing ever crashes.

The train/val split is made by random sampling of overlapping context windows rather than by cutting the corpus at a byte offset, so validation contexts overlap training contexts and val loss tracks train loss perfectly - the reported number is memorisation, and the customer's held-out data behaves nothing like it.

Positional encodings are computed but never added to the token embeddings (or added after the first LayerNorm and then normalised away); the model becomes a bag-of-tokens predictor, reaches a plausible-looking loss on character data where unigram statistics carry a lot of signal, and only the ablation reveals that the no-PE variant scores the same.

Post-LN is used with no warmup at an LR copied from a pre-LN config; the run diverges at step ~400, and three days are spent on the data pipeline before anyone checks the LayerNorm placement - the residual-path gradient growth with depth is the actual cause.
